speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But more than that, before embarking on this Paper, the Government had initiated a year-long series of nationwide Conversations on Women's Development involving Singaporeans from all walks of life.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It did so even as our nation battled a formidable virus which precipitated the worst recession since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The White Paper may have been prepared by the Government but it speaks with the voices of Singaporeans who care deeply about women.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the start of our debate, I would like to thank the many partners who have journeyed with us in the past year and a half.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They include the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO), the NTUC Women and Family Unit, the PA Women's Integration Network, organisations like Daughters of Tomorrow and Dads for Life.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We thank each and every one of the participants in the Conversations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: You shared your views candidly in the spirit of advancing women's interests.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We must begin by recognising that Singapore women have already triumphed over great adversity and made significant progress in so many ways.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Up till a hundred years ago, women were mostly confined to domesticity.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Sons had priority for education and parents decided on their children's marriages.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Some women suffered the indignity of being traded like property.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a teenager living in 1930s Singapore, my paternal grandmother, my popo, bore witness to the early winds of change.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: For example, about 700 brothels were closed after the Women and Girls Protection Ordinance was passed by the Legislative Council of the Straits Settlement.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 1932, the same Council banned the sale of young girls to rich families as "mui tsais".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Women could no longer be deemed chattel, to be bought and sold.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: During the war, many brave and enterprising women did their utmost to help their families and friends survive the cruel ravages of war – rape and murder, persecution and hunger, and untold personal tragedies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: There were many heroes – and heroines, too, including Elizabeth Choy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: After the war, women contributed to the rehabilitation efforts, setting up associations and mutual help groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Soon after we attained self-government, the women of Singapore achieved a historic triumph.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It also paved the way for greater protection from dangers like family violence and sexual offences.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More importantly, it changed the perception of how women should be treated in society and at home.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It gave women more autonomy in the roles they took up, fundamentally altering the social compact of its day.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Back then, only one in three women were literate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But schools for girls established by missionaries, activists, businessmen and intellectuals had already shown what women could do if only we educated them as well as we did men.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The trailblazers included Aisha Akbar, who, in 1950, won a scholarship to enter the Trinity College of Music in England.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She was only 20 then, and the first in Singapore to be awarded a music scholarship without having already qualified as a music teacher.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Ruth Wong, the first woman principal of the Teachers' Training College who later became the founding director of the present-day National Institute of Education (NIE).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She helped to transform the teaching profession and uplifted the education system, benefiting generations of girls and boys.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Free primary education starting in 1960 helped many more Singapore women triumph through education, achieving far more than basic literacy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Today, for every young man enrolled in University, there is a young woman.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In education alone, we, women, hold up half the sky.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also proved that, with education, we could triumph at the workplace and impact the lives of many others.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Her education led her to start Singapore's first family violence specialist centre, the Centre for Promoting Alternatives to Violence (PAVE).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Even today, PAVE offers valuable services in counselling, public education, research and advocacy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Then, there is Juliana Chan, a Singaporean scientist who holds four US patents.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Driven by her passion to enhance science communications, Juliana founded the Wildtype Media Group, which has become Asia's leading STEM-focused media company behind publications, such as the Asian Scientist Magazine and Supercomputing Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We also have Huda Hamid, a businesswoman and social entrepreneur, who has helped single mothers and women from low-income households become financially independent.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Huda was one of six winners of the 2020 Young Social Entrepreneurs Global Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More women have now taken on jobs previously dominated by men and stepped up to leadership roles.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Like Sudha, Juliana and Huda, they have proven themselves the equal of their male colleagues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Never before in our history have we had so many women in Parliament as we do now; and I sincerely believe Parliament is the better for it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In the past decade, we have continued to make good progress for Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Women are now better protected against harms and sexual offences, through the Protection from Harassment Act and Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Women are now better recognised for their contributions in the economy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Caregivers of the elderly and children, majority of whom are women, are now better supported.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: More facilities and higher subsidies have been made available.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Schemes, like Silver Support and the matching of CPF top-ups, help them in retirement.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: And, of course, we now have a woman as our President.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As many people noted in the recently released SPH Media book on Singapore’s battle against COVID-19, President Halimah has been a pillar of strength throughout this crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She stayed on top of things and struck a balance on difficult decisions, such as tapping into our national reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: By any measure, Singapore women's development has reached a very high base.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As a result, we may have felt no urgency to further strengthen the position of women in our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: As I mentioned earlier, almost the first thing the PAP did when it first formed the Government was to pass the Women's Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We believed it was timely to renew the pledge our founding leaders made so many years ago, to further elevate the position of women in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This is because, even as we were fighting hard to battle the pandemic, we remembered the daily battles women may still face: the battle with time to fulfil multiple roles and responsibilities; the battle for recognition of the challenges women and girls face, much more than men and boys; the battle with sexual predators who, having been tamed in analogue Singapore, now rear their ugly heads in our digital world; the battle with social expectations on what work we do, what chores we share, what words we say and even what clothes we wear; the battle within ourselves as to how much of "us" to give and how much to save for self-care.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To help women advance, we must not shy away from dealing with these battles.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: On the contrary, we must always see the progress of women as a journey without end, where every achievement is a foundation to aim for new highs.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In every generation, we have a duty to find new ways to uplift women.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: If half of humanity does not progress, how can the rest of humanity?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But where should the weight of our efforts now lie?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In all likelihood, these two lines of effort are the most challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Yet, they are also where we have the best hope to really move the needle for our women.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I believe this from the bottom of my heart.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In Mandarin):   Like many young working mothers, I struggled with guilt.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: How could I forgive myself if my child became sicker while I was away on a work trip?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: How could I forgive myself if my children fell far behind in school or became delinquent because I was not around often enough to guide them?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: At the same time, I also wondered if my boss would notice my divided attention.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Would opportunities be redirected because it was assumed I was no longer interested or up to the challenge?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, when my 82-year-old father suffered a fall and was hospitalised, my mother, herself nearly 80, became his sole caregiver.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: How could I forgive myself if she, too, became ill from exhaustion?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Questions like these trouble women all the time.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Almost all the women would find it difficult to balance their family and career at some stage in life.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part of the answer lies in additional legislative safeguards to uphold fairness at the workplace and also to uphold a more inclusive workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Part of the solution lies in providing better support to caregivers.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But these efforts taken by the Government can only go so far.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: No law or tripartite guidelines can dictate the norms in a family, or the detailed practices of workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Had my husband not stepped up as an involved father, had my brothers not stepped in to provide relief to my mother, had my father and father-in-law not given their blessings, I could not have continued to work with relative peace of mind, let alone stepped into public life with a degree of confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Throughout my working life, I was blessed to have bosses like Lim Swee Say and ex-Chairman of EDB Philip Yeo who made room to accommodate personal passions and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Twenty years ago, in the months following the birth of my twins, my former boss Lee Yi Shyan gave permission for me to work from home, long before telecommuting became a formalised policy and telecommunications infrastructure was mature.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: I will never forget the trust and the spiritual and practical support I have received from my bosses.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: (In English): Sir, this is why I firmly believe men's support for equal partnership with women is so important.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It is also why I firmly believe collective action, beyond what the Government will do, is essential.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We can put in place legislation on workplace fairness.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But the lived experiences of working women depend on the understanding and support of employers and colleagues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Standing in the Chamber today, these triumphs ring louder than ever.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: This will only happen when men and women partner each other as equals in every domain.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It depends on how we, as family members, share in caregiving and act as role models for our children.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It depends on how we, as a community, signal our protection and respect for our women.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: It depends on how we, as employers, empower women colleagues to dream bigger and fly higher.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Women in Singapore can continue to triumph, not through our words, but our deeds.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Since Independence, Singapore women have made tremendous progress.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Minister Josephine Teo shared about the many remarkable Singaporean women who have laid the foundations of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Allow me to share about one woman who has made a great impact on social work development.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Across the island, MSF provides a key line of social support in our local communities, enabling families to bounce back – achieving stability, self-reliance and social mobility.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is through a network of 48 Family Service Centres (FSCs).

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This all started with Ms Thung Syn Neo.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: She was a pioneering social worker, a giant in the profession.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We owe Syn Neo our gratitude for laying the foundations of our FSCs, which have uplifted and strengthened thousands of Singaporean families to this day.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This was the outcome of the Government’s intentional efforts to steward the progress of Singapore women, decade after decade, because we believe in a fairer and more inclusive society, where men and women are equal, valued members of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: My Ministry and the many Ministers that came before me, have been at the forefront of this endeavour.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have led the charge, legislatively, and through our policies and programmes; nudging at times, and earth shaking at times.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I was proud to share how far we have come at the G20 Ministerial Conference on Women’s Empowerment in Italy last year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Developing countries had problems providing access to education for their girls, and developed countries complained how their girls were still stereotyped to be educated for roles like teaching and nursing, and few were in STEM.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I was also glad to see many men participating in the Conversations – some of whom are in the Gallery today – because, in the next lap, we can only achieve this goal if we work together, men and women, in a whole-of-society approach.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One of whom said, and I quote, “Men and women both play a part in shaping the society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: If we all start to do the right things, the future generation will not have to go through what we went through.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We should start now while we still can.” This is one of the big conclusions of the Conversations: the collective responsibility that we, as a society, including we, men, must play, if we want to advance our women’s progress.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This means forging new societal norms – one that is based on respect and partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because only then can we progress further, to truly empower both men and women to pursue their aspirations freely and fully.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This requires collective commitment – individuals and families, people, private and public sectors, all segments of society, to step up and walk the talk.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In this respect, I believe that we, men, can make a difference for our women and, in the process, for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We can step up, we can do more and we should.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Be role models, not only in words, but also in deeds.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because we must believe in equal partnership between men and women, with respect as its cornerstone.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I want to state very clearly that this is not a zero-sum game.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: From time to time, such beliefs or misperceptions come up, whenever we talk about advancing women’s progress.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our approach is not about asserting the rights of one over another.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As men, we have a big part to play to encourage equal partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In our homes, as fathers, it is our responsibility to teach our sons what it means to respect all women, starting from a young age; instil in them the right values and be role models ourselves through our actions, for them to grow to be gentlemen.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Our children are social learners of the world, watching our every attitude, word and action.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They model after us and assimilate perceived social roles.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: More tangibly, we can play a much bigger role in sharing the weight of caregiving.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Because, in a partnership, we can build on one another’s strengths and be better together, for our children and generations to come.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I echo what Bryan Tan, who leads the Centre for Fathering, wrote in a recent commentary that says, and I quote, "Fathers are not 'substitute mothers'" and that "marriage is an equal partnership", unquote.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have cited it in our White Paper, but I thought it is worth reiterating.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Seven years ago, Saiful left his job in the creative industry to be a stay-home dad and the need arose because they had a young child in the family.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: While Saiful’s wife continues to work, she is always there supporting him.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Her presence enables him to overcome the challenges that he faces.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: First of all, not only did he challenge the traditional gender expectations and norms; second, it shows us that when men and women partner together, we become better as one.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We honour and respect our women because it is the right and moral thing to do, and this is not something new or just a feature of modern society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Respecting our fellow women is a natural evolution from our values, because we have been nurtured to honour, love and respect the most important woman of our lives – our mothers.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We can identify this in an Asian society like ours, culturally or religiously.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Chinese know the devotion of Mencius’ Mother, how she single-handedly raised Mencius after her husband passed away, and Mencius’ deep honour and respect that he carried for his mother.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: One account described the great length and extent that he went to bury his mother and to mourn for her when she passed away.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: When asked, he said that "the devotion that one owes one’s mother should be expressed fittingly at all times, and certainly through her funeral and mourning rites".

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: From the Ramayana, the Indians cherish Rama who was banished for 14 years to live in the forest by his mother Kaikeyi to make way for his half-brother, Baratha, to become the King.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And he dutifully left the city in obedience to his mother.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: When the Prophet was asked who a person should honour the most, or give the best treatment to, he replied, "his mother".

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And when asked again, "then who?", he said again, “his mother”, and again the third time, "his mother".

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Only at the fourth time did the Prophet say, "his father".

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In honouring our mothers, it shows we are also taught to cherish and honour our wives, sisters and daughters.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It is why we honour our Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As families, as a society and as a nation, we are stronger when our women, every woman, can flourish and realise their aspirations and their potential.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Thus, we must be part of the solution.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: And we will build upon this as a society – in workplaces, at home and in our community.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: At workplaces, our women contribute to a diversity of values, perspectives and capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: MSF will continue taking a multi-stakeholder approach that empowers stakeholders to collectively address underlying root causes.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For instance, the Council for Board Diversity raises public awareness of the importance of women on boards and works with corporates to develop a pipeline of board-ready women.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This would be more effective than setting mandatory quotas, which does not address root causes of the issue that have to do with culture and tradition.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Over the years, we have also greatly increased support for our caregivers.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: In Singapore, strong families form the bedrock of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: They are a key pillar of strength and our first line of support, providing unconditional love and support, through the ups and downs of life, such as that of our caregivers.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Their role is irreplaceable but there will be those who need more support, beyond that from one another.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We recognise their contributions to our families and society, and we will support them.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will elaborate, including the enhanced Home Caregiving Grant that would better help with caregiving costs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Through the enhanced Silver Support Scheme and the Matched Retirement Savings Scheme, we have also boosted the retirement incomes of Singaporeans, including caregivers, who may not have a chance to earn higher incomes during their working years.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We have also made major moves to make quality preschools more accessible and affordable to families to enable working parents, especially mothers, to pursue their career aspirations with peace of mind.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: These are just some of the many Government-led initiatives to support caregivers and their families.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The community has an important role to play, too.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Caregivers can benefit from strong community support, especially fellow caregivers who share similar experiences and can offer practical and socio-emotional support.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Allow me to share Richard's story, which is also featured in the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Richard left his job 22 years ago to care for his father who had cancer.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Things became challenging when his father then developed dementia.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: His father would sometimes get violent with him and people around him.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Fortunately, Richard received support from his neighbour and benefited from caregiver support programmes by the Caregivers Alliance Limited.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Now, Richard gives back and volunteers with them to help other caregivers find strength and solve the issues that they are facing.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Like I said earlier, men must play their part in shaping societal norms towards a more equal partnership between men and women.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling will speak more about this.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: I would also like to add that even as our society progresses, there are still persons who experience violence.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Protecting women from violence and harm requires partnership across all spheres of society between men and women.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Minister Shanmugam and Minister of State Sun Xueling will elaborate more on this.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The Government will work with community partners and the wider public to design and develop the garden.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: The roving exhibition will celebrate our journey on women's development.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: It also aims to build awareness and ownership of the action plans amongst Singaporeans from various walks of life.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: (In Malay):   In Singapore, we believe in equal partnership between men and women, with respect as its cornerstone.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We honour and respect our women because it is the right and moral thing to do.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is an integral part of our cultural values, because we have been nurtured from young to honour, love and respect the most important woman of our lives – our mothers.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: Just as we honour our mothers, we are also taught to cherish and honour our wives, sisters and daughters.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As men, we can and should step up to do more to support our Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: For instance, we can play an active role in caregiving for our children and elderly.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: We should also support our women as they pursue their aspirations at the workplace and in society.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: As families, as a society and as a nation, we become stronger when our women are given the opportunity to flourish and realise their full potential.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M)
text: This is what will take us forward in the next bound.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we take a look around, we will realise that we are surrounded by so many inspirational Singaporean women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In one IWD panel, I met with four such inspirational women with very, very diverse life stories.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chef Judy is a successful chef and, after a very painful divorce, she used the baking skills she learned from her very supportive ex-mother-in-law to become a successful cafe and baking school business owner.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Gwendolyn has a degree in political science and is also thriving as a Rota commander and firefighter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Cheryl struggled with mental health and is now a beauty queen and passionate advocate for mental wellness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sophia left her job to focus on raising her young family but, in the midst of it, upskilled herself and is now the proud owner of a very fulfilling business of supplying wedding flowers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These stories and achievements of our ladies reflect the strength and determination we possess as we strive for excellence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is, in part, made possible by the considerable improvements and opportunities, protection and safety nets that Singapore has developed over the years – evident in the increase in women graduates and women employment, along with the growth of women in leadership and board positions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in our efforts to honour our women who #breakthebias, our actions need to continually reflect the inherent challenges that women continue to face in our society, communities and families.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If our laws and policies are to reflect the standards we, as a society, desire, then this House must continue to look to pursue choices that seek to achieve a fairer and more inclusive society where both men and women, as equal partners, are free to chase their aspirations to the fullest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The NTUC recognises its pivotal position in spearheading efforts to achieve greater gender equality in Singapore and has, through the decades, been a progressive and relevant voice for our women, from the women's programme under Mdm Yu-Foo Yee Shoon to the Women's Development Secretariat led by Mdm President Halimah Yacob to its current incarnation, the NTUC Women and Family Unit.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, the creation of a more inclusive society does not differentiate on gender and relies, first, on the ability to provide equal opportunities for women.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Today, our women are flourishing in careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), IT, entrepreneurship, services, manufacturing and our choices are often limited only by our interests and passions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, our work is far from being completed.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Apart from developing favourable policies that elevate women in the workforce, the Labour Movement sees the pertinent need to widen the field for women by re-imagining and refreshing our career choices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to the promotion of STEM careers, the NTUC Women and Family Unit has identified even more opportunities and market gaps in critical but neglected professions that are traditionally dominated proudly by women, such as dressmakers and nannies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond new tripartite guidelines on FWAs, we call on employers to take steps to ensure fairness in the appraisal and performance management of workers on FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers must be clear about their duties, expectations and deadlines when they are on FWA.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women go through many seasons and we recognise that women at different points of their lives would leave, enter or re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many face difficulty re-entering the workforce after an extended hiatus as there is a mismatch in expectations and support between employers and women returners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement has sought to bridge this gap by providing training and mentoring that women can leverage to give themselves a leg up.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement, through the NTUC Women and Family Unit's Women Supporting Women mentorship programme, grants women at all levels, including PMETs, access to women mentors who provide support and guidance, allowing our women to have a better landing when they are returning to the workplace or even to pursue better and shinier pathways at work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I witnessed the journey of some 50 mentees who benefited from this programme and I would like to share the experience of one Ms K.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A single mom to three young children, Ms K quit her job five years ago as she was constantly taking childcare leave to take care of her young children.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When she joined the programme, she was taken under the wing of unionist sister Daphne Ng from the Singapore FinTech Association.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This six-month journey together culminated in sister Daphne recommending Ms K to a full-time role that provided flexible work arrangements (FWAs), which catered both to Ms K's caregiving and professional needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such success stories have spurred the Labour Movement to bring the Women Supporting Women mentorship programme to more local communities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Earlier this year, a survey conducted by the Women and Family Unit and the PAP Women's Wing revealed the worrying trends of gender discrimination that our women of today face at their workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not only did the report show that women perceive that they are disproportionately facing workplace discrimination, it also highlighted the prevalence of a lack of company know-how and policy against such workplace discrimination and harassment.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is, in particular, amongst companies that do not enjoy the abundance of resources and manpower.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has long championed actions to address discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We were party to drafting the tripartite guidelines on non-discriminatory job advertisements that were issued in 1999.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We co-led the formation of the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) in 2006 to promote fair and equitable employment practices as well as to provide an avenue for workers to report such unfair practices on them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: TAFEP, subsequently, formulated the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices in 2007, which has helped guide companies in adopting fair and merit-based employment practices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC has also been advocating for measures to level the playing field between Singaporeans and foreign workers for opportunities since 2011.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These were implemented in the form of the Fair Consideration Framework and the National Jobs Bank in 2014.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are heartened that these calls made by NTUC will be reflected in the move to enshrine the TGFEP in law.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the time I have stepped into this House, I have seen the concerted effort of our nation and this House in supporting the development of women in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we have made progress over the years, NTUC has identified multiple significant challenges that women continually face as they pursue their career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: NTUC believes that one's gender should never be an obstacle or a hindrance in the workforce and we will make every effort to provide opportunities and resources that work towards championing our women and the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many Members of the House are speaking today on this very important topic and I will focus my speech on jobs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Specifically, the need to provide women with equal opportunities at the workplace, so that we can support their aspirations to have both a fulfilling family life and a rewarding career.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Women face headwinds at every stage of their professional careers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Early on, while studying and choosing which career path to take, some hesitate to jump into male-dominated sectors, such as those in the Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) industries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Women also face challenges when they find out that they are expecting a child.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some tell me that they worry about being penalised in their appraisals when they go on maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Others shared with me that they had to suspend their job search because employers do not seem to want to hire someone who will need to take months off soon after being employed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For mothers who chose to leave the corporate world temporarily to care for their children and are looking to return to work, it can be daunting to return to a workplace that has changed significantly in the time that they were away.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many women also struggle to find opportunities to earn additional income while being a full-time homemaker or primary caregiver to their children and their elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For our young millennials, they have a vastly different outlook on what work-life harmony is, as they are more educated and have higher levels of career confidence.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many of them are rightfully ambitious and want to shine on the global stage, but do we have the right structures in place to support their aspirations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To address these challenges, I will focus my suggestions on three areas: jobs at home, jobs closer to home and jobs away from home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, let us provide better support to women, especially those with caregiving responsibilities, who wish to continue working from home.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But we can, and should, accelerate the implementation timeline.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While I understand that it takes time to engage the industry and ensure that there is consensus on the Tripartite Guidelines, we should strike when the iron is hot – in Chinese, we call this 打铁趁热 – and roll out the guidelines when many employers are still fresh from having the majority of their workforce telecommuting.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We should also support the aspirations of enterprising women who start home-based businesses to supplement their household income, while being a full-time caregiver or homemaker.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During my house visits, I have met many enterprising "mumpreneurs" in Radin Mas who have started their festive cookie businesses, bakers who specialise in customised cake designs, and one woman who even started her own trading company right from the comfort of her own living room!

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government, trade associations and self-help groups can provide better support to help aspiring home-based entrepreneurs kickstart and grow their businesses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One good example of a self-help group is Project Cookoh, a community effort that helps housewives in Jalan Kukoh start their own home-based business.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Project Cookoh mentors mumpreneurs, subsidises the cost of cooking classes and provides an online platform to help the women market their products.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We plan to start a similar programme in Radin Mas later this year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To help more aspiring mumpreneurs, I hope the Government can introduce a Home-based Business Grant to help defray the start-up cost of equipment and tie up with schools, such as SHATEC, to provide subsidised training courses for baking, cooking and safe food preparation, for example.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, I believe we can do more to help women find jobs that are closer to home, so that they can better balance their work and role as a caregiver.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This has been particularly helpful for single mothers, as they often hesitate to take on jobs in locations that require long travel time.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government, through our Community Development Councils and working with the NTUC, can scale the Jobs Closer to Home programme nationally and help employers tap into a ready pool of women who wish to work for companies that are based near their homes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, let us better support the aspirations of our millennial women.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This disconnect between aspiration and reality is concerning.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In many companies, going on international assignments and having extensive global experience is a precondition to reach senior management levels.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A persistently low participation rate of women in international assignments will, ultimately, affect gender equality at the leadership level.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Good mentorship is, therefore, vital to provide women with the assurance to venture overseas for their postings.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One good example can be found in the Financial Women's Association (FWA).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a community, we can do more to support the aspirations of our Singaporean women to have both a fulfilling family life and a rewarding career.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With our ageing workforce and inability to recruit and retain competent resources, the risk of an unsustainable economy and a rise in inequality may increase.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, are we doing enough in this competitive and fast-evolving global economy?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Are our institutional mindsets adjusted to attract more Singapore women to have a more significant role in our workforce?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We have made some progress in the development of women since the passing of the Women's Charter some 50 years ago.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The role of today's women is no longer just about gender equality, preconceptions or biases but diversity, inclusion and the social development of communities and families.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The White Paper on Women's Development is timely, with its recommendations in empowering women to play a bigger role in more economic sectors and to helm leadership positions across various industries.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the past decades, several organisations have successfully tapped talents from the female workforce.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They have provided women with opportunities to excel in the workforce and such opportunities provided the path to senior roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: More opportunities must be provided to women in predominantly male organisations and companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am passionate about the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and one area that our women can contribute to would be our defence sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Recent conflicts around the world have reminded us starkly that we cannot depend on anyone else to protect ourselves, our nation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In reference to a Straits Times article published in February 2016, in the next 50 years, the number of male Singaporeans between 15 and 24 years old is expected to halve.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Should we be seriously considering more Singaporean women to be part of SAF?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: When I joined SAF as a helicopter pilot in the Air Force some 25 years ago, there were only five women pilots in the entire Air Force and we were limited to flying transport planes and helicopters.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are, currently, more women pilots and they are flying mean machines like the F15SG Eagles and F-16 Falcons.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some of these women pilots are even helming the fort as Squadron Commanders.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, there are breakthroughs made in various combat units in the Army and the Navy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: SAF's efforts to continue to attract and retain women and placing them in frontline combat roles are very encouraging.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, we will have to do more in attracting women to be part of our defence team.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It has been more than 35 years since the very first combat servicewoman was recruited and I am looking forward to the Minister for Defence's assessment of the progress in this regard, specifically on the measures to increase the proportion of servicewomen and progression pathways for our women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Women have made some progress over the years in the Singapore Police Force.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Women Police officers can play a key role in enhancing the security and safety of our society, especially when the nature of crimes has evolved and technology has enhanced our ability to conduct surveillance and crime prevention.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us try to bring up the percentages of women Police officers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If physically and mentally demanding roles in the SAF and SPF have made progress in the representation of women over the years, employers, such as the Civil Service, Statutory Boards and MNCs should also set an example by recruiting more women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In fact, some Nordic countries had implemented gender quotas in their parliaments and in the board room.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These practices can assist in expediting the progress of women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Where there is a shortage of talent and keen competition to recruit and retain capable staff in the sunrise and fast-growing sectors, such as sustainability and IT, companies should look beyond their usual hunting grounds and tap half the manpower talent pool in the female population as a solution to their problems.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: You may like to know that in the early days of the United States' space programme, all the "human computers" were women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These are the staff at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) who performed highly complex mathematical calculations for aviation experiments and, subsequently, spaceflights.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, have no misconception that women do not have the IT aptitude.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Women's low representation in STEM careers has been described as a "leaky pipeline".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In our Primary and Secondary schools, girls often perform as well as the boys in science and mathematics.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: But as they progress to the tertiary level, fewer opt for STEM subjects, especially when it comes to engineering and computer science.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A women's contribution can only further assist in the field of engineering and science.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I also agree with the recommendations made in the White Paper to enhance equality in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is important to make a concerted effort to encourage our young women to chase their dreams and develop their fullest potential in their careers without any hesitation and with the fullest support.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As the Paper has pointed out, mindsets about what jobs are appropriate for which gender will need to shift.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is crucial to showcase the wide and diverse range of possibilities and opportunities for women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the years, many trailblazing women have paved the way for our younger women and provided them the much-needed inspiration and confidence to achieve their goals that will, in turn, help Singapore to progress.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   Earlier in my speech, I mentioned the progress made by the Singapore Police Force in women’s development over the past decades.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Beyond the Police Force, Mdm Zuraidah was also the chairperson of the Malay Heritage Foundation and currently serves as the Chief Executive Officer of self-help group MENDAKI after her retirement from the SPF.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am heartened that outstanding women have been given accolades like Mdm Zuraidah.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The stories of these outstanding women have inspired younger women to challenge themselves and excel beyond their predecessors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Over the years, we have seen more women athletes excelling in sports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am hopeful that more women national athletes will make Singaporeans proud.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The media and entertainment industry has an impact and plays a vital role in the amplification of women in society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Often times, women are portrayed second to men and that stereotyping is blindly amplifying certain biases.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Not all women are Bond girls whose sole responsibility is to wait for their handsome male hero to come home to them or behave like the female protagonist in constant distress, as portrayed in Korean drama "Crash Landing on You".

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I certainly hope the next Bond star will be a female lead and more female being portrayed as heroines in dramas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to reshape the archaic perceptions of how women are portrayed in our society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our local media must work towards shifting the narrative by placing equal emphasis between men and women by sharing aspirational stories with a positive reflection of fairness and inclusivity for all genders and races and not just for the rich or powerful.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must curate positive stories that will inspire and amplify the right values.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other than the media, public events and fora featuring female speakers, discussing issues that are of concern to the women community are important informal ways for women to share their experience and learn from one another.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In Sembawang West, women corporate and community leaders attend our annual SG Women's Festival event to share their experience and discuss best practices in areas, such as career, financial planning, health and wellness, caregiving and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These platforms help to create informal interest groups and build a support ecosystem for women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, the SG Heroines Award, CNA Women Award and Her World Women of the Year Award are important recognitions that inspire and rally women communities to do more for the society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I support the White Paper's proposal to develop career mentorship and networking opportunities for women.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need more professional and informal women bodies to recruit, retain and network with women in the various sectors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, the Women Aviation International SG chapter was set up in March 2021 to encourage more young women to join the aviation sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: While it is an initiative started by women for the benefit of other women, there is sincere support from our male counterparts who understand the need to attract and retain the best talents into this industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Being a participant in their programmes, I am heartened by the support from agencies and companies, such as the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore, Association of Aerospace Industries (Singapore) and Airbus Singapore, for example.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since both men and women contribute in the workforce, it is necessary for the Government to provide better facilities for homecare.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I fully support the call in the White Paper for more equality in the family and society, because caregivers themselves also need to rest and be cared for.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am glad to note that access to affordable and quality preschool facilities will be enhanced.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I urge the Ministry to pay special attention to estates with many young families and provide adequate childcare facilities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, in ageing estates, the Ministry must ensure senior day-care centres are easily accessible and affordable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With a rapidly-ageing population, we can expect more demand for migrant domestic workers to assist with caregiving for seniors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is not sustainable for the nation in the long run.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We will need to provide more and better institutional care and community support for seniors so that their children can go to work with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: People should also be better informed about geriatric care and the community support system available.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Working women tend to juggle one too many roles at home and at work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Prolonged periods of heavy loads can be draining on their own physical and mental health and may even cause burnouts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Mr Speaker, when moving the Motion on Empowering Women last year, I spoke about how we stand on the shoulders of those who forged the way before us and how we must continue to build on the progress that women have made to get us to where we are today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I spoke about society and the economy at large and how they benefit from greater equality for women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also shared my hopes that my sons would grow up in a fairer society and do their part to ensure that women and girls are not only given equal opportunities to forge their chosen paths in life, but that they will also be respected as equals and see outcomes that are on par with those for boys and men.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All these remain relevant today with the release last week of the White Paper on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Conversations on Singapore Women's Development were launched in September 2020 with sessions taking place through the year that followed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The year 2021 was also designated the year of celebrating SG women with its attendant events and activities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, despite being over a year in the making, the White Paper was released barely a week ago, leaving Singaporeans with precious little time to go through the White Paper and consider its recommendations before the issues contained within are debated here in Parliament.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There was just not enough time for my residents to provide feedback on the over 100 pages of its contents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Contrast this with the no less consequential population White Paper which was released on 9 January 2013.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That 41-page long paper was debated and passed in Parliament a month later on 9 February.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The seeming haste raises questions about whether the rushed timeline is necessary, or even beneficial to public debate and understanding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: An invitation for full and rigorous public scrutiny is one of the key tools for managing and countering misinformation and disinformation, and goes a long way towards dispelling unwarranted and unwelcomed conspiracies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That said, I am happy to see the paper acknowledging that a whole-of-nation approach has to be taken.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleagues and I will address some of these during the course of today's debate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To start, the White Paper specifically targets Singapore women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I feel we can do better: the principles and aspirations contained within the paper should form a blueprint of what we, as a society, stand for and what we value, no matter who you are.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the protections and aims should apply to all women in Singapore, regardless of nationality or status.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague Mr Leon Perera will elaborate further on these issues.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The latest publicly available study conducted in 2018 and published in 2020 by MOM showed that there was still an adjusted wage gap of 6%.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this pay gap is on the decline, it, nonetheless, still exists and I hope we will go beyond the points suggested in this White Paper to close the gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our efforts at reducing this pay gap must persist until women in Singapore achieve equal pay to their male counterparts for equal work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also need to ask about what the adverse effect the pandemic and our recovery from it has had on the gender wage gap and the effect of the chronic under-valuing and under-paying of jobs that are traditionally the preserve of women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Millions of us in lockdown around the globe found out first-hand how critical these workers are for the functioning and well-being of our economies, societies and families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The real gender wage gap also should take into account the number of women who do not "lean in" to seek higher paying jobs, promotions or careers, due to reasons, such as a lack of confidence, familiarity or just plain discomfort with what is seen as "too male" environments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, will speak more on this.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the 2020 MOM study asks but does not answer why such segregation exists.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It mentions data from two years with a 16-year gap – 2002 and 2018.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This information must be made publicly available, in aggregate form.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only with such publicly available basic data on a regular basis, could we have a better idea of the problem and move to close the gender wage gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will help employers increase access to a wider talent pool, enhance the diversity of their workforce and better attract and retain capable workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, the adverse impact on women's purchasing power does not stop at the gender pay gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There has been more attention in recent years given to the study of the phenomenon of what is known as the "pink tax", loosely defined as producers and providers charging more for the same products and services once these are marketed at women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Back home, a study by the Sunday Times of 10 retailers found women paying more for half of them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It appears that such gender-based pricing penalises women for, well, being women!

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The scope of this phenomenon and whether it is actually justified warrants a study in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The burden is also on her shoulders to ensure that the children are watered and fed, and that she not only has to coordinate the schedule, but is also expected to take time off work to attend to medical and other appointments of their dependants.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Member for Aljunied, Mr Gerald Giam, will speak more about what we can do to ensure that our unpaid caregivers – both women and men – are recognised and supported.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is no wonder that there are also increasing recognition and data showing that women are disproportionately affected globally by rising costs of living – because they start from a weaker economic position that is exacerbated by all the factors mentioned above.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have, in this House, spoken at length about climate change and its effect on Singapore, yet I note that in an article earlier this year, UN Women wrote, "the climate crisis is not 'gender neutral'.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Women and girls experience the greatest impacts of climate change, which amplifies existing gender inequalities and poses unique threats to their livelihoods, health and safety." Such climate-driven inequalities do not affect only developing nations, but also high-income ones, such as Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also cannot help but notice that most of the jobs in the traditional energy sectors are almost entirely male-dominated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The green transition, therefore, represents a chance for us to ensure that women are well and justly represented in these new "green jobs" and we must work to ensure that the gender gap in STEM skills does not prove to be a barrier to greater gender equality in a low-carbon future.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The White Paper, too, would like us to challenge these stereotypes, to push women to take leadership roles and to support entrepreneurship.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, removing barriers to female entrepreneurship will not only drive national economic growth, but also contribute to empowering women to be financially self-sufficient.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The establishment of the Singapore Women Entrepreneurs Network by SBF last September is a welcome step to create a community of support for existing female entrepreneurs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would this initiative be expanded to support budding, prospective female entrepreneurs, with an emphasis on women in traditionally male-dominated industries, such as energy and STEM?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would there also be any special emphasis on Femtech?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What about women who own micro businesses with different concerns?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while I am on this topic, and since we are discussing mindset shifts today, perhaps it is also time to do away with gendered terms like "girl boss" and "mumtrepreneurs", which, to me, seem to suggest that there is something out of the ordinary about women or mothers taking a lead in business.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to representation at the top, having more women in decision-making leadership roles has many benefits and gives young women role models to look up to.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A resident also pointed out to me that the multi-Ministerial task force to fight COVID-19 was an all-male affair when it came to the co-chairs and other public-facing figures – which, surely, causes some dissonance, given that the paper itself acknowledges that women are disproportionately more affected by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is undoubtedly true that we cannot make progress without "allies", I hope we do better at giving women a public leadership voice when we "build back better" coming out of COVID-19's long, long shadow.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague Sylvia Lim spoke about this extensively last year and I would like to repeat her call for change to make it conducive for women to step up to the political forefront.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, legislating against discrimination would make such practices illegal and, presumably, will come with attendant penalties for non-compliance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is why we are still even talking about the issue today, and the White Paper includes tackling discrimination as one of its topics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The guidance approach is just not good enough.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need legislation and policies that actually work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While mediation is an option, there needs to be proper mechanisms for monitoring, investigation, adjudication and deterrence in place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that we will take reference from other jurisdictions to see how thoughtful legislation outlawing such discriminatory behaviour can benefit women and other vulnerable groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would now like to turn to a major role that many women play: becoming a mother.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When I was pregnant with my youngest, his eldest brother, who was only aged four at the time, came up to me at bedtime and told me, "Mama, I am glad I am not a woman." When I asked him why, he told me very seriously that it was because "it’s so hard to be pregnant".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And, indeed, while parenthood brings much joy and growth, I do distinctly recall how lost and bewildered I felt the day we brought him home from the hospital.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having gone through 26 hours of labour and finally giving birth to an almost four-kilogramme baby, I was exhausted, in a huge amount of pain and just felt as if I had been run over by a bus, multiple times.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Baby’s constant wails and demands for food also left me frantically trying to find answers from my phone – with my husband being equally panicked.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My mother, from a generation who were told that "formula was more nutritious", was also unable to help with the challenging task of breastfeeding.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Despite this rocky start, I was extremely fortunate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For a village quickly grew up around me: aside from my parents assiduously ensuring that I had all the food and nutrients needed to recover in the immediate postpartum period, cousins and friends, who were themselves young parents, also offered all kinds of assistance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These ranged from offers for respite care in various shapes or forms, helpful recommendations and also late-night conversations on WhatsApp as we, together, stayed awake nursing or rocking fussy babies into the wee hours of the morning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For new mums who do not have a village growing up around them, it is vital that they are given the right care and support in the vulnerable weeks and months that follow childbirth.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They should also have easy access to non-judgemental advice and education about dealing with common issues ranging from lactation support, baby sleep advice and the change in relationship with their partners and families with a new baby.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that a task force will look at instituting practices, such as having specially-trained health visitors to routinely call on new moms just before delivery and during confinement, to answer questions and provide reassurance at home in a more relaxed, non-clinical environment as part of the norm.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We also should learn from traditional practices like doing confinement and jamu, and retain those practices which promote postpartum recovery and well-being, as these contain, after all, the wisdom of generations of mothers who came before us.
