speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the early days and months, issues, such as mom guilt – where moms feel guilty for having to leave their children with a career while pursuing a career – and bearing a disproportionately larger share of the mental load, must also be addressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The task force must also consider how to support new fathers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not uncommon to hear that fathers often feel at a loss on how to support their wives and that they can feel alienated during the pregnancy and postpartum journey, all the while wondering how to bond with their newborns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This can have an adverse impact on them playing a greater role in bringing up their babies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: More attention must also be paid to closing any gender health gaps that may exist.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: International studies show that in many areas of healthcare, women experience poorer outcomes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The UK's House of Lords had a debate last year on improving women's health outcomes and whether there is a gender health gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some societies have seen situations where women have longer life expectancies, but spend a longer period of time in ill health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These studies show, too, that women and ethnic minorities tend to experience bias when being treated for pain, and note that, generally speaking, healthcare systems and research have been built around men, leaving women chronically misunderstood, mistreated and misdiagnosed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also concern that, historically, women are left out of medical research, which is concerning, as recent research is shining a spotlight on how there is a gender impact on health and illness and that males and females respond differently to treatment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is heartening that there is targeted support for women's health outcomes and progress has, definitely, been made, but I believe we have not enough information publicly about how the concerns I raised above are being addressed in the Singapore context.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must go beyond just promoting women's health but also need to play our part to address any biases and ensuring that the research gap, when it comes to medical and health issues that affect women, is addressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, we should not see house and care work being the preserve of women and must be mindful of ensuring equal male and female role models are well represented.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The rest of us must also do our part and be aware that our words and deeds matter.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What we say and do are a reflection of our beliefs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is, as my grandmother used to say: "sim hor; sia hor; da hor".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We need to acknowledge the progress that Singapore women have made and the journey continues.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The White Paper covers five important areas affecting women's aspirations and development, with concrete recommendations for action.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would not be able to do justice to the work that has been done in all the areas covered in the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I would like to focus my speech today on the areas of providing equal opportunities for women at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are four points that I would like to touch on: one, why it is imperative for businesses to attract and retain women in the growth sectors; two, the approach to Flexible Work Arrangements (FWAs); three, the utilisation of parental and paternity leave; and four, mindset changes required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I welcome the new workplace fairness legislation to provide a safe environment for women and those facing discrimination or harassment at the workplace to speak up without fear.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having role models to inspire women and greater participation of women in leadership and board positions are important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Beyond these actions, I would like to bring attention to the need to attract, develop and retain more women in the growth sectors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Growth sectors offer better job prospects, growth and remuneration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If not as many women are participating in growth sectors, then, eventually, it will lead to a gap in the progress and development between women and men in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As companies push forward with their efforts to transform their businesses and with the growing importance of technology in business, STEM roles will be in demand.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: More can be done to understand why women in STEM roles are lower than in other sectors, so that the appropriate actions can be taken in partnership with businesses to attract and retain more women to STEM roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not just saying that the companies need to hire more women, we need to make sure that women want to be in these roles; and we need to understand why they are not – it is increasing, but it is not there yet.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Giving equal opportunities to women also has direct benefits for employers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The labour market is tight and businesses are facing challenges in getting the talent they need.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Data released last week by MOM reported an increase in the number of job vacancies in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A significant proportion of these vacancies are PMET jobs in growth sectors of information and communications, financial and insurance services, professional services, health and social services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Since 1980, women make up 50% of the proportion of University graduates.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In 2019, the number of women taking science, technology, engineering and mathematics in our local Universities was 41%.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It just makes good business sense for companies to hire women in STEM roles.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If they are not, they are missing out on tapping on half of the talent pool.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Recognising that women still tend to have the greater responsibility for caregiving, the White Paper has called for companies to provide FWAs to support more women to enter the workforce and progress.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Work practices must be supportive of employees' needs but we should recognise that business and operational considerations cannot be ignored.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In order to provide good jobs, businesses must be able to operate effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do agree with the balanced approach that the White Paper is taking in advocating for employers to consider FWA requests fairly and properly while recognising that FWAs are not an entitlement.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That would mean that it would be a year and a half before this happens.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I appreciate that time is needed to allow for consultation and to work on the new guidelines, if we believe that FWAs will enable fuller participation of women in the workforce, could we not start earlier and learn and refine from these experiences?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from the pace of the introduction of the Tripartite Guidelines for FWAs, I do want to highlight a few points on the approach to FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For clarity, let me just refer to what we mean by FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Taking what has been outlined in the Tripartite Standards for FWAs, it is defined as variations from usual work arrangements to include: one, flexi-load, for example, part-time or job-sharing; two, flexi-time, which is staggered hours and compressed work weeks; or three, flexi-place, for example, telecommuting.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If any good had come out of the COVID-19 pandemic, it is that it showed that businesses and employees could pivot to variations of FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While there were initial challenges, there were real benefits of adopting FWAs for both businesses and workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With FWAs, despite the restrictions, operations were able to continue, work could be done and jobs were retained.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Beyond COVID-19, employers can also benefit directly from implementing FWAs to achieve productivity; to gain access to a larger talent pool, and I am not talking about just women but men, too; and to have business agility.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While not all work can adopt FWAs, do not get me wrong, I am not saying that everything has to have arrangements made for FWAs – and some cannot.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as we look to strengthening the guidelines for FWAs, I think more can be done to encourage businesses to review and incorporate FWAs as part of business norms as there are real business benefits.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The approach and mindset of how we implement FWAs will also set the tone and the culture in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I believe that for FWAs to be effective, it cannot be just about requiring employers to give fair evaluation and consideration to employees' requests for FWAs when they require it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This approach, while seen as supportive of employees' needs for balancing their work-life responsibilities, does indirectly send a signal that FWAs are not the work norm or culture, and, hence, hesitation of both employers and employees to adopt FWAs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am supportive of the measures to encourage utilisation of parental leave as this will support employees, both men and women, in caregiving as parents.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I fully support the drive for both men and women to be actively involved and share in the responsibilities as parents to care for their children, because I think that is a benefit to not just the sharing of load, but really benefit to families and also benefit to the children and society as a whole.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I want to make a point about maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I agree and encourage men to utilise their paternity leave, so that they can share with the care of the child to allow mothers to recover well during their maternity leave.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But let us not forget, when we talk about sharing of leave, sharing of time and all that, let us not forget, women need to take care of themselves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Their bodies have gone through a lot, both physically and mentally.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have three children, and I will tell you, I love all of them, my deliveries were very, very short, my third one was 15 minutes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I will tell you, the nine months were challenging, your body just goes through a lot and the afterbirth is tough.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I would say to everyone, do not forget that and, women especially, do not forget that you need to take care of yourself.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while actions are important, let me now touch on an equally important point, my final point, on mindsets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is going to be fairly embarrassing for me, but I thought it would make the point, because it is a personal story.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I am going to share a personal story about mindsets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Many times, we do not realise our own inherent and sometimes unrecognised stereotypes that we all hold.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I personally think that I try my hardest to be quite open-minded, but the pin-drop for me one day – this was a few years ago when I had a very important client and we had arranged for technical briefings and very deep technological briefings for the client with very deep experts coming in and we came to a very important topic – and I was looking around the room when I said to my colleagues: "Where is the speaker?" It was very important and I was looking around and we were all looking for the speaker, at the expert.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And then, finally, I was told, "the speaker is in the room" and we looked around.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And then I realised: "Oh dear, are you sure that is the speaker, can you all please check?" That is what I said to our team.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Well, the speaker came on, spoke and, in my head, I thought it was going to be a disaster, or at least a mediocre session, but it turned out to be a very good session, because the speaker was a deep expert and, not only that, could actually relate it back to my clients' business and relate it back, a very deep technology area.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It was not a gender thing, but it was an age thing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I was looking for someone, because this topic was so complex and still is a very complex area, that I was looking in my head, a deep expert had to be one that "looked the part".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And the pin dropped for me, because I was so embarrassed and this happened many years ago, and I still cannot forget that, because it is a check for me to say that: "We do not think we are, we do not think it is, but we do it"; we do it all the time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And that is why, beyond actions, I think mindsets are important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I did a check yesterday, and this individual that I am talking about, by the way, is world-renowned, and she is still doing very well, and she is one of the world-renowned experts in this area and she is doing very well in that area.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But let me now come back to this point.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I encourage all of us to move forward to achieve this aspiration that we have for all of us to realise our full potential.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the White Paper.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I will elaborate how the Sunlight AfA, which seeks to support the Digital for Life (DfL) movement, tries to close the digital safety gap for women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam will share more about how MCI is responding to calls made by the Sunlight AfA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Online harms, especially those experienced by women and girls, are not something that can be understood in the abstract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Not everyone is aware of such online harms or what they look like.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, you can feel the devastating impact of such harms on individuals and their families even if you have never been directly targeted.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: All you need is to listen with an open heart to the story of someone who has gone through such an experience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I have heard several of such tales from personal acquaintances, each of which has remained deeply etched in my mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The first that I recall occurred more than 10 years ago.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A woman journalist related to me a harrowing experience, where her photos and contact number were posted by a person or persons unknown on websites that falsely profiled her as a prostitute.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She was harassed and embarrassed by phone calls from strangers wanting to obtain sexual services from her.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: She had reason to think that this was part of a campaign by those who wanted to punish her for writing pieces that they disagreed strongly with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In another episode, a father reached out to me because intimate photos that his daughter had taken of herself had been stolen from her phone and found their way onto blog sites that specialise in collecting and sharing such photos of young Singapore women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He went to great lengths to get the photos taken down.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I will always remember his anguish when relating the severe trauma that this had caused his daughter and his fear that he might lose her forever should she do irreparable harm to herself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Thankfully, in both cases, the women and their loved ones were able to overcome the harm they experienced and put these terrible episodes behind them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Another common form of such harms is hyper-sexualised communications on direct messaging platforms, typically involving the sending of lewd and sexually explicit photos.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are aimed at eliciting a response from the women and girls being targeted and linked to sexual grooming and eventual exploitation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The impact caused by such online harms can have severe consequences on the victims who are made to feel humiliated and ashamed, violated and unsafe, isolated and withdrawn, depressed and even suicidal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Their families and loved ones are also not spared.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: How many untold stories of scarred psyches or diminished lives are there?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: How many women and girls are out there who would never regain their self-confidence and peace of mind?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hearing about these episodes makes me and many others who care about the well-being of women and girls want to do something about it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This goes beyond our sympathy and indignation on behalf of the victims and their families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are wider and more insidious implications on society, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: What do these online harms have in common?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They stem from seeing and portraying women and girls, primarily, as playthings, for the sexual gratification of men.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is a deplorable and backward mindset, one that I believe most men do not subscribe to, but is, nonetheless, difficult to eradicate from society completely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It may be rooted in age-old inequalities between the sexes, but is unjustifiable by any modern standard of morality or law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Generations of women – and men who support women – all over the world have pushed back against this mindset and fought for the dignity and safety of women and girls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over time, like many other societies, we have developed clear laws and strong enforcement to protect women's safety in real life – against sexual assault, hurt crimes and trafficking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore is now one of the safest cities in the world for women and girls, so much so that many of us take it for granted that we can go about our daily business alone and unaccompanied.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But the exploitative and backward mindset towards women has found new means of expression in the Internet age.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Perpetrators believe they can hide behind the cloak of anonymity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The digital publication and dissemination of information, allows for viralling at speed and the impact on victims becomes more severe and wide-ranging.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Such harms can also be weaponised in a malicious and cynical manner to threaten and inflict trauma on individual women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Unsurprisingly, more women than men feel unsafe from gender-based online harms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If left unchecked, online harms that promote exploitative and disrespectful attitudes towards women and girls may discourage women from being active online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are not just talking about women deciding to make fewer posts or comments on social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But avoiding important and meaningful undertakings, such as leadership roles or advocacy in real life, that might increase one's chances of encountering haters who wield online harms as a weapon.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If this mindset is left unchecked, it may erode the real-life safety that women in Singapore have come to rely on, by undermining the value of respecting women and girls as full human beings that we have worked so hard to build up over the generations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some who are intent on doing real-life harm to women and girls are also availing themselves of online means to identify and isolate their potential victims – hyper-sexualised direct messaging being one of such means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: No society that respects and values women can stand for this, much less one like Singapore where women have achieved so much freedom and confidence in real life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our women and girls must feel as safe and confident online as they do in real life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is, certainly, relevant to many of the topics being discussed in the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Therefore, while I was at MCI, with support from my former colleagues, I decided to make an appeal to those who care equally about women and girls' online safety, so that we can come together and do something about it collectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I was moved by the number of people who came forward because this cause resonated strongly with them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This included not only women but also men.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The number of men reaching out and supporting the AfA affirms and strengthens my belief that men are absolutely vital partners for improving digital safety for women and girls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As fathers, husbands, brothers, sons, friends and colleagues – they care for and want the best for women and girls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is only ever about women and men working hand-in-hand to push back against mindsets that exploit and victimise women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: IPS Senior Research Fellow and Sunlight AfA member Dr Chew Han Ei exemplifies this solidarity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He joined the AfA because he wants to help shift societal mindsets and norms to empower men, as supportive allies of women, to speak out against behaviours that reflect and perpetuate retrograde and exploitative mindsets about women.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are men and women who recognise that online harms, which men and boys may similarly encounter, cannot be dealt with solely via Government action in the form of greater regulation and enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government's role is necessary but not sufficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Concerted efforts from the public, private and people sectors, to formulate approaches to victim support, undertake public education and engagement, and have Internet companies step up to do their part are also needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indeed, groups like the Singapore Council of Women's Organisations (SCWO), United Women Singapore, TOUCH Community Services and AWARE are among the organisations that AfA members hail from.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I also wish to express my gratitude to the many officers from MCI who believe in the cause and contributed so much of their time and effort to provide the AfA with secretariat support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam will share more on this later.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will work with community partners to develop public education initiatives to drive awareness about online harms and promote digital safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam and I are grateful for the support of all alliance members, including those who expressed interest in sustaining initiatives in the longer term.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The AfA has been a platform for many of our members to forge new friendships and explore common areas of interest, including wider advocacy for the protection and advancement of women and girls, beyond tackling online harms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I am encouraged and look forward to new engines of activism in our society in support of women and girls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Beyond the AfA, we have seen the cause attract wide resonance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: More broadly, we welcome interested community partners to join the Digital for Life movement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There is room for many of us to amplify efforts to build a safer digital future for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Very recently, Straits Times journalist Malavika Menon wrote courageously about her personal encounter with online harms, including that of a sexist nature.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Her piece reminded me of that first conversation I had, all those years ago, with a different woman journalist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We all share the goal of a gender-equal society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For us in the Workers' Party, this is a very important goal, which is why Ms He Ting Ru and I moved the Motion in this House on gender equality last year.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Personally, what keeps me invested in this ideal is when I think about my family members – my wife, my mother, my daughter and also my son – and how I want them to live in a society where every individual is judged not by their gender but solely by the content of their character – to paraphrase something that Dr Martin Luther King Junior said in the context of race.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While we broadly agree on the end goal, we have some differences in our approaches to define and, ultimately, achieve that goal, which is why, in our speeches in this debate, we are focusing on where we see gaps in the White Paper and where we have different views and policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In my Motion speech last year, I spoke about the challenges facing us on this front.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Online, we do still see views from some quarters stating that moves towards gender equality and fairness for women reflect "misandry" or the hatred of men.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He had reportedly called for the abolition of Korea's Ministry of Gender Equality and Family and had blamed the country's low birth rate on "feminism".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is a sobering turn of events, though it should be noted that the victory was by the narrowest of margins, with some Korean gender equality activists suggesting that the result showed that the momentum was on their side.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I cite this example not to argue that we should not go too far or too fast so as not to provoke a backlash from those with different views.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On the contrary, my Workers' Party colleagues and I argue that we should be bold and ambitious in our gender equality strides.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A great deal is at stake, including the empowerment to lead full lives and contribute back to society of half the population.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I bring up the Korean example to emphasise the importance of having conversations with Singaporean men and, perhaps, some women who may not fully buy into the vision of gender equality as well, to convince them that society moving in this direction is fair, right and not a threat to them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have to carry all Singaporeans on this journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must not allow anti-gender equality sentiments to fester and brew into something more bitter and more sinister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government can support non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and think tanks in conducting rigorous regular research and publishing the results about the areas in life where women still face inequality – from the unequal burden of housework and domestic violence to sexist discrimination and sexual harassment in the workplace and on campus.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of us in this House can and should help publicise such data, as should other stakeholders like NGOs, trade associations and chambers and student groups.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such data being widely accepted can help individual Singaporeans have informed conversations with other Singaporeans to move the needle on mindsets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In truth, the battle for mindsets was never mainly about policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is about us as a people keeping an open mind to new facts, research and trends, being willing to relook at established conventions and winning people over, one person at a time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We all have a role to play in this journey.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If every person who believes in gender equality can change the mind of just one person who harbours sexist thinking, whether man or woman, a revolution in our culture and thinking will be achievable within this generation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Here, I am not referring to violent or physical abuse, such as rape or molest, which is addressable under the laws that exist, but to verbal abuse and inappropriate behaviour, lewd and derogatory comments or instructions given in the workplace or on campuses, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Victims can also pursue recourse through the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA) Court, filing a Magistrate's Complaint or through litigation, which is costly and time-consuming, which would deter many victims, especially since victims may often be disadvantaged in terms of power or socioeconomic status vis-a-vis male perpetrators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, in the absence of any legislation defining sexual harassment of the employer's liability for the same, the outcome of such legal action is uncertain.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Other countries have used legislative tools to tackle this issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This can be found in the UK Equality Act and in the US.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Under this law, both men and women can commit acts of sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not suggest a rush to legislate right now but would make three suggestions here as steps to consider taking before considering the issue of legislation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, can this not be a requirement or a plus point when awarding certain large Government contracts and economic incentives?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, can the MOE be more prescriptive in requiring Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to adhere to certain baseline minimal standards of compliance with respect to sexual harassment?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These will include implementing a national code of conduct for IHLs as well as ensuring comprehensive sexuality education that includes the concepts of respecting consent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In Taiwan, for example, as cited in the AWARE report I mentioned, the government has enacted the Gender Equity Education Act, which, specifically, addresses the problem of gender-based bullying, which is referred to as sexual bullying, under the Act.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All of us, I am quite sure I can say this, have dealt with such cases among our constituents.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I dealt with one such case recently in the Serangoon ward of Aljunied GRC and I would like to share it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Olivia – not her real name, of course – is a foreign national on LTVP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They are parents to a Singaporean girl, Anna – also not her real name.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Anna is in Primary 4 at one of our schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She struck me as being just like my own daughter at that age.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At his wake, I met both Olivia and Anna.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I took down their details so as to write appeals in aspect of Olivia's continued LTVP status since she does not have a living husband as a sponsor any longer; and in respect of their continued stay in an HDB public rental flat since the family is of very low income – and, in fact, now has no income at all – since Olivia does not work, though she would now want to and need to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Olivia will have to start working even though she faces uncertainty as to her immigration status and ability to work in future as renewals of permits are never assured even though she is the mother of the Singaporean child; and Anna, who is part of a family unit with the mother and whose mother faces all of this uncertainty while having to raise her single-handedly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This suggests that many such couples have to deal with the stresses and difficulties arising from uncertain residency status for almost a decade before the migrant spouse acquires PR or citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For female migrant spouses, in particular, this means years of insecurity, compounding their vulnerability to family violence." According to an earlier Parliamentary Question reply in this House, 98% of LTVP renewals sponsored by non-spouses are approved but this still leaves uncertainty on the part of the spouse who loses a Singapore Citizen spouse or whose Singaporean spouse no longer wants to sponsor her LTVP application.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, LTVP is not a stable status and does not amount to residency, subject, as it is, to regular renewal after short-time intervals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The time taken for foreign spouses to become citizens and the uncertainty surrounding this have implications for, firstly, stress and mental well-being, as uncertainty clouds their ability to plan their lives.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may also affect the well-being of their Singaporean children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, access to housing options open to citizens and PRs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Though rental housing can be granted to non-citizens, the perception – and usually, the reality – is that it is harder for such cases.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Third, access to legal employment, which may lead them to take up cash-based forms of employment that do not have a legal basis, which will leave them vulnerable to exploitation with no legal recourse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not all foreign spouses have LTVP+ or MOM's approval to work.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be beneficial to tap on this pool of manpower for our economy since these individuals are living in Singapore anyway?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, access to certain forms of social welfare assistance reserved for citizens and PRs, as with housing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, access to subsidies for primary healthcare, which may inhibit behaviours, such as seeking medical treatment and going for health screening, and which may have an impact on the health of the wider community if LTVP holders succumb to communicable diseases, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sixth, enhanced vulnerability to domestic violence since the perception remains that it is harder to get a renewal of LTVP without spousal sponsorship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: AWARE has cited evidence of cases where the husband threatens to cancel the LTVP if the wife reports domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is why, in its General Election 2020 manifesto, the Workers' Party called for a clear, transparent and time-based fast-track path to citizenship for foreign spouses who are parents of Singaporean children.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In a previous reply to a Parliamentary Question, the Government outlined its rationale for not instituting a more transparent system for evaluating citizenship applications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two reasons were given: not wanting people to "game the system" and not wanting foreign nationals to accuse the Government publicly of unfairness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is true that most countries do not grant immigration rights automatically to foreign spouses of citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, many other countries publish transparent material for such decisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The subsequent application for permanent residency includes a "Life in the UK" test to demonstrate good knowledge of the country's language and lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The criteria, typically, cover age, level of education, appropriate skills and work experience, a job offer and proficiency in the local language.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In New Zealand, having close family members is also one of the criteria that is taken into account.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, we can institute more points for skillsets in short supply in our economy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To revisit a subject I have previously spoken about at some length in this House, to get more Singaporeans into good redesigned trade jobs like carpentry and plumbing, for example, one approach – not the only approach by any means – is to convert experienced foreign craftsmen and trades experts into citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As for the argument that foreigners should not be able to stir up anti-Singapore sentiments if there is no systemic national bias in granting citizenship, as one assumes there is not, this should not be an issue with a transparent points-based system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Opacity, on the other hand, can just as easily fuel such sentiments.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some may say that more transparency may encourage foreigners to marry Singaporeans in an exploitative and cynical fashion solely to gain an assured pathway to citizenship.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But not having transparency does not appear to have deterred Singaporeans from marrying foreigners and having children in very significant numbers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All the current regime does is create uncertainty for the foreign spouse and the mother of Singaporean children and, hence, for the family and the children themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It only makes things worse for everyone after the fact.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The advantages of a points-based immigration system include the following.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, creating predictability and a perception of fairness and transparency, better enabling participants in our national life to make decisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, attracting and encouraging the right applicants, for example, those with skills in short supply.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Third, creating a dynamic system that can be adjusted, for example, based on labour market needs, with those adjustments being publicly signalled and, hence, influencing citizenship application behaviour in a positive way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, within such a system, foreign spouses of Singaporean children can be given clear, transparent, time-based pathways to PR status and citizenship via a points system, without having to depend on a "black box" evaluation process which breeds uncertainty and an inability to plan ahead.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But with the advent of COMPASS, we have taken a major step in that direction for the Employment Pass regime.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is no reason why we should not do the same for our immigration regime.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, Sir, the fourth and last topic I would like to touch on, and in the spirit of gender equality, I would like to call for changes to our spousal maintenance laws to foster more fairness to certain types of men who may be at a disadvantage under section 69 of the Women’s Charter in the event of a divorce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the Women’s Charter debate earlier this year, the Government said it has considered the possibility of allowing maintenance applications to be made for husbands without the condition of incapacity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Its position on section 69 was that there was no need for such gender-neutral legislation because there is a higher chance of women giving up their careers to get involved in care work while the partner continues working.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In developed countries, approaches to spousal maintenance vary, with some countries like England giving generous maintenance to the financially weaker party and others focusing on time-limited maintenance, so that the spouse can get back into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I recognise that the specifics will continue to be debated more fully at some point in time, but one common idea I support is that, regardless of sex, a spouse must be able to file for maintenance without the requirement for incapacitation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One, it should not be the case that we decide this law on what tends to happen, but rather, what can happen, especially as the current cohort of young adults has reached a point where a higher proportion of women than men have post-Secondary educational qualifications.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It will not be a rare situation, going forward, that couples decide that the husband should be giving up his job to take on care work because he earns less or for some other reason.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, at the very least, we should not bind the Courts in granting maintenance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And my third point here also concludes my speech.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government facilitate and encourage employers to adopt fair practices to hire pregnant staff?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will we be able to include such fair practices as part of the MOM framework in the consideration of the application of EP and other work passes?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be good to have a platform to highlight companies with fair practices with regular testimonies by their staff and, perhaps, as part of the consideration of the Best Employer Award.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I appreciate the action plan to entrench FWAs as a workplace norm.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our experience during the pandemic has proven that it can work very well, with benefits for both employees and employers, as well as the environment, as we cut down on commutes to the office.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, each of us has at least one important person in our life.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They hold us in their wombs for nine months and take good care of us as we grow up.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, women hold up half the sky.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must also put ourselves in their shoes and understand the challenges and pressures they face.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, you cannot have the best of both worlds and you have to give up certain things and make sacrifices.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we cannot dismiss their sacrifices and take it for granted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot have the cake and eat it.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, we all have the responsibility to do our best to support and encourage them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am grateful to the Government for the great support it has given to low-income families over the years, including giving them a substantial subsidy for childcare.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOE also provides free breakfasts to those disadvantaged children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Government can also increase the childcare subsidy for children in the sandwiched middle- and low-income families to further assist them and ease their burden.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will help mothers who have to juggle work to supplement their household income.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Government will consider giving subsidies to mothers who are unable to join the workforce due to difficult circumstances.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Sir, next, the focus of this White Paper regarding caregiving has been on recognition and support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The enhanced respite care options and Home Caregiving Grant and the broadened scope of the Household Services Scheme are all excellent proposals.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But these may not apply directly to certain families, who need to depend on migrant domestic workers for caregiving and yet cannot afford to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry consider additional necessary support, including financial help, for young children with challenging illnesses who come from dysfunctional families or are being cared for by divorced single moms, such as by ring-fencing partial funds from their fathers’ CPF accounts, for their healthcare expenses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although the current CPF Act does stipulate the existence of a special trust account, the Courts have no power under the legislation to direct and/or to set aside amounts from their fathers’ accounts to help pay for the healthcare expenses of these children during the divorce proceedings or when the families are abandoned by the fathers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had, during the Workers' Party Motion on this matter last year in this House, spoken about a number of concerns about gender equality in the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To quickly recap, I had explained why womenomics in Singapore still had a way to go.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had also suggested a number of practical steps to promote greater gender equality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These include reservations for female representation on board memberships in GLCs, increasing the coverage of childcare and primary schooling facilities in demographically young estates, paid re-entry programmes for mothers and informal caregivers, and publishing aggregated and average pay gap information by industry sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I wish to share a number of reactions in response to the White Paper on Women's Development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Consistent with my earlier speech, I will focus on Area 1 of the White Paper on "Equal Opportunities in the Workplace".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Report highlights three action plans to improve female labour force participation: FWAs, career mentorship and flexible leave entitlements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will share about each of these separately.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Currently, MOM parental paid leave provisions amount up to 18 weeks paid, of which six weeks may be taken up by fathers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I think I can reverse engineer this figure essentially by adding up unpaid as well as paid infant care leave for each parent, perhaps the Government would be willing to clarify exactly how this discrepancy arises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Regardless of the calculations, while a move towards greater shared leave provisions, undoubtedly, represents an improvement, the policy still remains voluntary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Employers are only asked to consider FWAs "fairly and properly".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The only concession is that the consumption period for additional unpaid infant care leave will be extended for those in the Public Service from "within the first" to "the first two years".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On its face, these may seem to be distinctions without differences – 22 versus 24 weeks, a maximum of eight weeks versus a minimum of four weeks to be granted to the father.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if you will indulge me, there is, in fact, a material difference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By imposing a maximum that the father can take, the law, as currently construed, embeds, if you will, an implicit assumption that the father is, in fact, the primary breadwinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What if there is a couple where the woman out-earns the man?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this case, it would be financially rational for the woman to be the one returning to work while the man remains at home providing childcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Fixing a maximum of eight weeks for the father will preclude this possibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, this is not to deny the physiological changes a woman's body undergoes following delivery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And it is undeniably important that the body be allowed to rest and recover from the rigours of childbirth, lest the doctors in this House correct me on this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Research has shown, however, that the postpartum period can be divided into three distinct phases, with the second sub-acute phase where the body undergoes major changes in hemodynamics, genital urinary recovery, metabolism and emotional status lasting between two and six weeks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Postpartum depression would also, typically, present itself within this timeframe.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is why a 12-week minimum for the father makes sense, without ruling out the father as the primary caregiver thereafter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should also recognise that just taking additional leave, even when fully justified and accounted for, is not entirely costless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Being away from the office for a longer period will inadvertently delay or, perhaps, inhibit career progression and this is especially the case for mothers who end up utilising more of the leave entitlement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is another reason why minimum paternal leave requirements can also indirectly help limit the gender wage gap from rising even further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I applaud the effort to expand mentorship, I have mixed feelings about how far mentorship can take us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am a mentor, both voluntarily and professionally, to students, and I see the enormous value that close mentorship can offer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can be a wonderful idea if there are already sufficient women in positions of influence across a broad range of organisations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this is a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If potential female mentors available remain small in number, we run the risk of either over-taxing this limited pool of mentors or a failure to break into spaces where women are currently under-represented.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worse, we pile additional stress on this group, which may even, inadvertently, inhibit their continued career progression, because they have become preoccupied with non-professional commitments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The solution, it would seem, would be to encourage male mentors to step up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is certainly possible, but we would also do well to recognise the more challenging climate men face when asked to mentor the opposite gender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In a post-#Me-Too world, men have often become very cautious in both their language and advice, for fear of being accused of sexual harassment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They may choose to withhold their most strident criticism, even if such critique may be constructive, or refrain from banter, for fear of being perceived as sexist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This point was made by Anne Clarke Wolff, the founder and CEO of Independence Point Advisors, a women-owned investment bank and advisory, sometimes known in the business as “Salomon Sisters.” In an interview, Ms Wolff explained that the forces that led women to exit high-stress, high-remuneration jobs, such as those in finance, were not because they favoured shorter hours or lower commitment; au contraire, they left because they felt excluded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This absence of camaraderie may be ameliorated by genuine mentorship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is built over social settings, like drinks and dinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But many men today would be very uncomfortable engaging in such activities, even when above board, with someone of the opposite gender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One is also left to wonder just how such opportunities would apply to women in more blue-collar or non-professional occupations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, the origin of apprenticeships was to transfer artisanal skills in trades work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the mentorship and networking plan apply with equal force to lower-wage domains and occupations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The report takes the position that, while it wishes to encourage and support women in achieving their leadership potential, it shuns tokenism and, in particular, the "unintended consequences…   imposing hard quotas." On its face, this principle is surely indisputable; even champions of greater empowerment are likely to be uncomfortable with being granted a seat at the table, only by dint of their gender.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, perceptions of effectiveness of a female leader improves and gender stereotypes about the roles of women in public versus domestic spheres weaken.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After the advent of such quotas, gender gaps between males and females in terms of qualifications would also diminish and a female CEO would also be more likely to be appointed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, when mandated representation is actually pursued, both theory and evidence emphatically reject the notion that quotas would most likely be ineffectual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because quotas could improve talent allocation by overturning historical instances where such groups may have been deliberately excluded.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, nobody truly believes that being a man predisposes one to computer engineering, data science or finance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Overall, the body of evidence suggests that reforms of this nature have been successful in reducing historical inequalities, and power and norms do shift permanently, even in response to temporary interventions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All this points to something that is just as intuitive as a rejection of tokenism; that rebalancing the position of disadvantaged groups requires concrete corrective action, even if only for a season, to permanently shift attitudes and perceptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, in countries that have moved to embrace gender quotas on corporate boards, there has been greater enthusiasm for such quotas, as well as more professional and formal approaches to board selection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in countries where there are no quotas, there is a growing recognition that market forces will not fix the problem on its own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Undoubtedly, we should not go overboard with trying to squeeze round pegs into square holes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The evidence also suggests that firm valuations may suffer excessively when the existing gap between mandated and actual representation is larger, or when the costs of compliance are too great, due to the firm being too small to cope.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Here, again, the public sector can be the one to take the lead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even if we do not wish to excessively tie the hands of employers, will the Government at least ensure that all Government-linked firms aspire to this voluntary target?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And will the Government consider requiring board-level training on unconscious gender biases, similar to the current requirement that board members undergo one-time training on sustainability, for all listed corporations?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The book, which went on to spark a brief movement, explained how she believed that women had to be bold and embrace self-promotion, in order to succeed in the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This thesis has come under some criticism since, but the central metaphor – the need to be proactive in pushing for a seat at the table – applies, in my view, to how we should be advancing pro-women policy in our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is in this spirit that I have found the action points outlined in the White Paper to betray a somewhat lack of ambition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will, thereafter, make two observations about workplace culture and public policymaking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the Government's recognition that there is a need to enhance protection for victim-survivors of family violence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The extent of family violence tends to be significantly under-reported worldwide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We can understand why this is so for reasons ranging from emotional attachment to the perpetrator, to not wishing to incarcerate a breadwinner.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I was glad to see the footnote on page 49 of the White Paper, which recognises the need to look at self-reported data to supplement official data if we are to have a clearer picture of the prevalence of domestic violence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper affirms, among other things, that there is a need to strengthen societal attitudes against family violence and enhance preventive efforts for persons at risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was also stated that, for victims, reporting of family violence should be made easier and that immediate help should be available to reduce the risk of repeat violence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for perpetrators, the White Paper affirmed the need to increase perpetrators' accountability and rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do agree that tackling family violence benefits from a comprehensive approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, I am concerned that the proposed multidisciplinary first response may, inadvertently, result in a Police mindset that the social services will take the lead from the start.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the first response is, for want of a better word, "a softer one", there may be a perception among perpetrators that they can try to explain their actions away.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for victims, it is vital that they do not encounter responses that appear to decriminalise their experiences or, worse, attribute blame to them for precipitating the violence by the own behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If they do encounter such dismissive attitudes, they are unlikely to report again.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this note, I should mention the special vulnerability of persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is evidence from other countries that women with disabilities disproportionately experienced domestic violence and sexual violence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given that disabled persons may be less able to defend themselves, we must be mindful of our special duty of care towards them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was mentioned in the White Paper that frontline officers currently already undergo sensitivity training.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if there is any component or other training to equip officers to respond to victims of violence who are disabled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I next move on to discuss cases of repeat violence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Repeat violence is not uncommon in family cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides investigating cases after they have occurred, are the agencies looking into strategies to prevent the incidents in the first place?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In particularly high-risk cases, how much resources are agencies willing to put in?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At first blush, it might sound impossible for external persons to prevent incidents that happen within the house.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, it has been done to some extent, and successfully, elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate my point, I will take an example from the UK.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When they sensed that a violent attack was imminent, they could activate the alarm so as to open a voice channel to law enforcement officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The officers would then be able to hear what was going on in the home, talk to the victim if needed, and decide if a rapid response to the premises should be dispatched.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This initiative was, indeed, resource-intensive, but it reaped significantly positive results for victims not only in reducing repeat incidents but in reducing fear of crime, immensely improving the quality of life for themselves and, often, their children, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I cite this example to illustrate what a strong commitment to bringing down family violence might entail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Victims are usually in a difficult position as sending their spouses to jail often impacts the family economically and, in that sense, can be "unaffordable".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This, in turn, may lead agencies to face ambivalence from victims who report for protection and then withdraw when it comes to prosecution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The need to strengthen societal attitudes against family violence applies to frontline officers, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is not a new issue; neither is it confined to Singapore alone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Being a Police officer carries a certain, almost romanticised, notion of going after bad guys and girls.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While there may be other motivations, there are many officers I know personally who enjoy the adrenaline rush of handling murder cases and going after organised crimes syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some officers may not find handling family violence cases quite their cup of tea.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If they bring reluctance or disinterest to such cases, the public will feel it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is thus important for the official HR policy for career progression not to relegate such duties as unimportant and thereby affect that officer's career prospects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Beyond official HR policy, there is also the issue of the unofficial culture, that is, what officers talk about in the canteens, which may be much harder to overcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Hiring and promotion of employees on equal footing, male or female, are fundamental.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, like Ms He Ting Ru, I welcome the pending anti-discrimination legislation and stronger fair employment guidelines as steps in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a further aspect that is more insidious and, that is, again, culture.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How many women bear with unwarranted contact from male superiors because they want to keep their jobs?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A fleeting touch may seem harmless to some.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, it bears remembering that physical touching without consent could well amount to the offence of outrage of modesty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What about something less than touching, such as making loaded comments?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To cite a personal experience: decades ago, when I was a law enforcement officer, it was suggested to me by a male superior that I should put on make-up when I came to work.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I did not take offence at that time, as I simply dismissed the comment as crazy since we were not running a modelling agency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But thinking back about it today, the comment was probably made innocently, but was it appropriate?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would such comments impact other women much more deeply?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But to avoid undue pressure on females in the workplace, employers and society as a whole would need to step up and educate themselves, too.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is seen under the section on mindset shifts at Action 24: "Develop gender-responsive standards under the Singapore Standardisation Programme".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is express recognition that there is a need to improve gender diversity in the standards community so as to develop gender-responsive standards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is essential for meaningful analysis in gender-sensitive policymaking.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Related to standard setting, there is mention in the White Paper of the importance of having more women in leadership roles as CEOs and directors of companies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, it is also vital to have more women in political leadership, which I consider to be standard setting at the national level.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I was glad to hear Minister Josephine Teo earlier highlight the increased presence of women in this House and that society was better off for it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I had spoken on this topic in August last year on the Workers' Party's Motion on gender equality.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not intend to repeat myself here, save to say that this is a critical peg that we all need to work on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also touched on workplace culture and the impact on the experiences of female employees.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The White Paper on Singapore Women's Development is an important step to continue the progress and collectively drive the whole-of-nation commitment to advance Singapore women's development.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I believe that there is more that we can do to increase its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, to further ease the caregiving load, how can we continue to provide more affordable childcare?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic was a catalyst for organisations to adopt FWAs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: FWAs have helped both men and women better manage their workplace and personal responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Due to restricted access to the workplace during the pandemic, it became a "burning platform" for workplace norms on FWAs to evolve.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would go towards ensuring that we keep up the momentum towards making FWAs a norm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since many primary caregivers tend to be women due to our entrenched societal expectation, to increase the effectiveness of FWA in furthering Singapore women's development, we must also do more to promote job restructuring through flexi-load or job-sharing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This can enable those with caregiving responsibilities to continue playing a part in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Take, for example, Mdm Farhana from Pasir Ris.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She takes care of her elderly mother who undergoes dialysis three times a week.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If more organisations adopt job-sharing, flexible work hours and remote working, caregivers like her may have more opportunities to contribute to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women play many important roles in our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They contribute to the economy and shoulder a heavier burden of caregiving.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, while we enable FWAs to help both men and women better manage their workplace and personal responsibilities, the FWAs must also address the dos and don'ts of how to protect their privacy and family time at home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we practise more flexible work hours, workers will be working at different hours to manage their workplace and personal responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have heard of anecdotal stories of workers feeling pressured whenever they receive or have to answer emails late at night.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we do not want to go to the extreme end, like in France, where it is illegal to email an employee after office hours, we must recognise that FWAs mean that different groups of people will be working at different times.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, as FWAs blur the line between work and home, how can we get employers and workers to come to a new understanding about work-life balance and respect for personal space and time?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should also encourage employers and organisations to facilitate the re-entry of women into the workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
