text: Whether through developing mentorship or internship programmes, or by providing networking or retraining opportunities, the effort to enable more women to re-enter the workforce should be recognised and highlighted as an important consideration for fair and inclusive employment practices.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In a study conducted by PPIS on the aspirations of Muslim women in Singapore, one of the top aspirations of Muslim women is to be financially independent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many respondents shared that they felt less employable as they perceived that social inequality in employment opportunities still exist.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They also felt there was less exposure to different job opportunities and, interestingly, they felt that there were insufficient avenues to upskill for better paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we, as a society, come together to support and create platforms for our back-to-work mothers seeking upskilling and re-employment opportunities?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: PPIS President, Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim, also suggested that such programmes should be attended by spouses to provide the closest support for our back-to-work mothers, something which I do agree, that us, males, we must do more of.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, given that one in four Singaporeans will be above the age of 65 by 2030, will this be enough?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are our projected requirements and how can we have a whole-of-nation commitment to address the manpower needs of the respite care industry?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must explore how to better create awareness for the grant or any other grants for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of our Pasir Ris residents, Mdm Neo, who is in her 60s and currently unemployed, takes care of her bedridden husband.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I visited her a month ago, she happily shared that HDB has just installed the ramps and grab bars for her under the EASE programme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, through our conversation, it became apparent that she has not heard about the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure caregivers are aware of the support that is available and not just ask for it when they truly are at their wits end?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we have effective outreach programmes to help support our caregivers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we also segregate caregivers based on who they are caring for, for example, someone providing care for a person with disability, vis-a-vis a caregiver providing care to a chronically ill elderly?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both these caregivers need and deserve our support.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Should we have a one-stop portal that can serve all caregivers or at least provide the relevant information for any one of our caregivers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can we proactively engage our caregivers so that they do not feel that they are left to their own devices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another way to ease the caregiving load is to continue providing affordable and quality preschools.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must recognise that some women choose to remain at home instead of work, in order to provide adequate care for the young, or to persons with disabilities or developmental needs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are also some women who had to quit their job because of health issues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can do more to ease such pressures on our already stressed young mothers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Over the last 60 years, much progress has been made in women's development in Singapore in many areas, such as education, healthcare, the enactment of the Women's Charter, protection from violence and more equal working opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The White Paper on Singapore Women's Development is an important step to collectively drive the whole-of-nation commitment to advance Singapore Women's Development and I believe that there is still more that we can do to increase its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many respondents shared that they felt less employable as they perceived that social inequality in employment opportunities still exists.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They also felt that there was less exposure to job opportunities and there were insufficient avenues for them to upskill for better-paying jobs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What roles can bodies, such as MENDAKI and NTUC, play to create platforms for back-to-work mothers who wish to seek upskilling and re-employment opportunities?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: PPIS President Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim also suggested that married couples attend such programmes so that back-to-work women can receive support from the person closest to them – something that I really agree with.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Second, while we work towards changing the stereotype that women are primary caregivers and, hence, often shoulder a heavier caregiving load in the family, we must provide better and easier support to our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Third, to further ease the caregiving load, how can we continue to provide more affordable and quality childcare?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should provide support for our young women to find jobs in the growing industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mdm Deputy Speaker, ultimately, we all have a part to play to inculcate the values of fairness, equality and respect.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We all can address gender roles from young, at home and in schools and, in this way, help to build a fairer and more inclusive society where all Singaporeans have full and equal opportunities to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women represent our mothers, sisters, wives and daughters.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Every one of us has a vested interest in ensuring a supportive and inclusive workplace, free from harassments and discrimination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women deserve to feel safe and protected as they remain important contributors to society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must role model equal and mutually supportive gender relationships built on sincere care and concern for others.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will help determine how women in the next generation will be treated as we commit to build a fairer and more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In August of last year, I spoke in support of the Motion on Gender Equality tabled by my colleague Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I highlighted the unequal distribution of care responsibilities between parents and how this is linked to discriminatory social institutions and stereotypes about gender roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I suggested that the impetus for change lies with both the views held by the individual and society at large, as well as with us policymakers and how we shape those views.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Mr Gerald Giam, will be touching on FWAs and how both employers and employees gain from having FWAs as the norm, rather than the exception at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I have reiterated across various speeches over the last two years, I hope that the Government, businesses and society do not view FWAs as one which has unintended consequences of reduced employability or, ironically, creating rigidity in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is imperative for the Government to demonstrate leadership on this matter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first issue I would like to touch on is that of parental leave and its impact on the roles of fathers in society and in accelerating gender equality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The upheaval caused by COVID-19 and its impact on how we work have shone a spotlight on gender inequality that exists at home, with working mothers often the ones who have to pick up the slack.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I previously highlighted a study by market research firm IPSOS Group S.A. and United Women Singapore, which showed that a mere 47% of mothers are happy with the division of household and care responsibilities, as opposed to 78% of fathers – a clear difference in perception that we need to shift.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These shifts in societal perception that we seek do not happen in isolation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Policies play a large part in shaping these views and, on this front, I was a bit disappointed to see that the White Paper has fallen short on concrete policy changes to encourage fathers to take on a more active role in household and caregiving responsibilities, especially around a more equitable distribution of statutory parental leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is a growing body of evidence that suggests that the immediate aftermath of a child's birth represent a golden opportunity of sorts to shape lasting good habits among young fathers that persist throughout a child's lifetime.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Fathers who spend more time with their infant children develop greater confidence in their own childcare abilities, perpetuating a virtuous cycle that leads to lasting egalitarian split of responsibilities between mothers and fathers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is also a suggestion that women in more equitable households can focus more energies on career development, leading to better gender equality both at home and at work.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The impact is not limited to the parents involved, but also has far-reaching impacts on society at large.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A study by the IZA Institute of Labor Economics in Germany from 2017 showed that in the decade after Germany introduced reforms in 2006, to encourage fathers to take at least two months of parental leave, there was a marked shift in the attitudes of not just the current generation of parents towards gender equality, but also the grandparents' generation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Both grandmothers and grandfathers, whose grandchildren were born after the reforms, were less likely to agree with the sentiment that " omen should be more concerned about their family than about their career".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Since my last speech on this topic, some of you would know that I have welcomed a new addition to the family and our little baby boy is now just over four months old.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am extremely grateful that my employer is understanding and a strong believer in FWAs, but many other young fathers do not share the same experience.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By increasing the statutory entitlement to fully-paid parental leave for fathers, we can, at the very least, eliminate some of the direct financial considerations from the mental calculus.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are heartened by the Government's move to lead by example in encouraging public officers to utilise their full entitlement of parental leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This will go some way towards breaking down stereotypes and misconceptions in the workplace that lead to lower take-up rates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But we can, definitely, go a step further with actual policy changes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And I can imagine the challenges mothers face in reducing their paid maternity leave, especially when we consider that our parental leave policies are not exactly world leading, with the 16 weeks of maternity leave below the OECD average of 20 weeks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A further expansion can come in the form of "sharing bonuses" awarded if fathers take up their full minimum entitlement of shared parental leave.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, as an added incentive, consideration could be given for an additional bonus number of weeks to be awarded to the pool if fathers utilise the full four weeks of minimum parental leave they are entitled to.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The hope is that, over time, these increased entitlements become entrenched as social norms – as has happened in countries like Germany – as more parents utilise their full entitlement, initially to benefit from the bonuses, and, over time, because it is simply the thing to do.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These new social norms will encourage fathers to spend more time with their children and take on a greater role in the child's development, take on their fair share of household chores and lead to an overall uplift in our society's perception of gender roles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second issue I would like to touch on is that of providing support to parents and, especially, mothers beyond childbirth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We all recognise the importance of parental care leave in allowing mothers to properly recover from giving birth to her baby and for parents to care for and bond with their newborn child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while we have a high standard of medical care provided at childbirth across all our hospitals here in Singapore, I believe more can be done to provide greater postpartum support to mothers, especially to first-time mothers, and families who may not have the economic resources to obtain post-birth support services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To many parents, including my wife and I, having a trusted confinement nanny to support our transition from a clueless couple to proud parents is a godsend.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such services do not come cheap, however, as they range in the thousands of dollars, and made worse in the last two years due to the border closures.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, even for those of us who are lucky enough to have the dedicated care and support of a live-in confinement nanny, the immediate aftermath of a confinement nanny's departure is still one characterised by high levels of stress and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: They say it takes a village to raise a child and I find it to be especially true after the birth of my second son.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One might think that, as experienced parents, things will get easier and we might enjoy some efficiency gains.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But my personal experience suggests that caring for two young children is more than double the amount of effort.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are extremely thankful for the village that was our families and extended families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, not everyone has easy access to their very own village and, for many others, the parenthood journey can also be a lonely and alienating one.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond providing informational support, could we bring the proverbial village to all mothers out there, to ensure that community support and services are available, especially to those without a strong informal support system, to fill the care gap?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, spoke about this point earlier as well, with her suggestion being instituting practices, such as having specially-trained health visitors, to routinely call on our new mothers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To reduce inequity and inequality during the foundational years of our children's lives, we need to strengthen access to continuous care for the health and well-being of our parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is merit to the ground-up consultative approach adopted by AfA, but, in parallel, more can already be done to correct systematic discrimination faced by single parents under the law.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One of these areas is the differential treatment currently accorded to unmarried single parents – often single mothers – in contrast to their peers who are single parents by virtue of divorce or who are widowed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This contrast shows up most starkly on the issue of housing access – with far-reaching consequences for both parent and child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, a stable home environment is one of the leading indicators of positive developmental outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At present, HDB recognises single-parent households of divorced or widowed parents as a family nucleus, for the purposes of public housing eligibility, as well as for access to public housing grants.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Outside of these concessions, unmarried single-parent households have to avail of the schemes targeted at singles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The eligibility schemes and grants targeted at singles are often more restrictive and have lower monetary amounts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the challenges that single parents face do not discriminate based on marital status and are, in fact, more pronounced, especially when we consider that single parents have to singlehandedly shoulder the burden of both being the primary caregiver and primary breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This struggle was experienced first-hand by one of my constituents who is an unmarried single mother with her daughter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She shared the challenges she has faced over the years and how she has fought to overcome them to do right by her child.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition to battling social stigmas and stereotypes, she was discouraged by the various Government policies, such as that for housing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a young father, I understand the trials and joys of parenthood, but I cannot begin to imagine the sheer weight of responsibility faced by single parents, such as herself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The challenges faced by unmarried single parents are large enough without the additional burden of being viewed differently in the eyes of the Government for access to public housing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Financial worries are not uncommon for single-parent households and every cent counts.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Families also qualify for the family grant, which can rise to $50,000, double the $25,000 maximum awarded to singles.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While HDB is free to assess cases individually and make exceptions if appropriate, it does not appear that the exception is commonly made.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is but one example of differential treatment under the law for unmarried single-parent households.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Elsewhere, single parents are not eligible for the Baby Bonus Cash Gift and Cash Gift Baby Bonus Plus, which amount to $8,000 in total.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Parenthood Tax Rebate and Working Mother Child Relief (WMCR) are also not extended to single parents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If the WMCR is to encourage married mothers to continue working after childbirth, the reality for many single mothers out there is that they simply cannot afford to not continue working after childbirth.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: No matter the express objectives of our Marriage and Parenthood policies to promote and strengthen the institution of family, and to encourage parenthood within marriage, children are not insulated from the impact of our policymaking.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is also these policies which could inevitably contribute to inequality at birth and beyond.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, I would like to raise my concerns on women's retirement adequacy and financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While women had higher average CPF balances as compared to men up to the age of 35, this could perhaps be explained by the roughly two years of National Service commitments or that women in these age groups are, generally, paid more favourably compared to men.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Men across all other age groups had between 6% and 35% higher average CPF balances, compared to women within the same age groups.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The gender gap in retirement adequacy, especially when we have a defined contribution type pension system linked to employment, is one which needs to be squarely addressed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is thus imperative that we redouble our efforts to strengthen social safety nets with an emphasis on adequate retirement adequacy for women.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On financial literacy, the OCBC Financial Wellness Index 2020 report found that only 60% of women surveyed had investments, compared to 75% of men, noting that more Singapore women than men see investing as gambling.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But for women with the confidence and knowledge to conduct their own investments, their investments do better than men.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This perceived lack of knowledge or confidence is also reflected in an earlier survey conducted in 2019 by UBS Wealth Management in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While 64% of women believe they would outlive their spouses, with most women heavily involved in household daily expenses, a dominant 72% let their spouses take the lead on long-term investment and financial planning decisions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the White Paper compared literacy rates for women between 1965 and 2021, given our social security system which emphasises on individual responsibility and self-reliance, I hope the Government will commission an in-depth study to examine the levels of financial literacy amongst Singaporeans, with a particular emphasis on empowering women to take charge of their own financial well-being.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allowing all Singaporeans access to a simple and fuss-free investment solution to earn higher expected returns for their CPF as envisioned by the CPF Lifetime Retirement Investment Scheme will also go a long way to enhance retirement adequacy for all, which, I believe, will also significantly benefit women who are less inclined to invest on their own volition today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To conclude, Mdm Deputy Speaker, the four issues I have raised – parental leave, providing support to parents beyond childbirth, supporting single-parent households and raising women's retirement adequacy and financial literacy – are not entirely new.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Around 200 years ago, the first organised women’s movement started in the UK.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They were called the suffragettes, fighting for suffrage or the right to vote.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It was only in the last century that women obtained the right to vote in most countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Women were also required to attend school and encouraged to join the workforce and did well in both areas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Women have enjoyed equal rights at law for a long time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, equality at law was the start of the journey.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Equal rights, in substance, are a longer journey and this White Paper facilitates that journey with concrete actions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The 25 action plans are comprehensive and touch on many of the issues women face today.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there are many initiatives I find interesting, I will focus on two broad areas in this speech, namely: (a) equal opportunities in the workplace; and (b) the recognition and support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In simple terms, these initiatives strive towards substantive equality at work and at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I had spoken in favour of anti-discrimination legislation in earlier debates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is relevant to many contexts, including protecting against discrimination based on gender, race, religion and, back then, it was nationality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the absence of legislation, MOM had given effect to the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices by linking companies’ rights to tap foreign workers to compliance with these guidelines.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, Singaporeans had to be given fair consideration before you could employ foreign workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Grievance handling procedures and protection of complainants will also be required.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I expect this will require a cultural shift amongst employers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For a long time, we had a strict contractual interpretation of employment rights and it was easy for employers to both hire and fire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, employers will need to make hiring and promotion decisions more carefully and, in practical terms, will likely need to properly document decisions to prevent allegations of unfairness.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also legislation envisioned in relation to FWAs and new tripartite guidelines that envision requiring employers to fairly consider requests for FWAs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many employers had to radically rethink their work arrangements over the last two years with the work-from-home requirements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Hopefully, the lessons learnt from this experience will not be lost but will, instead, be utilised when we return to business as normal.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Of course, flexible work is a lot more than just working from home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It includes the option to work shorter hours or fewer days in a week, which will require employers to put in more thought in the work scope of individual employees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Again, though, these FWAs should be equally available to men and women to be effective.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is so that, for example, in certain households, if men wish to play a bigger role in caregiving, they may also need to avail themselves of FWAs to play this role.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Otherwise, if FWAs apply only to women, it may have the perverse effect of forcing women to continue to bear the caregiving load using these arrangements.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is being done through changes in the listing rules and the Code of Corporate Governance.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Again, I note that diversity is not intended to cover gender alone, but also other forms of diversity, which I assume would also include race and professional backgrounds of members of the Board.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As Boards provide leadership to companies, having diverse boards would provide companies with a greater breadth of perspective as well as having a positive knock-on effect within the ranks of companies, as diverse boards are more likely to pick from a wider pool of talent for leadership and executive positions in the company as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These legislative changes detract somewhat from the "freedom to contract" model we have adopted in relation to employment law, but I believe that these are necessary derogations as these initiatives protect employees in vulnerable positions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The combination of more FWAs as well as fair consideration principles being legislated could go a long way to allow men and women the ability to remain in the workforce and not be embarrassed or discriminated against if they decide to take different work arrangements to attend to caregiving needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When we move from the workplace to the home, we also find that women often bear the bulk of caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second set of actions, 7 to 11, provide a wide-ranging suite of measures to lighten the caregivers' load.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The financial strain will be eased with grants, such as the Home Caregiving Grant and the expanded Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund, with further future support envisioned.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Access to affordable preschools is going to be enhanced and there is also a focus on the mental and physical health of caregivers, with support networks being set up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These options are important because they, significantly, ease the load many women carry at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Again, as with FWAs, I would suggest that all these grants and support be provided on a gender-neutral basis, so that if the caregiver at home is the man, these grants and support should be equally accessible to them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In addition, I would suggest that it may help to have support networks that are specific to male caregivers as they may face a different stigma from female caregivers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A newspaper feature on stay-at-home fathers who did the caregiving while their wives were the primary breadwinners highlighted the stigma that many of them face.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, these are the best examples of men supporting their wives with their aspirations and should be celebrated.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If this gets more normalised, this may have a much stronger impact on the overall journey to gender equality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   Last year, I discussed in this House the experiences shared with me in one of the dialogues on Women's Development that I attended with Ms Indranee Rajah with women from the Indian community.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of the issues raised now see benefits through direct action plans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Measures are also in place to protect those who speak out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additional support is also being rolled out for those caring for persons with disabilities and children with developmental needs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The above are just a few examples of changes in this wide-ranging paper that aims to create a more equal society for women, both at home and at work and support the important role they play in both areas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Deputy Speaker, I support this Motion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We are colleagues at the workplace, also mothers, wives, sisters and daughters to our families, Therefore, as we debate in this House about how we can better support women, we are, indeed, debating about how we can create a better future, not for Singapore women alone, but for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have made good progress in empowering women in Singapore and we should be proud of that.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, women make up almost half of the labour force, literally holding up half the sky.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many more women are entering and excelling in what are traditionally regarded as male-dominated sectors, such as STEM, construction, professional services and becoming leaders in their chosen fields, many of whom are in the Chamber today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will continue to encourage and support women in pursuing their career ambitions while respecting women's choices on the sectors that they wish to contribute to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Given our manpower constraints, it is crucial that we enable both women and men to be part of our workforce as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I share the story of a dear colleague of mine.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She lives with her retired husband and mother-in-law who has dementia and is bedridden.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Although they have a helper, her husband started to face burnout a few years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In her previous job, she felt extremely helpless as she was working long hours and was unable to work from home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She contemplated early retirement to better care for her family.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Thankfully, after changing jobs, things improved for her as she is now able to work from home regularly and is given time off to run errands when needed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: She appreciates the workplace flexibility that allows her to continue working and be financially independent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With a more balanced share of caregiving load in her family, everyone enjoys better physical and mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Experiences like this show how important FWAs can be.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With workplace flexibilities, women who are caregivers will be better empowered with the choice to continue working and progressing in their careers, thereby reducing career lags for women and helps to close the gender pay gap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: FWAs apply not just to women, but also to men.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With greater workplace flexibility, coupled with a supportive workplace culture that recognises both men and women have a role to play in caregiving, more of us will be able to manage work and family demands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is why we must press on with efforts to sustain workplace flexibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As safe management measures gradually eased, we may be tempted to revert to pre-pandemic ways of working.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, if we do so, we will lose the many benefits that FWAs bring to employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The tripartite guidelines will prescribe fair and proper practices that employers should adopt, such as having a proper process to assess employees' requests for FWAs and communicate the outcome of such requests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This will establish the norm that it is acceptable to request for FWAs while maintaining employers' prerogative to approve or reject the requests based on their business and operational needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Melvin Yong's suggestion to implement the tripartite guidelines on FWAs earlier, it is important that we take a calibrated and enabling approach to enhance access to FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to equip employers with capabilities to manage a more flexible workplace – not just remote work but also flexi-time and a flexi-work load – and also ensure that employees also understand the roles that they play in making FWAs sustainable for business operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should build confidence and capacity instead of seeking to use legislation for every workplace issue that arises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Otherwise, workplace disputes will arise and the mutual trust and understanding between employers and employees which we have carefully maintained over the years will be eroded.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over 10,000 companies have already adopted the tripartite standard on FWAs, covering more than one in four employees in Singapore today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We welcome more companies that are ready to come on board even before the tripartite guidelines are introduced by 2024.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Public Service has adopted the tripartite standard on FWAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Government also encourages and recognises companies with progressive HR policies, including FWAs, enhanced leave schemes for caregiving and sabbaticals, employee leave schemes, many of which were raised by Ms Poh Li San, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Louis Chua.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I think these are all positive steps and we encourage companies to do so if it suits their employees' needs and their business operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Alliance for Action for Work-Life Harmony has been championing these forms of work-life support since last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ultimately, companies with progressive policies will be able to better attract and retain talent, which is good for business.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: From the Conversations series on Singapore Women's Development, we also heard stories of how some women who chose to leave the workforce for a few years due to family reasons faced difficulties returning to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: All employers ought to practise fair and merit-based hiring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: If employers screen out applicants because of so-called resume gaps or last-drawn salary, they risk losing out on good candidates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: A better, smarter approach is to make a robust and fair assessment of each candidate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOM will continue to partner the Institute for HR Professionals (IHRP) to uplift HR standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will help HR professionals develop capabilities that allow them to better tap on back-to-work women as a talent pool.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For back-to-work women who are ready to return to the workforce, they can tap on Workforce Singapore's (WSG) and NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute's (e2i) career coaching and job matching services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: They can also benefit from Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs) to reskill for new jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: WSG will broaden its partnerships with various organisations, such as Mums@Work Singapore, Daughters Of Tomorrow and MENDAKI, to reach out to back-to-work women and support their journey to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I am heartened that there are organisations out there, such as NTUC Women and Family Unit, SHE BRILLIANCE and Financial Women's Association, that have been active in providing mentorship and career guidance to moms who are trying to come back to work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I think we need more of such community support to help uplift women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms He Ting Ru spoke about the gender wage gap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to do more to reduce the gender wage gap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need to take a multi-pronged practical approach towards this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We have heard of some countries that have legislated equal pay for equal work, such as in some parts of the US and Canada, but the adjusted pay gap remains higher than that in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In Singapore, we take a much more practical approach towards matters like this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Here, we are talking about strengthening workplace fairness, introducing and entrenching FWAs, working with industry partners and community partners and using education to encourage and empower women to take on jobs in growth as well as in STEM sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: After all, the main reason for the gender wage gap in Singapore is occupational segregation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I agree with Mr Louis Chua and I thank him for raising this point.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some women, because they are caregivers, may have had disrupted careers and, as a result, were not able to earn as much as their partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Aside from providing a supportive environment for caregivers to continue working, MOM has also taken steps to help caregivers build their retirement nest egg.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, we encourage cash top-ups to CPF accounts of caregivers through tax incentives and Government matching grants for eligible seniors, many of whom have been women who benefited from these schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Second, they can consider monetising their homes under the HDB Lease Buyback Scheme and the Silver Housing Bonus to unlock their housing value and enhance their retirement income.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Third, we supplement the retirement income of seniors who had low incomes during their working years and now have less in retirement through the Silver Support Scheme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For more women to succeed in their careers, we must also tackle discrimination and harassment at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some participants in the conversations shared that women still face prejudice due to perceptions that they would be less committed at work due to caregiving and pregnancy reasons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: When instances of discrimination or harassment were reported to their employers, some felt that their concerns were swept under the rug.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Others hesitated to come forward because they were afraid to lose their jobs or of "getting marked" by their colleagues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: All of us have a role to play.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We want to send a strong message of assurance that help is available and that those who seek help and recourse can do so safely and will be protected against retaliation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I must say this is really a long journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Looking as far as back as 2016 in Parliament, Mr Patrick Tay had already been pushing for anti-workplace discrimination legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, numerous times, various Members of Parliament in this House have raised this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I am really glad that, finally, we are taking that big step towards legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The committee is looking also at the legislation to include requiring employers to have a proper process to handle grievances reported by their employees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Like many of the shifts in the White Paper, the eventual workplace fairness legislation will not just benefit women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In giving greater assurance to women at work, we are also giving greater assurance to all workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, we all know that legislation is not a panacea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We need mindset shifts and collective action for real and sustained impact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As Ms Yeo Wan Ling highlighted, employers must educate and equip themselves, their supervisors and HR professionals to create fair, respectful and safe working environments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices (TAFEP) and the tripartite partners can help employers with this, with further support available for SMEs if they lack knowledge or the capacity in implementing proper policies and grievance handling processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I urge companies to take ownership and tap on such help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To individuals who encounter workplace harassment, TAFEP's Workplace Harassment Resource and Recourse Centre is here to provide advice and assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We assure you that you are not alone and it is safe for you to reach out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Our community partners, such as grassroots leaders, union leaders, Daughters Of Tomorrow, Mums@Work Singapore, SCWO, AWARE and more, are among those working with us to augment outreach and support to those affected by workplace harassment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Together, we are enlarging the safety net to protect and support women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As colleagues or friends, each one of us can make a difference, too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Instead, call out and stand up against unfair and unsafe work practices and support those who are affected.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should work towards a vision of zero workplace discrimination and harassment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Before I conclude, let me highlight our key actions in Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will enhance our systems so that our work environments are safe and free from harassment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: (In English): The benefits of our efforts will well extend beyond the workplace, where our children can grow up in more supportive family environments with greater parental involvement, where there will be stronger relationships between parents who share responsibilities at home, and where women and men partner each other as equals, progress together and pursue their aspirations freely and to the fullest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I am heartened to hear this joint call and commitment to action being strongly echoed by Members of Parliament who have spoken thus far.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, today, let us join hands as a society, regardless of our political affiliation, to commit to making our workplaces fairer and more inclusive, for an even stronger Singapore tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In my opinion, the policy and legislative changes that will be implemented have the ability to catalyse a mindset change in the whole community on how gender roles are perceived in today's context.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: To do so, we can, firstly, look at the gender pay gap.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Both the adjusted and unadjusted measures of gender pay gap are used for policy-making.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The gender pay gap was attributed to various factors.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Women frequently play the primary role of a caregiver, be it to their children, the elderly as well as those with special needs.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is significant and can be explained by occupational segregation.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Examples include the effect of occupational choices which may be dictated by a woman's multiple responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) in 2020 also shows further evidence of the motherhood penalty in which the gap widens, particularly when women reach their peak childbearing or childcaring ages.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: So, what can be done to narrow this gap?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am very heartened that the White Paper has taken a multi-pronged approach to tackle this.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, minority women may have to deal with biases due to gender as well as race.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In June 2021, a woman applying for a preschool teacher job was allegedly asked to remove her hijab at work.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, whether a woman decides to get married or start a family should not be asked in interviews or play a part in whether job opportunities are offered.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is disheartening that we are now in the 21st century and yet women are still having to contend with questions on their childbearing motivations at the workplace and upon being hired.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is very welcomed that we will be enshrining the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices in law.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so will afford better protection to women who are victims of discrimination and prevent retaliation against those who whistle-blow.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In particular, I would also like to ask if specific legislation and policies will be introduced for women going on maternity leave.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If there are cases in which a pregnant mother has to go on maternity leave, she should not be automatically given a lower band by default during her subsequent appraisal simply by virtue of taking what is a statutorily mandated leave.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Guidelines should be available for the employer to objectively evaluate her performance and for the employee herself to be able to fulfil them reasonably.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This can help to address the unequal pay or promotion which can slow down further career progression down the road.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, what provisions or measures can be introduced that would ensure women are not discouraged from taking their statutorily mandated maternity leave at risk of penalty to their career progression?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: While the White Paper champions autonomy of choice for women, I am concerned that women may be presented with a false choice and come under increased pressure to view their recovery during the duration of the maternity leave as optional, especially for women who aspire to hold leadership positions in future.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, they may either opt not to take the full duration of their maternity leave or choose to continue working throughout the duration of their maternity leave.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Anecdotally as well, it seems a handful of employers may encourage women to work throughout their maternity or seek to postpone or do away with their time away with the promise that doing so would lead to greater career progressions.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I think a stronger message needs to be sent that maternity is not an optional leave but one that is statutorily protected because Parliament recognises there is a need for women to recover from the procedures and many bodily changes introduced by pregnancy and labour.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There is a greater social good being encouraged by preserving the maternity leave for women and ensuring that it is observed.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: There are many ways FWAs can be implemented, whether flexi-place, flexi-time or flexi-load.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Being able to do so would allow employers to adopt the best practices to manage their workforce while, at the same time, allowing them to tap on talents that they may not have been able to traditionally.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is also a major step forward to weaken gender norms.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of work structures that reward employees for pulling more hours at work, a transition to one which is supportive of a family-friendly work culture would encourage both parents to balance work and family commitments.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, such benefits should not be solely used by women as the perceived costs of hiring them will increase.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Fathers are worried that it might affect their career prospects.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Employers also have to ensure that colleagues are willing to cover the fathers' duties in their absence.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that the White Paper will be tackling this aspect in Action 4.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, may I ask whether there are similar upcoming plans to ensure increased utilisation of FWAs, not by women, but by men as well?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This will be a strong signal to the community regarding the importance of shared gender responsibilities as equal partners as well as towards enhancing the support of women in low-income families as well.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, it is evident that everyone plays a part in the progress of women's development which is why I believe mindset change is the most critical step in this whole endeavour of policy, legislative and structural changes.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is reflected in the choices that we make every day.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Only with everyone taking a conscious step and working hand-in-hand will our efforts bear fruit much faster with far-reaching effects.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The White Paper encapsulates the collective aspirations of women in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Importantly, it tackles the deep and long-running concerns and stigma and discrimination our women face at home, at school, workplaces and the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Regardless of where women are in their lives, we, as a society, must support them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Importantly, we saw how FWAs allowed organisations to remain productive while allowing workers to juggle other commitments at home.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This alleviates the mental burden faced by women who are caregivers but, at the same time, it allows the husbands the opportunity to share the load.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Importantly, it can also encourage women who have not been working for some time to return to the working world with ease.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I commend efforts, such as Mums@Work, Career Navigators and MENDAKI Sense's back-to-work women programme, which mentor women who wish to get back to the working world, retain them, retrain them and partner companies to ensure a smooth transition.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I hope that the Government can push the deadline earlier and explore accreditation models for companies that support FWAs and have concrete back-to-work women HR policies within their organisations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Staff welfare clubs for women or the set-up of childcare arrangements within the building can also be implemented to allow women to have a strong support group within workplaces and allow their children to be near them while they work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I hope more companies can consider rolling them out to allow more women to return to the workforce.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When my mother was born, her father passed on soon after.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My grandmother raised seven children on her own.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: She was a religious teacher teaching Quranic recitation; she was a seamstress, sometimes doing clothes for free so that the children in the kampung can have nice clothes; she was somewhat an entrepreneur, she cooked and sold epok epok in the kampung, too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: She held a tight ship, ensuring ends meet and that the children were well cared for.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My mother, being the youngest, had sisters who were doubling up as mothers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In situations like this, the elder ones usually make way for the younger ones to support their education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Although things turned out okay for my family, I have seen families of similar profiles within my constituency who are facing challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: During a recent house visit, it pained me to find that the elder siblings who have yet to complete Secondary education, forgo their studies so that they can help with the family income.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There were also times I found children who were without preschool education due to multiple constraints faced by single parents.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We can help alleviate their worry and better support them mentally and emotionally by focusing our resources on supporting their children's well-being.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to get the children in school, focus on their studies and set them on the multiple pathways of success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, we can have more child-minding or student care services in schools and within clusters of low-income families, so that children from vulnerable families can get access to care conveniently while their mothers go out to work and focus on their careers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we can focus our resources on the well-being of children, I am optimistic that we can help our women from vulnerable families get back up and provide better for their families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, I welcome the tabling of this White Paper on Singapore Women’s Development and support all the actions being proposed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my English speech earlier, I have touched on two areas, namely, career aspirations and support for children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: More Malay women are now serving as members of the Mosque Management Boards, as well as Malay/Muslim bodies in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, compared to the number of men, the number of women has yet to reach 50% in terms of those becoming members of board of directors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In MUIS, five out of its 19 Council members are women.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What about the number of women appointed as members of the mosque management boards?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am thankful that during my service as a mosque Chairman in the past, I have worked with many capable women.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We already have a woman President of the Syariah Court.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, our President Mdm Halimah Yacob is ranked 37th on the list of 500 most influential Muslims in the world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Perhaps, it is time for us to have a woman mosque Chairman?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that more opportunities and spaces are open for our women to assume leadership responsibilities in our institutions, not just in MENDAKI, MUIS and mosques, but also in Malay/Muslim bodies and private companies, so that a diversity of opinions can be obtained through discussions and policy presentations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, we still see many single mothers and mothers from low-income families facing many challenges.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These include those who have to quit their jobs to look after their children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the tabling of this White Paper can further enhance support and assistance for women and children from needy families, especially in terms of providing more preschool and after-school childcare services.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To my fellow men out there – husbands, fathers, sons – let us ask ourselves what kind of future do we want to create and leave behind for our women, our daughters?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want our daughters to be respected, what are we doing within our homes or within the online space?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If we want our daughters to succeed in their careers, what kind of work culture are we practising in workplaces?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In general, we support the plans outlined in the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are a few areas we wish to add on.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The participation rate of women in the labour force has been rising over the years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women have taken on more economic responsibilities, but their share of caregiving and family responsibilities has not been decreasing correspondingly.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should not surprise anyone if this situation makes marriage and having children more daunting.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the White Paper correctly pointed out, mindsets on gender roles need to change.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our current parental leave structure reflects the old mindset that needs to change.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the mothers getting a much longer leave than fathers, it reinforces the idea that childcare is primarily the responsibility of mothers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The default equal share of parental leave between the couple underlines the belief that parenthood is a responsibility that should be shared equally by both parents.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Equal parental leave would also give less reason for employers to discriminate against female employees.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Various studies have shown the beneficial effect of fathers taking paternity leave and taking on a bigger role in parenting.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An NUS study found that children are less likely to have behavioural issues and fathers experienced reduced conflict, stronger family relationships and increased satisfaction in their marriage.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another study found mothers get improved maternal postpartum-depression outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2019, the take-up rate was only 55%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A key reason cited was work culture that does not support the taking of paternity leave.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should, therefore, look at incentives for employers to provide better work-life balance.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will move on to financial support for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Home Caregiving Grant is given to defray cost of caring for persons with disabilities who require assistance in performing three or more Activities of Daily Living.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This grant is given regardless of whether the caregiver is a paid professional, foreign domestic helper or an unpaid family member.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Therefore, it is more a financial support for the disabled person, rather than for the caregiver who may have had to give up a full-time job.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same applies to the Senior Mobility and Enabling Fund which subsidises the cost of mobility devices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can MOM provide the number and percentage of caregivers who received CPF top-ups each year and what was the average amount of the top-up?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this a measure we can rely on to ensure the retirement adequacy of caregivers?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, would the Government consider a scheme where a portion of the monthly CPF contribution of the working spouse is transferred to the caregiving spouse?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is fair for a married couple who share the responsibilities of family and work to also share the rewards.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A third area that I wish to bring up is that of foreign spouses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would like to see greater transparency in the criteria for residency for foreign spouses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the implementation of COMPASS, we have moved towards a more transparent model for approval of work passes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A similar move towards transparency on residency criteria for foreign spouses would benefit our citizens worrying over how to ensure long-term residency for their foreign spouses and the recurrent cost of visit passes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many good plans in the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the end of the day, we need to measure reality.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the indicators that will be tracked to monitor if we are achieving the objectives stated in the White Paper and what are the targets set?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, we can set a target for female representation on the Boards of Directors.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since Statutory Boards and IPCs can achieve about 30% female representation, it shows that 30% is a realistic target.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Listed companies have a female board representation of under 20%.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another area that is very important to most women would be the sharing of parenting and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Government be tracking and setting a target for this as well as the utilisation rate of maternity and paternity leave?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As I listen to them relate how they looked after their loved ones in their final years, I am filled with admiration for their immense dedication and sacrifice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken to an elderly wife who changed the stoma bags of her husband, who was a cancer patient, for a period of time until he passed on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have conversed with a son in his 50s, who changed his elderly mother’s soiled diapers several times a day, in a reversal of parent-child roles.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have a 72-year-old resident who continues to juggle her roles working as a cleaner and the sole caregiver to her disabled adult son and mentally incapacitated husband.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These unsung heroes press on out of filial devotion to parents, duty to spouses, responsibility to their adult children and, most importantly, love for their family members.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unlike caregivers of young children, caregivers of elderly or disabled persons face a heavier load over time as the health of their loved ones deteriorates.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They do not experience the same delight of young parents watching their children grow up.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their care recipients may not be able to express their appreciation well or may even inadvertently make hurtful remarks due to conditions like dementia.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For caregivers, every day brings new challenges and new heartaches, until that inevitable day when they see their loved ones pass on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Caregivers of children with disabilities face an additional stressor of worrying about who will care for their children if they outlive them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is a very heavy burden to carry.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We, as a nation, society and community, can and should do much more to share some of the weight on caregivers’ shoulders.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These percentages have surely gone up since then and will likely increase further, given our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I will focus on Area 2 of the White Paper – the caregiving aspect.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While caregivers in Singapore are more often women than men, I will not take a gender-specific approach to the problems or solutions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The role of caregiving does not solely apply to any gender and, most certainly, should not be borne only by women.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Unpaid caregiving of family members incurs substantial direct expenses and opportunity costs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The majority were women aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In his paper published in Insights in Public Health Journal, Dr Wayne Chong pointed out that unpaid informal caregivers of older adults not only pay the lion’s share of mental, emotional, social and financial costs of care, they also fork out non-trivial opportunity costs associated with caregiving, including lost wages, personal freedom and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is time for Singapore to provide a more comprehensive package of financial support and compensation to caregivers for their economic and social contributions to the nation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, employers play a big part in creating a society that values the contributions of caregivers and shares some of their burdens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All employers should provide FWAs for their staff to better balance work and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Managers should be given training to have a greater understanding of the unpredictable nature of caregiving so that they can be more empathetic towards their staff.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government aims to create a workplace norm where employees "feel it is acceptable to request for FWAs, while maintaining employers' prerogative to accept or reject requests taking into account their business needs." Can the Minister for Manpower clarify if this means that employers can reject FWA requests without providing valid reasons?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If so, it will give employers an escape clause from their FWA obligations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I repeat the call in the Workers’ Party’s 2020 Manifesto that all informal caregivers of elderly or disabled family members should be entitled to ask for FWAs that are feasible for their line of work and fair to both the employer and the employee.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Employers should be required to provide reasons if the request cannot be met.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It is in the interest of all organisations, large and small, to have meaningful FWAs in place.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Employers who fail to do so may lose capable employees to competitors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In fact, having good FWAs can be a company’s competitive advantage in attracting talent.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The underlying premise is the basic principle that "a happy worker is a productive worker".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Second, we need to legislate Family Care Leave.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Most caregivers remain in paid employment, which places extremely heavy demands on their time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The demands of both work and caregiving responsibilities are often concurrent, making it difficult to set aside one to handle the other.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Civil servants are currently eligible for two days of parent-care leave per year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, according to an MOM survey, only 20% of private companies offered such leave benefits in 2018.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
