text: There have been many calls for the legislation of Family Care Leave by Members of Parliament from the Workers' Party, PAP, Nominated Members of Parliament, as well as AWARE and the Singapore Alliance for Women in Ageing, among others.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government should legislate Family Care Leave soon.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will help in recognising that caregivers’ contributions are on par with that of parents with young children.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Family care leave can supersede the current Childcare Leave.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: An additional two days should be granted if the employee has more than one care recipient.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This means that if an employee has one child and one parent to care for, he or she will be entitled to eight days of paid Family Care Leave, of which three days are paid for by their employer and five days by the Government.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Government rejected previous calls to legislate eldercare leave, citing business cost concerns by employers, manpower constraints and the employability of caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Having the Government bear more costs of Family Care Leave will limit the financial strain on employers and minimise any employment discrimination against caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Third, we should recognise the skills and work experience of caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During the caregiving years, a caregiver gains important skills, such as people management, negotiation, conflict resolution and budgeting, as well as domain knowledge, such as healthcare, food and nutrition knowledge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Employers should consider caregiving experience as work experience, just like the Civil Service does for National Service, with corresponding salary increments.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Recognising caregivers’ skills and experience could also open up employment opportunities for them in the care sector, which, in turn, can contribute much-needed manpower to our health and social care system as our society ages.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Public Service should take the lead to steer this mindset shift, and the Government should encourage the private sector to do likewise.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such a paradigm shift will signal that caregiving is, indeed, valued by society.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fourth, we need to adjust our approach to financial support and compensation for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Caregivers should be provided more financial support to offset the costs of home-based caregiving.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This support should aim to match the subsidy given to patients in long-term care facilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To qualify, care recipients must require assistance to perform three or more Activities of Daily Living (ADLs), such as eating, bathing, dressing or toileting.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am also concerned that some patients with dementia may not qualify for HCG.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is because the behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, such as forgetting, impulsivity, wandering and getting lost, are different from the ambulatory and dexterity competencies of ADLs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: HCG is meant to defray the cost of caregiving expenses rather than financially compensate caregivers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, any financial compensation schemes in place are mainly through family members, such as the Retirement Sum Topping Up Scheme.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Over and above financial support, family caregivers should receive some form of financial compensation for their caregiving work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This would mean allowing them to claim a modest allowance on top of HCG so that they will have more savings for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the caregiver and their family members are low-income earners, the Government should step in to top up their CPF Special Accounts or Retirement Accounts, without the need for matching contribution by family members.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fifth, home-based caregiving services must be made more accessible to all households, especially lower-income ones.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper proposes broadening the Household Services Scheme (HSS) to include basic child- and elder-minding services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the HSS is not currently subsidised by the Government, even though households likely to benefit most are those without the means to employ a live-in domestic worker.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At $20 an hour or more, the cost of home-based caregiving services is a stretch for many such households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MSF should extend means-tested subsidies to Singaporean families which procure home-based caregiving services for their elderly or disabled family members, if those members are not able to attend centre-based programmes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By caring for their loved ones at home, caregivers save the Government subsidies it would otherwise disburse to care centres.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of these savings can be passed on to families by increasing subsidies for home-based care.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sixth, short-term and ad hoc respite care services will allow caregivers to run errands, respond to unexpected developments or just get a short break from caregiving.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All full-time caregivers deserve an option to take a day off a week, where they can draw on a shared pool of suitably-qualified respite home care workers or place their loved ones in care centres during their day-off.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Full Government subsidies should be made available to those from lower-income households.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Currently, respite care services are provided at some senior care centres and nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a very small number, considering there are some 210,000 caregivers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many requests for respite care did the Agency for Integrated Care receive in 2021?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is there sufficient public awareness of the availability of respite care services?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What plans does the Government have to expand the availability and accessibility of respite care?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some elderly caregivers lack the strength to even lift their disabled spouses or adult children to bathe or transfer them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some elderly care recipients are single, with no children to care for them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There continues to be high demand for nursing homes and adult disability home places in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How much of our population's future demand will this expansion meet?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: What are the Ministries doing to ensure that care homes are able to attract enough qualified professionals, including Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, they continue to press on, out of love and duty to their family.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a nation, we will need a paradigm shift in our thinking towards caregivers and share some of their burdens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the support of the Government, businesses, community and Singaporeans, we can strive to be a more inclusive society and better recognise the sacrifices of our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.58 pm until 5.20 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not need to speak about the history of women's rights in Singapore or the issues women face, the details are in the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are important, but the topics have been well-covered.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, the psychological significance of the White Paper and, secondly, I will update the House on our approach to violence which is targeted at women in the family context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, on the psychological significance of the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you try and deal with large issues, like equality of men and women, one, you have to make a list of specific things that need to be done to achieve the end goal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the White Paper lists the many areas where more action needs to be taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The House has discussed them and I am sure will continue discussing them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To get a change in thinking at the individual level and to have it deeply set in is never easy.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Are we able to say that equality for women is part of our culture that is deeply set in?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the answer is, it is still work in progress.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the process we started in September 2020 has moved the needle, quite some.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The progress women have made in many fields since then has made the idea of equality more real.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The scale, the depth of the Conversations and follow-up have registered in our collective consciousness.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has helped in the process of our collective psyche in accepting equality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you want to know whether something is fundamental and accepted by most, you test it by checking.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I were to ask this question to a group of right-minded people, will they say, "Yes, of course, it is so", or will they express different views?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they will say, "Yes, of course, this is so", then that is your answer.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you apply that to the idea of equality for women in Singapore, after the Conversations and the White Paper, if someone were to stand up in a group in Singapore and ask about equality for women, will people say, "Obviously, yes"?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or put it another way – in a mixed group of right-thinking people, how many will dare to say, "Men and women should not be equal"?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is an achievement that, regardless of whatever one may personally think, if people realise that expressing a contrary view would be against social norms, that means people understand what the norms are.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we must not underestimate the power of such collective norm building.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Conversations and the White Paper have helped a fair bit in this process.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over time, if properly acted upon, that can change behaviour on how men and women perceive women and their roles.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The current situation in Singapore may look like, well, this is normal, this is the natural order of things.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the US, a headline in the last few days caught my eye, that women now have to travel outside the state they stay in, in some places, to get abortions because of tighter and tighter rules on abortions in some of these states.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The issue of a woman's right to have a medical procedure autonomy of her body versus a life, is subject to laws in many countries, including Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it gets difficult when the issue becomes politicised and if you tilt too far away from giving autonomy to a woman over her own body.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Singapore, a woman's autonomy is given considerable weight.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you move to Australia, another matter that has received some attention is the experience of women in the Australian parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am referring to these examples not to criticise other systems and approaches.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am looking at them as illustrations which can remind us of choices we have made, we make on the journey we have travelled and can travel.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Coming back to Australia, there were several allegations about how women were mistreated in the Australian parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In November 2021, a report, known as the "Jenkins Report", was published on what has happened in the Australian Federal Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It sets out in graphic detail some of what happened, quite shocking really.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have prepared an annex that lists some examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the list, an MP leaning over, grabbing the victim and stuck his tongue down her throat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a member of parliament doing this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At an after-work drinks session, a senior party member put his hand up the victim's skirt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A male colleague asked the victim intrusive questions about her personal life and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Leaders made jokes about employees' sex life, asked them out for dates, propositioned them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parliamentarian was completely naked when a worker walked into his office and addressed the worker as if nothing untoward, and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For us here in Singapore Parliament, you can understand this is quite unthinkable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not mean that in a self-congratulatory way, nor do I seek to draw any conclusions on morality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just looking at it, factually, our laws and framework and what we expect of behaviour in Parliament, all are different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the consequences, if you breach our laws, are quite severe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can expect to be caned if you are a man; and I will come back to the examples here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the conduct in the Federal Parliament of Australia, one is tempted to ask: is this the result of a different culture on how women are perceived and can be treated?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know enough to draw any conclusions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Members can see, where we are in Singapore and the road we are on, was and is not pre-ordained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is because of the choices we made and the work we have put in to treat women properly, with respect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members look at the examples, on the right-hand column, in Singapore, just a couple of examples – a man, previously with NUS, holding a PHD.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In another case earlier this year, a masseur molested a customer during a massage session.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We look at it in the context of how we treat women and what the laws are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of these fit in together to make sure that there is a certain status, respect and expectation of behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will refer to Australia in another context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, in one of the conversations that I took part in, there was an Australian lady.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was taken aback by what she said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said – and these are in the notes that our civil servants take – and I quote verbatim, "to Minister's question on her experience in Australia in terms of career opportunities for women as well as support for mothers, the lady said that Singapore offered much better opportunities and support for women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Companies in Australia often took a male-centric perspective and women tended to be politically disadvantaged, especially in rising to leadership positions." Again, a small vignette.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we move forward to the UK, I can recount to the House what a relatively senior female diplomat from the UK told me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, quoting from the notes, "on caregiving, Minister said that we were exploring how we could provide better support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One way was to recognise the caregiving role in monetary terms" – I will skip her name – "said that UK had not seriously discussed the question of monetary compensation for caregiving." On my list of examples, let me also share some things that have happened recently in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I say Malaysia, Singaporeans and, probably, Members of Parliament, too, sometimes tend to say on social issues, Malaysia is not a real comparison because we have taken different paths on social issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We were part of the same country until 1965.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were deliberate choices and they have led to very different results, and that is worth reflecting on to consider carefully what path we should continue on and what we can do to strengthen the respect and the idea of equality for women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will refer to two events: one early in the pandemic and one just a few weeks ago for Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In March 2020, Malaysia, like Singapore, was dealing with the pandemic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Movement Control Order, I think, had been in place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Malaysian Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development posted infographics on social media on how to ensure harmonious households.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a document that was obviously intended to be serious and it gave advice to wives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ministry's post, as you can imagine, drew a lot of response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I understand it, Doraemon is a male robot cat, so, not quite sure why women should speak like a male robot cat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were many takes on the ministry's post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With Speaker's permission, can I have this video shown?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Besides this, the same ministry, on 18 March 2020 also stated that only the head of the household should leave the house to purchase necessities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think almost in every household, the man assumed that that was them and only them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Fast forward to this year, 22 February, the Malaysian Deputy Minister, again from the same ministry, the Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development, she gave this advice to husbands and wives, that husbands should try the "physical touch" approach by striking their wives "gently" and to discipline them if they do not stop "unruly" behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And wives should seek husbands' permission before speaking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And wives should speak to their husbands only when the husbands are calm and relaxed, and after the husbands have eaten and prayed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Members will not even consider it possible for either MCCY or MSF to issue such statements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People may think this is a joke, but the differences in approach underlie and make a serious point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The path taken in 1961 and continued has led us to a very different place in terms of how we in Singapore view women and what we consider acceptable to say to women about how women should behave.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The White Paper pushes us further along that road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our cultural norms are now different from Malaysia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have, as opinion leaders, the power to strengthen and solidify those norms with more action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can look at positive examples from other countries for us to emulate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of them are in Scandinavia, not in all aspects, but in some important aspects.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is still much we can learn from others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To summarise my first point, Sir, the impact on norms and values, the internalisation of the idea of equality – I see that as among the most important outcomes from this process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the whole, if you look at women and how they perceive their safety and security, we have done well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have told the House before, SPF does regular surveys.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have made several legislative changes to give better protection to women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just touching on the changes in the last three years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2019, we amended the Penal Code to deal with sexual crimes which use technology; we repealed the marital immunity for rape; we introduced enhanced penalties for offences against victims in an intimate or close relationship with the offender.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Usually, women were the victims, even though the legislation is neutral about which sex.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the same year, we amended the Protection from Harassment Act to enhance protection for victims of harassment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The victims are, again, usually women or, quite often, young women.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Last year, we increased the penalties for sexual offences, including outrage of modesty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for today's purposes, I will deal specifically with violence in the family context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For violence at home, women, again, are more likely to be the victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proportion or ratio is three to one, roughly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members would have read about some cases which were in the news.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A woman was abused by her husband on several occasions – punched her, held scissors to her face, cut her hair while holding onto her head.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An elderly mother was abused by her adult son for years, starved, not allowed to shower, physically assaulted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She did not report him to the Police, despite volunteers asking her to, because she said she did not want to affect her son, despite suffering all this abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The task force came up with 16 recommendations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One common situation, for example, is the threat of violence at home or in a flat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The husband is angry, he is threatening violence; the woman fears for her safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Police turn up at that point, nothing much can be done because if there is no actual violence and no imminent threat of violence, then it is very difficult to do anything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Her husband denies it anyway that he is going to hit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The woman and the children stay in the same flat in fear, and then something bad can happen.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once these measures are able to be implemented – the task force's recommendations – MHA and MSF will respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the situation is serious, if there has been violence, it may proceed as a criminal case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We try not to criminalise all of these situations because that then does, quite often, irreparable harm in the family context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But where it is necessary, it is processed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is no actual violence but there is a significant threat of violence, the wife may be offered the option of being moved to a safe space, depending on the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be her choice even if there is no criminal offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She has the option that she can take the children and leave immediately, go into the safe space, then consider her next steps, instead of facing the threat of violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could also include moving to a temporary shelter arrangement while working out longer-term interventions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That gives the parties the opportunity to cool down, provides an opportunity for reconciliation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see, however, what we hope to achieve.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For a woman in Singapore to be truly unencumbered to pursue her aspirations and make real choices in her life, we need to address challenges that many women still face today and facilitate the path for her to seek opportunities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I join this debate to speak on two salient challenges: coping with caregiving duties and seeking a safe digital space.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Their contribution is part of what makes Singapore a thriving and caring society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am encouraged to see many men share caregiving responsibilities at home as husbands, sons and fathers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, some stereotypes remain and women continue to take on a higher load.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: During the Conversations on Women's Development, many women shared that they struggled with balancing what they were traditionally expected to do as caregivers against achieving their aspirations, and often had to choose one over the other.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They hoped men and women could take on a more equal share of caregiving duties.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am glad to hear the calls made by my colleagues in this House for men and women to partner each other as equals.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Each family should find their own balance, with family members pitching in to care for loved ones and giving each other real choices to pursue their aspirations, regardless of gender.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a vision we must continue to work towards.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government understands that caregiving can be a heavy load to shoulder alone.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We need to provide more support to caregivers, both men and women alike, so that they can find the balance between caregiving and pursuing their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some may choose to dedicate more time to caregiving.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Greater support will help them to manage the load better.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Minister Masagos Zulkifli earlier shared about efforts to support families with young children.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Allow me to share more about our plans to strengthen support for caregivers of seniors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We are proud to be a society where children feel an innate sense of responsibility to care for their elderly parents, but this duty can be challenging.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will build on these efforts to recognise and empower caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Caregiving can be a long journey – a marathon, rather than a sprint.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Crystal Lee is one example of a caregiver who has had a long caregiving journey.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She started at the young age of 13, caring for her father, who suffered from various cancers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Later on, she also took care of her mother who suffered from a stroke.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More than 20 years later, Crystal continues to care for her mother.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Crystal shared that her mother goes to the nearby day care centre, giving Crystal time to rest and recharge.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She also taps on the Home Caregiving Grant (HCG) to help her reduce her care costs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These alternative care arrangements have given Crystal space to pursue her hobbies and continue working as a part-time nurse.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Today, we have a range of eldercare and respite care services that help to ease the caregiving load of caregivers like Crystal, allowing them to rest and pursue other goals, with peace of mind that their loved ones are well cared for.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This provides another option for caregivers to tap on to take a break.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Nonetheless, some caregivers shared during the Conversations that they were unaware of the respite options available.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Others hoped to access respite care more readily.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Over the years, we have expanded the capacity and range of eldercare services to meet the care needs of our seniors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many seniors and their caregivers have benefited from these services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Gerald Giam have asked whether our care infrastructure will continue to be sufficient.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, as our population ages, the caregiving load on families will grow.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Household sizes are also shrinking, with fewer members to share caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many of our seniors also prefer to age-in-place at home.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We want to continue to fulfil their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To do so, we need to build on the range of services and support structure in place today, to better care for seniors at home.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some seniors may be less mobile and need more help with activities of daily living throughout the day.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Others may need support beyond the typical service hours of their nearby day care centres.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together with the various initiatives announced in the White Paper, we aspire to provide wraparound care for seniors residing within the community, even for those with higher care needs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This way, our caregivers can continue caring for their elderly loved ones in the community, instead of in nursing homes.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Another area of concern is financial support for caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our caregivers care for their children and elderly parents out of love and not for hope of reward.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This value of family support and filial piety is something we should continue to treasure and uphold.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Nonetheless, caregivers shared that they feel the financial strain of caring for their loved ones at home, in spending on care options and daily necessities.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More financial support can go a long way to help caregivers obtain the help they need to ease their caregiving journey.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2019, the Government rolled out the HCG to defray caregiving costs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The grant has since supported more than 39,000 beneficiaries.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In February 2022, we also rolled out an expanded Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund, which is expected to benefit more than 38,000 seniors in 2022.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Since then, we have reviewed the HCG and enhanced it to recognise caregivers' contributions and further reduce caregiving costs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Members of the House have expressed their support for this enhancement, and rightly so.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The enhanced HCG builds on multiple layers of financial support provided today to defray the costs of care for those living at home.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As a start, the Government already provides generous means-tested subsidies of up to 80% for centre- and home-based eldercare services.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Other support includes grants and insurance schemes like CareShield Life and ElderShield.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together, these go a long way in helping to lighten the financial load on caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Some Members have made suggestions calling for even more financial support.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These are not new propositions requiring paradigm shifts.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have and will continue to study these carefully.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, we must recognise that any additional support comes at a cost and will raise our long-term healthcare expenditure and impose pressure on our fiscal resources.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Beyond helping caregivers afford the help they need today in their caregiving journey, we also need to ensure they are cared for, especially in their old age.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Those who have cared for their loved ones for most of their life may have lower savings for their own retirement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government has put in place various initiatives to help build up the retirement adequacy of Singaporeans, including older caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Silver Support Scheme provides quarterly payouts to seniors who had low incomes during their working years and now have less in retirement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Families can also play a part by topping up the CPF accounts of their loved ones.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will support you with tax incentives and matching grants for eligible seniors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Caregivers of seniors and those with mental health conditions can look to the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) as a one-stop resource, be it for referrals to care services, applying to financial schemes, or tapping on respite care options.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: MOH and AIC will also build on existing caregiver support networks and outreach teams to provide more sustained support.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To improve visibility of these efforts, AIC and MOH will launch a publicity campaign starting this year, to raise awareness of available resources and where to seek help.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This is a journey we need to embark on together to support our caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Employers can be more understanding towards caregivers who need flexible work arrangements (FWA) because of their caregiving commitments.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: When like-minded caregivers are brought together, they can provide a listening ear, share experiences and even lend a helping hand.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Minister of State Low Yen Ling will share more about the Government's plans to form community-based peer support networks for caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Together, as a community, we can lighten the load for all caregivers.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In Malay):   I thank my colleagues for sharing their views on the need to support Malay/Muslim women.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We have, indeed, sought perspectives from all levels of society in Singapore and across various groups, including the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Hence, we had also involved groups, such as PPIS and the Muslim Youth Forum, in the discussion.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Besides Government initiatives to support the development of Singapore women, community efforts through our M3 agencies and Malay/Muslim organisations have further strengthened support for women in the areas of marriage and parenthood, employment and others.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, in employment, we have strengthened support for women to return to work through the Back-To-Work Women programme by MENDAKI, which provides opportunities for women to gain new skills and suitable jobs.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many women are strong and resilient and can uplift themselves if given the opportunity.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Therefore, we see more women being appointed as leaders, including in religious institutions and Malay/Muslim community organisations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In 2019, for the first time, a woman, Ustazah Dr Rohana Ithnin, was appointed as one of the four full members in the Fatwa Committee of the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The achievement of women is something that we can be proud of.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We will continue to enhance and build on efforts to empower Malay/Muslim women to achieve their aspirations.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I would now like to address the issue of enabling all women to navigate the digital world confidently and safely.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Singapore's digitalisation journey has benefited many women by unlocking new employment opportunities, such as in the cybersecurity and technology sectors.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Digitalisation has also enabled many women to better manage their responsibilities at home and work.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, as more of us go "digital", some have, unfortunately, fallen victim to online harms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann explained how women have been particularly impacted by this phenomenon.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Government seeks to build a digital society where everyone can have a positive digital experience.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Whole-of-society efforts like the Digital for Life movement, which brings together partners from the people, private and public sectors, are needed to nurture a safe digital space for all.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The Sunlight Alliance for Action (AfA), which I co-chair with Senior Minister of State Sim Ann, was launched in support of the Digital for Life movement.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: To date, AfA’s work covers Public Education, Victim Support, Youth Engagement, Research and Volunteerism.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann has elaborated earlier on the importance of creating a supportive environment for all women online, as we do in the real world, and how the community has worked together through AfA to ensure women and girls benefit from our increasingly digitalised society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Apart from Sunlight AfA, we have also seen various community partners contribute to the ecosystem to tackle online harms.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: These include the Defence Guild SG, which was launched in June 2021 by a group of lawyers following an offensive online poll sexualising women asatizah.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Member of Parliament Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim is part of this effort.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition to initiatives by the community, legislation is also needed to enhance online safety.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Many countries, such as Germany, Australia and the UK, have introduced or are looking into new regulations to tackle harmful online content.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Closer to home, the desire for enhanced measures to protect users from online harms is strong.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In addition, respondents felt that companies and platforms have the most room for improvement in tackling the issue.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Given the fast-evolving digital landscape, continued research will be critical in generating insights to help us protect our people in online spaces.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: However, some stereotypes and challenges remain that impede our progress in creating a fairer and more equal society.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: As we mature as a society, our mindsets need to change collectively.

speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Communications and Information and Minister for Health (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Everyone has a part to play, be it in caregiving or in ensuring a safe digital space for all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, let me ask, what is the place of women in our lives?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will share a bit of my own circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My grandfather and grandmother, they had nine sons, I have no aunties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Of whom, my father was the second eldest.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They lived in a kampung in Lorong Chuan, now part of Aljunied GRC.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I grew up watching the men in my family breed fishes, plant vegetables, rear livestock, repair cars, there was a workshop in our kampung.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the women cook, clean, look after the children.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There was "men's work" and there was "women's work".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, when my grandfather fell gravely ill, I saw it was my aunties, that means my uncles' wives, particularly my 阿姆, in Teochew, who took care of him.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, when he died and during the last rites, I could see the men and the women had distinct roles and there were protocols during the last rites observed at the funeral.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, from young, I felt some dissonance because I was in Primary school then and, at that time in class, there was hardly any differentiation between boys and girls.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If anything, the girls were often the better students while the boys were more playful and many of us were struggling to keep up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: School lessons at that time already included stories like 花木兰, Marie Curie.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And so, from a young age, we had both men and women as our role models.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, my parents moved into their own flat in Toa Payoh, next to a temple.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, my mother was the outlier, the only woman in the family.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But what changed was her role in the family.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She was a teacher, which meant she had to go to school very early in the morning, came home, marked the examination papers, marked the homework and then cooked, cleaned, looked after my brother and me; and also coached us in our homework.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in her, I saw a very strong woman who, in her world, carved out a role for herself that was equal but different from my father.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To me and my brother, she was our disciplinarian and also our anchor.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Growing up, therefore, my family was mainly men, and women were the outliers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My wife and I had our own children and the situation changed completely.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, today, after my parents' passing, the people I love most in this world are all women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The dissonance I felt as a kid, slowly developed into a deeper understanding of the struggles and aspirations of women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am not sure I totally get it, but I am trying to get it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After all, in Singapore, our daughters have a good education.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are growing up in a world where women can be CEOs, professionals, leaders of nations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as parents, we will support them to fulfil their ambitions and their aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But soon, I realised it was not so simple.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I saw it through the eyes of our daughters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One example was when our daughters were just toddlers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During Chinese New Year visits, relatives would glance at them and then turn to my wife and ask, "When are you having sons?" My wife will always reply, "I am happy with two daughters!" And I know our daughters heard those conversations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, as a young girl, my elder one, when she first learnt of the concept of dowries, she had a shock.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not know how it came up.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And she started asking, "Why must the groom's family give the dowry?" We are talking in terms of Chinese tradition, "Why the four pieces of gold for the Teochews, why the roast pig for the Cantonese and Hakkas?" She had all these burning questions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My wife calmly answered, "Because in Chinese tradition, the girl marries out." That got her even more upset.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She said, "So, this is like a transaction?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will be sold?" I tried to make things better by explaining, "The money can flow both ways.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And in some cultures, it is the bride's side that provides the dowry in recognition that the husband will incur costs in taking care of the bride."   It was not a helpful intervention.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would say, if this was a supplementary question, it was a very badly answered supplementary question.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And these are beyond Government policies and legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, policies and legislation, especially those in Singapore, are meant to remove discrimination and promote equality.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, we have biases deeply embedded in our social practices and our constructs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think they probably had their roots in nomadic bands, where the men mainly hunted; the women mainly gathered.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then, these roots probably grew deeper in agrarian tribes, where the men mainly ploughed the fields and the women took care of domestic matters.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The tribes decided to come together to form complex societies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And then, the key problem statement was: how do we, as different tribes, live peacefully together and not kill one another?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The answer is to make everyone stakeholders of a stable and peaceful society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that stake is the betterment of the family, of whom members are bonded by blood and DNA.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It follows, therefore, that blood lines must be drawn to define the family.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The basis to do so in most societies was the patriarchal structure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The expectations of sons carrying the family line, daughters marrying out, dowries flowing whichever way, sons having the greater share of inheritance – often, protected and reinforced the system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot undo all these longstanding anthropological practices and history in one generation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But no matter how entrenched, that past is challenged by the present.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think there are at least three driving forces: one, education; and two, technology.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And they combine in a powerful way to force a rethink of the status quo.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Young girls in Singapore grow up in an environment that their grandmothers would not have imagined when they were children.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Education has become the great equaliser of most societies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With equal opportunities for education and development, women are now able to enter vocations and professions that were, historically, male-dominated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And education, as a driving force, is now turbo-charged by the advancement of technology.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What used to require physical strength can now be automated or done by machines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, neither men nor women are better at numerical calculation, more empathetic or more meticulous.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is individuals that have varied strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During that time, I met many women engineers working in LTA, SMRT and SBST.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I was Education Minister, I met many male students training to be nurses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And, now, as Health Minister, I see many of them serving in hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In my GRC, we have two successful women: one, Mariam Jaafar, who was trained as an engineer; two, Poh Li San, she was a Super Puma helicopter pilot.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The lines that were once perceived between male and female-dominated occupations are blurring and, the overlap, I believe, will enlarge over time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The patriarchal structure will evolve faster if people now conclude that, as a society, if we treat men and women more equally, it is better for the welfare of our families and our loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Society must also play a part, that means, you and I – everybody, every family.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are many BTO units and many young couples have moved into them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I can see many husbands are now significantly involved in household and child-minding responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some families even have a breadwinner mother and a stay-at-home father because this is the best play of the family's strength – unheard of in my growing up years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Employers can decide, without the compulsion of law, that it makes better business sense to get rid of gender bias in hiring, promotion, appointment to boards and succession planning.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Having said that, the push for greater equality between men and women is a nuanced and long-term exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have highlighted the existence of societal biasness that we need to correct.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But at the other end of the spectrum, there are inherent differences between women and men that cannot be ignored and should, in fact, continue to exist.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I often say to people who tell me that they would like to serve the poor as I do," and Mother Teresa would tell them: "What I can do, you cannot.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But together we can do something beautiful for God.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is just the way the differences between women and men." Many women I know, including my wife, are against gender biasness in society, but they will also fiercely guard the difference between women and men.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because they know daughters have a special bond with their parents that is different from the relationship that sons have.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A woman, in a room full of men, is often able to articulate a different perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It comes from carrying the child for nine months, manifested in a mother wanting to nurse the child after birth.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is by a Hollywood star, Denzel Washington.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: He was paying a tribute to his late mother in one of the talk shows, I think.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And he said this, I quote, "A mother is a son's first true love" when he is born; "a son is a mother's last true love" when she dies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Single or married, mothers or women without children – women have special roles to play in their families and society because of these differences between women and men.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, where does recognising inherent differences stop, and biasness and stereotypes begin?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a very difficult and sensitive question, which I have no answer to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: During this debate, we hear many examples, many suggestions: how about enhancing this scheme, that scheme?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But let us have that broader philosophical question in mind.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We want to get rid of biasness but there are also inherent differences between women and men, beautiful differences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We only catered for maternity leave in our Employment Act decades ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And that was a world where women needed to recuperate after childbirth, and where child-minding and taking care of the infant were mostly performed by women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2022, should we, therefore, declare all these as family leave, to be equally shared between men and women?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Is it equality or are we no longer recognising that there is still a difference between men and women?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, let us be wise when we make such suggestions and choices.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On this, let us also have some perspective.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is not difficult to ask for more subsidy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Taking the Home Care Grant (HCG), for example, $400 is not enough, increasing from $200 to $400 is not enough, so, let us increase some more, give to more people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: From a technical perspective, the HCG is not universal but broad-based.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No doubt, if you transfer someone from a nursing home to a homecare environment, the Government saves on subsidies and we can think about how to help such individuals and such families more.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when you implement HCG, it does not cater to just this group.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is, actually, quite broad-based – whoever meets the means-tested criteria is eligible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we will continue to find ways to support families: from housing to education to, generally, having a safe, peaceful environment to bring up children as well as for homecare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, let me speak as a man, to fellow men.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I say let us all be stakeholders in a fair and equal society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the most basic level, let us respect women through our words and actions.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Offences against women are clearly wrong and the vast majority of us agree with that.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Perhaps what is less obvious is the occasional insensitive remark that reflects an unconscious bias or stereotype.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Understand and see things from a woman’s point of view.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Stop mansplaining, using diminutives, or doing things in the presence of women that they feel embarrassed by.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Let us be more proactive in supporting the women in our lives, just as they support us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This could mean undertaking the roles that society often expects women to do, like household chores, parenting, arranging for food during a gathering or conference or Parliament Sitting.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many men already do these things and we can, certainly, do more as equal partners in society, and in solidarity with women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I may be old-fashioned, but I personally think there is much virtue in men extending a special courtesy to women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To be honest, I often feel uneasy, just because I am a Minister, that people, including my female staff, will attempt to carry my bag or open the door for me.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I will always try to stop them and offer to open the door for them instead, often reminding them etiquette comes before protocol.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It does not lessen the person at the receiving end or imply that they cannot do it themselves!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are perfectly capable of doing it themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Instead, it adds a certain appreciation and complementarity to the relationship between women and men.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to make a special shout-out to our youths, having met many of them during my time as Minister for Education.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I say to them: be kind to all your friends, accord respect and courtesy to one another, listen to the views of everyone, girls and boys, keep the games and the jokes appropriate and tasteful – not from your point of view, but from theirs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sexual offences are a rising problem amongst your generation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The boys might be uncomfortable with hearing this, but I think it is important you hear this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Never be part of the problem, but be part of the solution.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When in doubt, always do the right thing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Watch out for the girls and, if it is late at night, offer to walk them to the bus stop, to the MRT station or to their destinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But on those rare occasions where you take a photo with your class, your CCA group or with the Minister, do not let the girls kneel in front and you stand at the back comfortably.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Or at least position yourselves freely as equals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Safe management measures (SMM) restrictions are now lifted, you can now take group photos again without one-metre spacing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A poem was written about her called "The Ballad of Mulan" or 木兰辞.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I thought the last few lines are particularly meaningful.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Chinese, it goes like this: 雄兔脚扑朔, 雌兔眼迷离； 双兔傍地走，安能辨我是雄雌!

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Roughly translated, it says: when you catch hold of a rabbit, the male will kick its legs; if you catch hold of a female rabbit, it will close its eyes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when they run side by side, you cannot tell which is male and which is female.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This was written in 400 AD, during the era of Northern Wei (北魏).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Even in highly patriarchal ancient China, there was recognition that there are inherent differences between men and women.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But there are many roles that can be equally performed by both women and men.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As our daughters grow up and start their own families, they will likely face the same dilemma as many women today, juggling multiple responsibilities and feeling guilty if they fall short of being the "superwoman" who can handle it all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But if my daughters decide as a life priority to start a family and spend more time as mothers to bring up their children, even at the expense of their career progression, I will be immensely proud of them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And if they decide they prefer to be single and use their talents to contribute to community and society, I will also be immensely proud of them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But whichever priority they put greater weight on, whatever life course they choose, they should not be pressured to do so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In that speech, I touched on how women tend to "leak out" of the promotion pipeline at the mid-career stage because the mid-career period tends to coincide with the stage of their lives where women experience heavy maternity and family commitments.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Due to these commitments, many of them either exit the workforce, take on an involuntary career slow-down or are assigned to what some may call the "mommy track" by their companies.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because of these reactions, the career gaps between women and men widen as the organisational hierarchy progresses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It would be that FWAs in the form of working from home and such hybrid work arrangements where time is spent between working from home are working out just as well as being physically present in the office, which is the more traditional working arrangement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many Members of this Chamber have already talked about FWAs and, indeed, FWAs are covered and highlighted in the White Paper.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: FWAs might just be the right solution that enables women in their mid-career to have the best of both worlds.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, as we are also lauding the merits of FWAs because they enable women to manage both their work and their family commitments, we need to be mindful also that there could be potential downsides for women when FWAs are applied in too broad strokes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A 2017 article written by Singaporean researchers from the Human Capital Leader Institute (HCLI) published in the Global Talent Competitiveness Index by INSEAD, highlighted the need to have a more nuanced approach when implementing pro-family policies to support women.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, for women in their mid-career to truly benefit from FWAs, companies need to be cognisant of the potential impingement of the formation of informal professional networks that may result from the prolonged reliance on such arrangements.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Companies, therefore, need to proactively assist women to manage the risk of such professional isolation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the ways that companies can mitigate this is to implement a system of corporate mentorship and sponsorship for female executives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentors and sponsors, senior executives are responsible for providing career guidance to female executives, helping them open doors to high-visibility projects, connecting them with professional networks within the company and across the industry, and also ensuring that they receive the resources they need for project implementation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through this process, female executives can continue to have a channel into the senior corporate network, thereby ensuring that they continue to have the corporate visibility and exposure they need to advance their career even though they choose to opt for a more FWA.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The second area I would like to speak on is specialised support for mothers who are returning to work.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
