text: Even though both men and women are equally susceptible to experiencing work-family conflicts, women are more likely to experience these conflicts more frequently and at greater intensity than men do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is largely due to societal expectations that place a greater degree of family responsibilities on women even when they are full-time professionals and a greater degree of social sanctions that women will experience than men when they fail to juggle between work and family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, many working women have chosen to take a break from work to concentrate on meeting their family responsibilities before returning to work when their children are old enough to be independent.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Juggling between work and family can be daunting, especially so for women who are returning to work after prolonged periods of non-work arising from the need to meet family responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An idea that is also worth exploring is to create more networks of entrepreneurs or business professionals to guide, mentor and advise mothers who are perhaps thinking of starting their own business.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has, definitely, resulted in the rise of more home businesses and, rather than return to conventional employment, perhaps some of these "mumpreneurs" might want to scale up their businesses, so as to allow themselves the opportunity to generate an income while also having the flexibility to attend to their other personal and familial duties.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, as we work towards parity, equality for women in Singapore, we are taking on what perhaps is becoming less and less of a "wicked problem", but still one that has no simple and easy solution.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My comments notwithstanding, I am supportive of the White Paper and hope that this will provide the foundations for Singapore women to grow, develop and thrive in our community and society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This marks yet another key milestone in Singapore's long journey towards removing barriers and empowering Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This House has seen many exchanges and recommendations on how we can empower and advance Singapore women over the past six to seven decades.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Personally, since entering this House in 2011, I have also heard many suggestions made by fellow Members of Parliament (MPs) and seen real policy changes implemented to resolve pain points and provide stronger support to Singapore women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Humbly, I, together with fellow PAP women MPs, have contributed modestly to the cause by moving a private Members' Motion titled "Aspirations of Women" in 2017.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, now that a White Paper is completed and introduced, this is certainly a significant leap forward as tangible actions will be taken to further Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And, of course, in this House, I have also covered a range of topics talking about women and place of women in tech, as well as digital competency.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But in this speech today, I would like to just share and address two pieces of feedback I have heard so far and some suggestions in the area of empowering women in their careers and protecting girls from harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One category of comments I have heard is whether we are overly promoting women's rights.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Comments include, some jokingly and some not so jokingly, whether we should also have a Men's Charter or White Paper on Singapore Men's Development and whether we should promote women to higher positions for the sake of it, thereby compromising meritocracy potentially.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, efforts to champion Singapore Women's Development cannot be to demand women's rights just because it sounds politically appealing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Rather, it is about ensuring fair play and choice.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is to ensure that, for instance, between a male and female candidate of comparable competency or potential, the female one does not get filtered out or be considered as a lesser candidate because of biases, such as "Oh, she is of childbearing age and may have to take time off to give birth" or "Oh, she has young kids and will have to take childcare leave or be distracted now and then".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This was something that I experienced in 2015, when I first gave birth.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I remember this as a comment during the General Election; this was levelled against me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Or that "women are more emotional, less decisive and harder to follow." Well, we need to address such attitudes and comments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, there is a need to make the entire environment – employers and society – to be more empathetic and supportive towards women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, just as women in Singapore today have control over our own bodies as law enforcement authorities do not turn a blind eye to crimes against women, there is also a need to punish and deter the worst abuses against women at the workplace as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is to ensure that women are not disadvantaged for recruitment and promotion.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, beyond breaking the biases, it is also putting in place support to free up women's capacity, so that they can pursue other worthy aspirations to be an equal partner.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We have seen women going places, we have seen how women are able to hold our own and make it out fair, and yet, we have to ask ourselves: is it enough?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Are there other barriers that are in place, that are prohibiting women from going out there to fulfil their fullest potential?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, with this Paper, and by supporting Singapore Women's Development, I believe it is also about fulfilling the potential that has been untapped.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, this leads to the topic of caregiving.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another feedback that I have heard is whether having a whole segment on caregiving in a paper titled "Singapore Women’s Development" will reinforce the gender stereotype that caregiving is exclusive to women.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Anyone can be a caregiver and it is a noble responsibility to care for another life, especially if the care recipient is a loved one.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Caregiving should ideally be a shared responsibility, regardless of gender.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the current reality is that women disproportionately form the majority of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, even as we continue to educate and change mindsets, we must address this caregiving issue now, so that women weighed down by caregiving duties can have the capacity to also pursue their other life aspirations.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I am glad that the White Paper recognises this current reality.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Furthermore, caregiver support policies are not exclusive to women but benefit male caregivers as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The grant will not fully compensate for caregiving and it is not meant to do so, but it recognises the sacrifices that caregivers make and reduces the trade-offs that caregivers face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The increase in grant may cross the threshold for the household to finally get help, so that the caregiver can take up a part-time job and keep her career on track.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, readily available and accessible respite care, especially for full-time caregivers, are important to reduce burnout.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, full-time caregivers would usually have been out of the workforce for some time and suffer relatively weaker finances.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On a note related to caregiving, though out of the scope of this White Paper, I wish to again highlight the topic of migrant domestic workers (MDWs).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The role of MDWs remains integral to how Singaporean families choose to provide care or supplement caregiving for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: MDWs, therefore, help to free women to focus on work and other pursuits.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, in many instances, the MDWs may have caused more grief than relief to their employers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I had shared the challenges faced by Singaporean families and, indeed, Singapore women, in my Adjournment Motion last November.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I should also note that the dire situation has improved as the supply of MDWs have eased.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nonetheless, there are still instances where employers feel that the system is tilted in favour of MDWs when disputes arise and employers are left to prove their own innocence to the authorities while scrambling to pick up the pieces at home.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Another point I wish to highlight is better protection of young girls from harm.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Several of my youth volunteers at MacPherson are passionate about this and recently organised a few webinars under the "Action for Her" movement centred on protection of girls against online harms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Issues explored ranged from body shaming to cyberbullying to sexual harassments.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This can be especially salient in complex family settings that are dysfunctional or where the parents are undergoing acrimonious divorce.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Children look up to their parents as role models and they pick up ideas from their surroundings.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They must not be led to think that the misdemeanours they are exposed to at home are normal.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And more importantly, to ensure that girls in such households and settings are not led to grow up thinking that they are weak and do not deserve happiness like any other.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must better protect our girls, intervene sooner when necessary, bring them into safer environments sooner, so that they can grow up with the right values and in an environment that brings out the best in them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader, would you like to proceed with the Exempted Business Motion?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite the ambitions, most will, at some point in their lives, find themselves being responsible for the care of a loved one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be a parent, grandparent, spouse, child, sibling or relative.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know many of my residents who are caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Hence, supporting caregivers is a subject that I take great personal interest in.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I agree with the various recommendations in the White Paper to enhance support for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Certainly, I also concur that men should take up our share of caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is usually more challenging than what is conventionally regarded as "real work", especially with the emotional attachment.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, unlike formal employment, there is no remuneration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is only sacrifice and the self-satisfaction of knowing one's loved one is well looked after.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Caregivers put their own aspirations on the back burner and this may cause some of them to face social isolation and suffer from low self-esteem, which may result in poor emotional and mental health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may worry about a time when they, too, will require caregiving, but lack the finances for it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the proposals in the White Paper are laudable, I would like to suggest more services and support with direct benefits for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the proposals in the White Paper are laudable, I would like to suggest more services and support with direct benefits for caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In the US, some states enacted legislation to create mandatory family leave insurance programmes, to provide caregivers with paid time-off.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Several EU member countries, such as Belgium, Denmark and Finland, have various forms of caregiving leave and benefits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to ensure that caregivers are not financially deprived from their caregiving roles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Paid caregiving leave, together with respite and day care for patients, will allow caregivers to take a much-needed break to recharge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I know caregivers amongst my residents who have not had a real holiday in years, since they started looking after family members with chronic conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a 24/7 commitment with no scheduled break.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are items required on a regular basis and the costs do add up.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also consider tax breaks for caregivers for persons with mental health problems, who may include adult children, spouses and siblings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is because the current recommendations are focused on mothers, and caregivers of seniors, children with developmental needs and persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond caregivers of seniors, this should also include caregivers of persons with mental health problems and children with chronic health conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Yio Chu Kang, I have seen how caregivers need additional support after their loved ones have passed away.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At times, they are lost and end up having prolonged grief, which then affects their own mental health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The support from AIC must be comprehensive, simple and accessible to all types of caregivers to seek help without requiring onerous research.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: AIC can better link up with the community and have better visibility.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To my knowledge, not many people may be aware that AIC provides support for caregivers, too.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I can volunteer Yio Chu Kang constituency to work with AIC on this effort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Like the SAF Day, businesses and organisations can provide discounts to caregivers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The logistics may have to be finetuned, but the goal is to appreciate caregivers for the essential role they play in our society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a family-friendly society, we can do more to care for our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us continue to explore more initiatives to provide the continuous and necessary support for women in our journey towards a fairer and more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: When this White Paper was released, I reached out to my female fellow union leaders, both young and mature, who are also female workers.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: From the exchange I had with them, I will just focus my thoughts on workplace opportunities and challenges, while in my Malay speech segment, highlighting the importance of appreciation and protection for women.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The question is, could it have been more and higher up the ranks?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Our collective immediate response must be an affirmative yes!

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Then, how do we entice and encourage women into the workforce, putting in measures and support that ensure not just a higher labour participation, but further raise the capabilities of our total workforce?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, what are the areas that we can identify, so that these women can both bridge the gap in capabilities, if any, and also towards achieving higher productivity, which can, in turn, boost our economy?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This may look easy on paper but, in reality, we need more employers to be more welcoming and embracing of women in their organisation, and also emplace them in leadership roles.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Women should continue to be given more opportunities for a higher role, based on their capabilities and merits.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Understanding women challenges, employers must also do their part by adopting and practising FWAs at their workplace, while, at same time, also applying fair performance appraisal towards women in their organisations.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I mentioned fair performance appraisal because this is also an area of concern to some women workers that I spoke to before.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: While these women really hope for the increase for a much-needed rest after each pregnancy and delivery of a child, they also expressed concern that there are instances where they knew of fellow workers losing out in their performance bonuses during this absence, or worse, some do even get less because they are seen to be less capable than their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I call on employers to be more accommodative and understanding towards your female workers in such circumstances.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us not demoralise the women for their absence but evaluate their contributions in a fair, constructive and also productivity-related work outcome.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Hopefully, by embracing an objective performance evaluation through adoption of tripartite standards of fair employment practices, this will, certainly, further increase and improve their morale.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Luckily, the clock is just 24 hours because the way women get things done, the clock does not seem to be just 24 hours.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: A female leader and worker recently shared with me a summary of her observations on the workplace challenges faced by women and I quote in her own words, "To be honest, over the years, there has been constant advocating against such societal stigmas, and we know, no matter what, the issue of gender inequality and stereotypes still exist today, regardless of within or outside of the workplace.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: The key question is, how do we provide the platform whereby these guidelines can be put into action and is more legally binding?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, setting a criteria framework of sorts for companies to adhere to?

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, the position or status of women in our society has progressed over the years and we have seen many women excel in their careers, on par with the men.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding their achievements in their careers, we also cannot ignore the ongoing perpetration of violence against women, both physically and emotionally.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Although family violence like these usually results in separation, there is one person who continues to protect the family's core.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: This is the sacrifice usually made by women because men do not have the same emotional capability as women.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In this situation where separation is inevitable, it is useful for the couple to make informed decisions in the interest of their children.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Each divorce does not only involve the couple, but others in the family, too, because it will have an emotional impact on their children.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: I also hope for more support for single parents who need to manage between earning a living and taking care of their children.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, find the time to be with your children so that your ex-wife can have her own personal time, just like you.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, especially for the wives, please love our wives, pamper them with the things that they want whenever we have the means to do so.

speaker: Mr Abdul Samad (Nominated Member)
text: Once again, I repeat, Respect, Protect and Care for Women at all times!

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As a nation, we will stride decisively ahead to realise greater equality between women and men.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is an important move to advance Singapore women’s development to higher levels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Although much has been achieved since the 1961 Women’s Charter, there is more to be done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For instance, women today still take the lion’s share of caregiving duties and many Members have talked about it during their speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: And some of the common products that we use on a daily basis are made based on men’s requirements, without addressing the needs of women users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: But this is changing and will continue to evolve with the plans that are put forth by the White Paper.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Since the start of the Conversations in September 2020, I have had the chance to speak with many Singaporeans of different ages and from all walks of life – from youths and working professionals, caregivers and educators, to corporate and business leaders, as well as our unionists.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Among the diverse views of nearly 6,000 participants of the Conversations, one strong common wish was for Singapore to build a fairer and more inclusive society, where men and women partner each other as equals, and pursue their aspirations freely and to the fullest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: To this end, let me share how three key action plans in the White Paper will uplift, protect and reflect the interests of Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Today, while women have made headway in terms of greater equality at work and in society, a disproportionate gap persists when it comes to caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Women are still the ones holding the fort in caregiving and shouldering the heavier load.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Although there is growing recognition of the need to balance this disequilibrium, it takes time to change long-held gender role stereotypes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Meanwhile, we must do all we can to support caregivers and women who carry out the tough work of caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the course of our Conversations in the past one-and-a-half years, many participants had suggested tapping on the "kampung spirit" to better support our caregivers, for instance, creating a community buddy system where caregivers can check in with one another and offer emotional support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will partner the community to push out three key initiatives to uplift and support caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This will help reinforce ground support for this group of caregivers who are especially vulnerable to burnout.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Volunteers who wish to be part of this effort can go to the C2C, which is the Caregivers-to-Caregivers training programme, to have a better understanding of the kind of mental health challenges that caregivers face.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Second, we will boost help for caregivers of persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For example, the mother of a five-year-old boy with autism, Mdm Feng, tells us that she has benefited from the valuable experience, advice and tips of other parents of children with special needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: They taught Mdm Feng how to use simple occupational therapy (OT) exercises to help her child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Third, we will co-create new solutions to cater to the needs of caregivers so that they can be better supported in their caregiving journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: NCSS and Montfort Care are leading the Caregiver Community Lab project.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It brings together caregivers, residents and community partners to ideate and co-create solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The project was first piloted in Radin Mas and will now be expanded to Tanjong Pagar.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Besides synergising the efforts in the two estates, this initiative seeks to better understand the barriers that our caregivers face in accessing support services and take steps to address the obstacles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Although my caregiving journey for my late father 12 years ago can be considered a short one compared to others, I know how strenuous and stressful it can be because, each day, while my late father was in the ICU and it was a total period of 10 weeks, we oscillated between hope and despair as we kept watch over him 24 hours a day over that 10-week period.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Many caregivers go through the roller-coaster emotions on the road of caregiving.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Having a network of support from fellow caregivers and care services will strengthen their resilience quickly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With greater respect and partnership in caregiving, men and women can contribute towards this important role which cannot afford to be neglected, else society and our families may suffer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Government will spare no effort to boost and bolster new structures of support and create new solutions to meet the needs of our caregivers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With greater community support, we hope no caregiver will walk the journey alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Just as how we are empowering and equipping caregivers, we are enabling women to have the freedom and security to excel in sports by providing them safe sporting environments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: During the Conversations, participants had expressed their desire for clear guidelines and measures to deter harassment and misconduct in the sporting arena.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This exercise involved key stakeholders, like sportswomen, psychologists and non-profit organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Second, the Safe Sport Commission has established a central case management service to provide a channel for reporting incidents of misconduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In addition, there is a network of counsellors and befrienders to provide psychosocial support for affected individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The Panel will decide on the appropriate penalties and sanctions to be imposed on alleged perpetrators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Fourth, we will continue to educate the sporting community and public on the Safe Sport Unified Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The online learning portal, "SportSG-ED" has specific modules for coaches and athletes to learn about their roles and responsibilities in sports.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last but not least, the Safe Sport Programme is testament to our zero-tolerance approach towards any misconduct that threatens the safety of our sporting environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: By upholding the standards of the Unified Code, we can keep our sporting environment healthy and positive for all athletes, especially women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Apart from setting respectful standards of behaviour in sports, we are also developing and upholding "gender-responsive standards" in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This means setting standards for products, services and procedures that consider and cater to the needs of both genders, including those of women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the past two years, we have to use masks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Some of us have to use personal protective equipment (PPE).

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Personal protective equipment (PPE), such as helmets, gloves and safety goggles used in worksites, and so on, need to also cater to the sizes and shapes of women for better fit and protection, instead of being uniformly designed, based on the requirements of males.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: It will be implemented across all committees under the Singapore Standards Council, such as biomedical and health, building and construction and quality and safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Our efforts are aligned with the vision of the International Organisation for Standardisation and their "Gender Action Plan".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Apart from developing gender-responsive standards, the Gender Strategy also seeks to increase women representation in the development of standards and raise awareness of their contributions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, I would like to use this platform to encourage and urge women with relevant industry experience to contribute their views and expertise to this important work of national standardisation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The ESG website has more details on how the public can participate with their feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We hope that in the near future, the products, services and procedures in Singapore will be increasingly gender-responsive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As addressing the unique needs of women become more a norm rather than an exception, our society will be one where men and women are recognised and treated as equal partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: These are fundamental values that will help us forge a Singapore where women and men stand as equals and where we each have the chance to realise our dreams and aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, Singapore has become a place of more equal opportunity for women, thanks to policy efforts by the Government, tireless advocacy by civil society champions and the encouragement and partnership of male allies.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, as we chase the aspirations that we rightfully deserve, we run into social barriers and our own voices are often dimmed by societal expectations and mindsets that have not caught up with the times.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But the types and trajectory of women's careers tend to differ significantly from those of men.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no lack of women at entry level but female representation tapers off in senior positions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Women are sometimes perceived as too much or bossy when they are assertive and decisive.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These women are then seen as less likeable or capable and, hence, less likely to rise through the ranks.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Leadership is not just about the boardroom or in politics.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But even stepping back from becoming a prefect in Primary school, for example, for fear of being unliked for the same qualities which are viewed positively in boys, is not something that we want for our girls.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many fast-growing and well-paying jobs are in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM).

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just 50% of women who graduate with STEM qualifications go on to pursue related careers in this male-dominated space.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Efforts like the mentoring programmes and workshops by Tech for She, a group of working professionals and youth and tech, are an important part of the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Institutes of Higher Learning as well have some programmes to attract and retain female STEM talent, such as NTU's Women@NTU initiative, which also supports early career female researchers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But a European-based Microsoft survey found that young girls become interested in STEM at about age 11 and may lose interest by age 15.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By focusing women in STEM efforts at the tertiary level, are we too late?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I look forward to hearing more about how STEM can be made even more accessible and relevant to girls in Secondary or Primary schools.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must amplify the story of women in STEM.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, a ground-up initiative, the Codette Project, which believes that every woman deserves an equal chance at success and that tech can get her there, launched an exhibition featuring minority women from different ages and backgrounds in the tech industry.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It sends a clear message that these spaces belong to people like us, too, and "success looks like this", the name of the exhibition.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, unfortunately, still a reality that women face a childcare penalty.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mother's wages typically stagnate and enter a permanently lower trajectory, especially if they take time off to care for their children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even when women do not become mothers, studies have shown that the mere perception of this possibility can lead them to being treated differently by co-workers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There are also times when women affected by societal pressures and unwanted reminders of ticking biological clocks hold ourselves back.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, "I should not put myself out there for a promotion since I should be trying for a child ASAP after marriage." I am heartened to note that there are plans to facilitate greater women's representation in leadership roles, strengthen workplace fairness and introduce new tripartite guidelines, calling on employers to consider FWA requests from employees fairly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond guidelines, I also hope that societal norms will change as both parents become more actively involved in raising children.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than embracing women as equal partners in the workplace, these shifts need to occur in our homes, too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One focus of the White Paper is on caregiving, as many of my colleagues have spoken about.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As noted last year, there are approximately 210,000 caregivers in Singapore, most of whom are women aged 40 and above.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my Meet-the-People Sessions, I have encountered women who told me the difficulties in securing migrant domestic workers' help during COVID-19 meant that they, as mothers, wives, sisters, aunties and daughters, had to make the tough choice to leave their jobs to ensure an elderly parent or child is looked after, while it was not even in the realm of contemplation that their brothers or husbands would do it instead.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many mothers also shared how the expectation always fell to them to take emergency leave in the case of an ill child.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I applaud the proposal to enhance the Home Caregiving Grant (HCG) which will now provide up to $400 in relief per month.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe there is room for the scheme to be expanded to better reflect the true value of unpaid caregiving.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Hawaii, for example, the government grants up to US$70 a day to unpaid primary caregivers of senior relatives to alleviate caregiving burdens.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singapore's population ages and care burdens increase, such models may be examined further, including how we may potentially finance them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the criteria which a care recipient of the HCG must meet can be expanded as well, as some seniors fall just shy of the three ADL criteria, but face other serious challenges that require dedicated care and similar expenses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also look forward to hearing more about how the Household Services Scheme can be broadened and make more accessible in a timely manner to meet demand.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Who will care for our caregivers in their old age, those who have given up hopes and dreams of their own, once the care recipients are no longer around?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am glad to hear the efforts elaborated by Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam earlier on this front.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When you get to your 20s, you are asked at every festive season, wedding and funeral, "When are you getting married?" After you get married, you are asked, "When are you having children?" When you have one child, you are asked, "Why are you stopping at one?" And when you have many children, you are asked, "Why do you have so many?" But it is not always within the control of the woman and such comments can be very hurtful reminders of what they hope for, but have not come true.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that society can consider for women who remain single because of personal decisions; women who have made a tough choice to leave relationships; women who cannot have kids because of infertility challenges either of their own or of their partner; or women who need to focus on careers because they are the only child who can look after their parents.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that in considering what can make a woman whole, we look at who she is and not just who she could be relative to someone else, like a wife or a mother.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope we can, in the words of Minister Ong Ye Kung earlier, consider the unconscious remarks that we make.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This benefits not only them but the children they may welcome into their lives in a planned, responsible manner.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a Member of this House who is a woman under 35 years old, it is something my peers and I have often discussed and I know that there are women slightly older who wish that they have this option, too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a topic that has prompted much discussion, and I hope that we can continue to have these important conversations in a way that is mindful of different beliefs and, ultimately, for greater progress.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With FWAs, leadership cultivation, this White Paper proposes actions that benefit many white-collar working women.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, any discussion on gender equality is incomplete without considering the experiences of women from lower-income backgrounds.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With limited resources, it can be all the more difficult for these women to have a voice and a choice despite their courage and best efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposed solution for lower-income women we often hear is, "Why don't you get a job?" Well, many jobs have irregular hours due to overtime while most childcare services have fixed daytime hours, making it more difficult to viably care for children without additional expenses.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And although childcare subsidies do exist, the burden of proving the work hours falls onto them, and sometimes are difficult to substantiate, especially for self-employed mothers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, these women face other barriers like aspirational poverty or lower social capital.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As ComLink scales up, I hope that there can also be better integrated programmes catered for women to achieve personal growth and empowerment beyond family and child-centric efforts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Additionally, specific groups of women need more support.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this House, I have called for more to be done for families of offenders.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Generally, there are 10 times more men than women in our penal population.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such initiatives could make a world of difference to the women whose struggles and aspirations may otherwise be overlooked.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recently chatted with two young women who co-founded their first business.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have worked with large tech companies, both in Singapore and overseas, and shared with me some responses they got when they introduced themselves as minority women founders, identifiers that they were proud of.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One response was, "Why do you victimise yourself that way?" The double-barrelled identifiers by race and gender were somewhat affronting to some people.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But why should minority and women mean victim, or less than?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why should not minority and women mean strong and capable?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   In my speech earlier, I touched on how Singapore, since long ago, has taken steps and provided opportunities for women to achieve our aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The White Paper on Singapore Women’s Development shows the Government's commitment to take firm action to support women in fulfilling our aspirations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I hope we will not just depend on laws.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a society, we should also play a role.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recently, we have seen an incident where misogynistic comments or a list that sexualised our religious teachers have degraded our women.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The community came together to condemn such acts, and incidents like this have encouraged more discussions on the importance of respecting and upholding the dignity of our women.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have we changed how we see the role of our mothers, older sisters, younger sisters, or wives at home?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A recent study by the Singapore Muslim Women's Association (PPIS) highlighted a concern faced by Singapore Malay women.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They face a dilemma of balancing their aspirations at work and at home.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is my hope that more Malay/Muslim women are given the opportunity to hold positions as company chiefs and leaders of community organisations.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In doing so, it will allow women to have bigger dreams so that other women, particularly our young, will dare to try and achieve the aspirations that they hope for.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Our position on Singapore Women's Development is for all of us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this Singapore, men and women can play to their strengths without labels.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know that all of us in this House, men and women Parliamentarians alike, will work even harder such that Singapore will be fairer and more inclusive for the generations of young women to come.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To our dear girls, "Don't let anyone or anything hold you back." Mdm Deputy Speaker, I support the White Paper and look forward to the collective action that we will take as a society together.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I quote, "I think the degree of a nation's civilisation may be measured by the degree of enlightenment of its people, of its women".

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Women today are no longer confined to the traditional role of homemakers alone.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, women in Singapore, including myself, have benefited greatly from the meritocratic system with equal educational opportunities for all and become contributors to nation-building and social progress through our own inspiration and self-determining efforts.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is thus very encouraging for me to know that the Government is putting forth wide-ranging action plans to advance Singapore women's development, with the vision of creating an inclusive and fairer society for all.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My speech will focus on some suggestions that could further enhance the actions to be taken in these two areas.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that mentorship is an excellent way to support women who intend to pursue career advancement, professional development or wish to return to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have been providing mentorship to younger women for several years and it has been most satisfying to see these women grow in their careers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Social platforms can allow those who are willing to be mentors to be matched with women who are seeking mentorship.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have spoken about the need to enhance caregiver support in my 2021 Budget speech and I believe that action plans in the White Paper to enhance respite care options for caregivers and Home Caregiving Grant will, indeed, be welcome measures to alleviate the caregiving load.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides the action plans proposed for caregivers' support, I would like to call for further support for caregivers of seniors by having the Agency for Integrated Care actively promote advanced care planning, especially at the early stage of caring for their senior loved ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is so that the caregivers can alleviate their concerns of what would be the most appropriate care to carry out, without being burdened or feeling guilty whether the right care was given to their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will likely help to ease their financial burdens to support the long-term care needs of their children when they become incapable of giving care to their adult children themselves.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Deputy Speaker, since our Independence in 1965, the role of Singapore women has gradually evolved from family-centred homemakers to career women in the modern era, making substantial contributions to our country and society.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I fully support the White Paper on Singapore women’s development.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The White Paper will help uplift Singapore women's status and lay the foundation for their development in the future towards a fairer and more inclusive society.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In particular, I support the action plans in two areas in the White Paper.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, equal opportunities in the workplace; second, support for caregivers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I am encouraged that the Government will be developing career mentorship and training programmes for women at work and those re-entering the workforce.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have been providing mentorship to younger women and it has been most satisfying to see them grow and succeed in their careers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government can provide a one-stop portal that can match women at work and those re-entering the workforce with a suitable mentor who can help them open a window of opportunity and fulfil their career aspirations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I am heartened by the recommendations to enhance female caregiver support proposed in the White Paper, such as the enhanced Home Caregiving Grant and respite services to lighten the financial and mental burden of caregivers.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can also pay attention to caregivers of seniors, by having the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) actively promote advanced care planning, so that seniors can ponder and plan in advance their personal care arrangement in later years.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By doing this, caregivers would know what the most appropriate medical treatment and care will be, based on the seniors’ own choice, without being mentally burdened or feeling guilty.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, uplifting the social status of women requires the collaborative efforts and support from both genders.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To collectively build a society where men and women are equals and all can pursue their dreams freely and fully, we need our fathers, brothers, husbands and sons to give their unwavering support and close partnership.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: May this partnership continue to enable Singapore to become a fairer, more inclusive and united country.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, embarking on this endeavour to advance Singapore women's development is a partnership between both men and women.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: May this partnership continue to flourish so that we, as a nation, can achieve greater heights together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We become better when women are more equal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Although many of the recommendations in this White Paper will make our job market more attractive, our economy more competitive, our long-term growth more sustainable, none of these justifies our adopting the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That women should have an equal place in society is right in itself, not because it promotes some other social good.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This poem "Mother and Son" written by Langston Hughes, a famous African-American poet, describes the process well.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It goes like this. "Well, son, I'll tell you: Life for me ain't been no crystal stair.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It's had tacks in it, And splinters And boards torn up, And places with no carpet on the floor – Bare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But all the time, I's been a-climbin' on." For many women today, life is no "crystal stair" and, today, when we see girls and boys in school and safe streets at night, there remains "tacks and splinters".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, there remains a wage difference between men and women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More women are likely to be harassed sexually and there are far fewer women than men on boards of companies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In our words and in our deeds, there remain many injustices and biases in society.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One White Paper and one Motion does not make a crystal stair but it is a step up.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, there have been many such step ups, leading to the more equal landscape that we see today.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is still a gap and the narrowing is slow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Earlier this year, I spoke on the issue of support for mothers who may be unemployed during divorce.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I also asked about support for parents with caregiving responsibilities, including greater flexible work support and other policies for better work-life harmony.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For the past 15 years, I have also spoken on the need to support single mothers as part of a broader commitment to single parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In all these policies, I have often wondered about the lines that are drawn.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, do we draw a line between the home and the workplace?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When we give more support to women as caregivers at home, are we making them better workers and colleagues?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another example, do we support single mothers or all single parents?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Do we support just mothers who are unemployed or do we do so for fathers, too, during divorce?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When we say "regardless of gender", do we mean we treat men and women the same?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Is that not the right thing to do?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, we support single parents whether they are men or women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We support all persons who require help during their search for employment regardless of gender.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, for NTUC FairPrice, our commitment in developing a wonderful workplace is anchored on our human resource practices, which adhere to the principle of equality and equal employment opportunity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We employ on the basis of merit and adopt a non-discriminatory stance on race, religion, gender or age.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices require us to provide employment opportunities to all, including part-timers and flexi-timers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many of these are women who juggle between home and work.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But in so doing, we make no judgement on whether it should be women or men who do this juggling.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the same way, all staff are also entitled to childcare leave and child sick leave.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have "family charity leave", which allows both men and women to either celebrate auspicious occasions with their family or to do charity work and bond with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We aim to ensure they are provided with not only competitive remuneration but also a safe and caring environment, a culture of continuous learning and a roadmap for career development so that every employee has the opportunity to develop to their fullest potential.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In that case, equality is the result of treating people the same.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But in some cases, equality requires us also to treat women differently.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, SMEs employ about 70% of the workforce and there are more than a quarter million of these companies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More women felt they had been passed over for promotion or career advancement, that their companies favour men when hiring.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They felt treated unfairly but they were afraid to report it to their management.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Clearly, equality here requires us to pay greater attention to providing equal respect for our colleagues who are women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Earlier this year, some SMEs have signed Memorandums of Understanding (MOUs) with NTUC, which will provide consultants and resources when they set up policies, such as on proper grievance handling procedures and disciplinary actions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The road to greater equality requires us not just to treat women like men, but to pay attention to the unfairness that exists today between them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The workplace is one of the most important spaces where such equality can be observed, can be measured and can be improved.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It has to do with the way we think, speak about and to women.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How many times have we interrupted women as they speak, explain to them matters which they already know – sometimes better than us?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How many of us do this to women more than men?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must not only refrain from openly disrespectful behaviour, such as those that I have listed above, but also patronising ones.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, I am sure all of us would have – well, I certainly have – experienced some senior corporate leaders, including senior civil servants, thank a male emcee by name and the female emcee by referring to her as "the beautiful young lady".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is a temptation to brush these off, not to take offence too easily.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, let us keep climbing and working together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Enough with the talking and let us put all these into practice.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In conversations with single women caregivers, a major challenge shared is their retirement inadequacy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Caregivers face difficulties holding down a full-time job while still providing care for the seniors, especially in households where the load of caregiving falls entirely on one person.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Those interviewed in AWARE's 2019 survey either cut down work hours or stopped work altogether.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These work changes negatively impact the caregiver's own retirement adequacy as CPF contributions are stopped or reduced.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Given that most caregivers are 45 to 59 years old, an age where they could be economically productive and be able to save up for retirement, the financial impact is significant.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The negative impact on retirement savings is compounded by the fact that women also, generally, earn less than men in their working life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One of the ways Singapore enhances old age income security is through the home ownership programme.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In their senior years, married couples have the option of downgrading their HDB flats for a retirement income.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, this is not an option for singles, who are already limited to buying higher priced resale or 2-room BTOs in non-mature estates or in prime locations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In short, singles, specifically women, expend their financial resources on care for their parents and face financial challenges in their later years for their own care, with little to, at times, no family support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, top-up of CPF from family members to caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Government could consider supplementing caregiver CPF contributions from the care recipient parents' CPF.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For those who qualify for MediSave care, care recipients can be given the option for the monthly cash amounts to be transferred to the caregiver's CPF instead of their bank account.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This can be done where children have been ascertained to be caregivers of a specific parent, to receive a monthly transfer from the latter.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There could also be an option for siblings who have met the Basic Retirement Sum to top-up their caregiving sibling's CPF, incentivised with an enhanced caregiver's support tax relief beyond current amounts for the contributions made, or complemented with greater subsidies for the parents' caregiver's services.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second suggestion: healthcare subsidies based solely on household income.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Having understood the concerns of some of my residents, I would like to propose a consideration for MOH relating to care recipients staying in properties of annual value (AV) $13,000 and above.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In MOH's current means-testing approach, even if the household income qualifies the recipient for subsidy, but the care recipient stays in a private estate where AV is very likely to be above $13,000, no subsidy will be given to him or her.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The rationale behind this is that if the senior sells their private property and moves to an HDB unit, they then should have sufficient income for healthcare costs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, this means that the senior would then, in their old age and ill-health, have to move in and adapt to a new environment, possibly away from the environment of the people they are familiar with.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In addition to ongoing caregiver responsibilities, the single caregiver will have to figure out the sale, search and purchase of a home and make arrangements for the move.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These stresses add on to the stress of change in health and care needed both for the caregiver and recipient.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If access to subsidies requires seniors to move their homes in order for caregivers to access subsidies, it will also go against the grain of encouraging ageing-in-place.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For care recipients with property AV of beyond $13,000, when the care recipient no longer needs to stay in the property, proceeds from the sale or rental of property could then be returned to the Government, as part of the agreement to receive subsidised care.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will help alleviate the immediate financial burdens of caregivers, ensure that the Government's subsidies are sustainable, while truly supporting seniors to age-in-place.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The third suggestion: workplace support for single caregivers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Childcare leave should be converted to a more general family care leave, to include those who are caregivers of parents, particularly single caregivers who have limited help.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The number of family care leaves for such singles should be mandated by law, instead of simply encouraging employers to provide for it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: While FWAs have been raised as a viable alternative, mandatory family care leave can still be added to complement FWAs, in the same way that parents are still entitled to take childcare leave, even when on FWAs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Extended family care leave should also be considered for those who have parents with dementia or conditions that require greater support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Instead of hiring MDWs for the work of caregiving, if children choose to give of their time and effort to do so, our policies should encourage it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I look forward to sustainable changes the Government would make to better support our single women caregivers financially, both in the immediate and long term.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is very needed momentum towards women's equality.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One, work and housing security for low-income women; two, enabling workplace fairness and equality; and three, ensuring sustainable distribution of care.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: While I welcome the recommendations in the White Paper to enable more women on boards and mentorship opportunities and PMET jobs, we need to pay special attention to lower-income women who struggle to access stable employment in the first place.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And I believe, we can do more to improve work accessibility for them as a society.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Non-PMET workers have lower incomes and lesser financial resources to outsource their care needs.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For example, most cannot afford to hire domestic help.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should provide them with more support to help them reduce work-care conflict.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Although I am happy that the Government would be extending the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) to more sectors, we need to make sure that these higher wages are not met with strategies by businesses to cut corners on the welfare of workers, which will have a very detrimental impact on low-income women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can incentivise businesses to adopt innovative work allocation strategies, primarily targeted at the low-wage job sectors.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This could be flexi-hours, flexi-shift, shift-swapping, compressed work weeks, core and stable scheduling, to name some examples.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Daughters Of Tomorrow (DOT) has advocated since 2018 for employers to take up core and stable scheduling.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To enable companies to adopt core and stable scheduling, perhaps the Government can consider giving wage top-ups to workers who may not have as many care responsibilities at home to take the shifts during periods when home care is most needed, usually these are the evenings and the weekends.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such a scheme could be called "Work-Care Grants" and some may argue that the higher hourly wages could cause these evening and weekend shifts to, in turn, become more popular instead.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, similar experiments of the international retailer Gap have shown that mothers with care responsibilities preferred to forego the marginally higher hourly wage, in favour of being able to be at home during care hours for the children.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to stable shifts at work, lower-income women need better housing security.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government will look seriously into communal housing for single mothers and extended rental subsidies for vulnerable families which are striving their utmost towards social mobility.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Single mothers in shelters face massive anxiety from being told that they can only stay for six months.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Shelters have to use this approach currently to ensure adequate capacity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Those who are in rental flats face similar uncertainties when weighing income opportunities against loss of rental subsidies when their salary increases.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents from public rental flats who sought my assistance after they have employment requested for reduction in housing rental.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Doing well at work, ironically, becomes a disincentive.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It holds back the progress of lower-income women that we want to see the most.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We already know that the average length of stay in rental flats before families move out into their own homes is seven years.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Reducing financial shocks during this period and helping the families to build buffers are critical for successful emergence from poverty.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I urge the Government to relook at the income criteria model for rental housing provision.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We must also, at the same time, explore more stable and sustainable alternatives, such as communal housing, in the long term.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: SHE Project showed that mothers with longer-term housing stability were better able to rebuild a path towards financial independence.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This model is already in use in the US and Japan.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can study their experiences to create a model that works for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Second, regarding workplace equality, I urge the Government to enable SMEs to build more progressive workplace cultures by supporting them in the culture and operational transformation journey.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The call for non-discriminatory hiring practices needs to come hand-in-hand with equipping SMEs better.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in February, I moderated a panel discussion at NTUC, together with TAFEP, where HR and business owners from SMEs gathered and came to hear about ways they can better tackle workplace discrimination and grievances.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The attendees who came found it helpful and they saw that grievance handling does not necessarily have to end up in lawsuits or firing someone but could be opportunities for education within their companies.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We talked about the possibilities of harnessing the energies of their own employee community to advance this cause without incurring high expenses as a form of internal corporate social responsibility.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The Government can help rally business associations to do more of such sharing sessions with NTUC and TAFEP to facilitate best practices and capacity-building amongst SMEs.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There is still stigma around men spending time away from work to take care of family.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Men shared with me their concerns that taking time off from work for care obligations could compromise their chances at promotions or create a negative impression of them at work.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One key strategy to change this mindset is to ungender care and normalise care work for both men and women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can deploy young people based on their aptitude in either the armed forces or the care forces.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Those who are physically unsuitable for the armed forces can be deployed to care roles in the community, such as respite caregiving, care coordinators, medical escorts, befrienders, mental health responders and so on, while those with the desire and physical aptitude can opt or be deployed to military positions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many families' caregiving needs increased.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Many citizens had to quit their jobs to care for the young and old at home.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In Switzerland, men can choose to do civilian service instead of military service, serving in healthcare, welfare, environmental protection, research projects or development assistance abroad.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If compulsory enlistment is too big a step for now, we can introduce CCAs in schools in the likes of National Cadet Corps or National Civil Defence Cadet Corps, perhaps called the National Care Corps for both boys and girls.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This will help to socialise young people from a young age to see women as equals and themselves as caregivers, giving them exposure to care work as a meaningful vocation.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When men and society take some care burdens from the shoulders of women, women can have more space on their shoulders for their aspirations and for daughters to stand on.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In doing so, we will create role models for both our sons and daughters, for a world that sees true and equal partnership between men and women and on this point about true partnership.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: True partnership requires recognising and affirming the inherent worth of women in all spheres of life.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It requires the eradication of the mindsets and the narratives that create barriers to women's worth being recognised.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: These narratives have conditioned society so much that, often, women doubt ourselves, we doubt our own worth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When Minister Ong Ye Kung said earlier about the comments that relatives make, an innocuous comment to say "When are you going to have sons?" could hurt a girl child very deeply, causing a wound on the perceptions of their self-worth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
