text: Because of this, mandated representation, alluded by our hon colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim earlier, saying that it is charity that should begin at home, is deeply patronising to women.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In a world where innocuous messages are sent constantly to women to make us feel lesser, the last thing that we need is a cloud hanging over our heads, making us wonder and doubt whether we have gotten a position out of our own merit or for anyone else to have that doubt.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, let us focus on doing the real work, the deep work that may not sound very ambitious but is important to help change the values and inherent unquestioned mental models that build these narratives that cast doubts on women's self-worth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need to build up women's innate confidence and the work that truly eradicates narratives and barriers are the ones that we need to do, so that they no longer stand in the way of women's self-worth and brilliance.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Stop making us doubt and stop making us choose.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: De-conflict our choices so that we truly can have it all.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: If not for us now, at least in the near future, for our daughters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of the Motion and, in particular, the action areas in the White Paper on increasing protection against violence and online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ending family violence and preventing online harms require a multi-pronged approach involving many parties.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Men – husbands, fathers, brothers, sons – can be advocates and allies for the cause.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But men can also be victims of violence or online harms as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am thus heartened to see the White Paper involving the feedback of many men and setting out what men can do to make a difference.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, we can raise awareness – make it easier to report, make help more accessible and make reporting safer not just for survivors but also for whistle-blowers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, we can help change mindsets that violent or misogynistic behaviours have no place in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, we can rethink the way we tackle family violence and rehabilitation efforts in our community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recently, in conjunction with International Women's Day, PAP Women's Wing provided a resource toolkit for activists to assist anyone facing online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was involved in this, together with hon Members Nadia Ahmad Samdin and Hany Soh.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Together with DefenceGuild SG, we held talks to raise awareness on online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: DefenceGuild SG is a ground-up initiative of lawyers which I founded, following the incident of the lewd online poll on female religious teachers in the Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Probono lawyers provide assistance and advice to victims of similar online harms and sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, there needs to be protection for whistle-blowers as well.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We need people who would either be brave enough or feel safe enough to stand up, speak out and take action against such behaviours, be it in the real world or online.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides awareness, we need a network of support and information accessible to those who need it and make it easier and safer for reporting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, in Taiwan, crisis shelters sometimes are held in the same building as the police station itself.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Late last year, France rolled out an initiative to facilitate the lodging of reports on family violence by survivors from where they have found shelter so that they can be in an environment where they feel safe.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am grateful that MSF has adopted my suggestion on the hand signal for the "Break the Silence" campaign to provide non-verbal cues for family violence reporting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Australia, such resource websites incorporate a "clear history" or a "quick exit" button which brings the reader quickly to a nondescript Google page, for instance.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through such awareness and efforts, we hope we can shift mindsets of our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Last year, Casa Raudha conducted a survey and a discussion between fathers and men at the Keat Hong Community Club to understand the impact of the patriarchal mindset on families and its correlation with family violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A third of the respondents agreed that having a head of family with a patriarchal mindset can destroy a family’s harmony.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Patriarchal mindset and misogynistic and violent behaviours have no place in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A mindset shift to bring about equality should start at home.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, this White Paper is important to everyone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Each of us is a leader of our respective families and able to portray positive traits that can be emulated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When family members help one another, the result is family harmony and prosperity in the community.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mdm Deputy Speaker, a change in mindset on family violence requires rethinking a more inclusive approach.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Australia, Victoria state's initiative called the Orange Door provides access to comprehensive services for those experiencing family violence so that they can feel safe and supported.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It also provides services for men who resort to violence so that they themselves can get help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, our Family Violence Service Centres also act like a one-stop centre for assistance and links survivors to other forms of help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such efforts would preserve relationships and the family unit in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is better for the family's financial and housing security, too.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Survivors of family violence are more likely to live in interim rental housing upon discharge from crisis shelters.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Of those who are employed, about 80% earn less than $2,000 per month.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These women face challenges in getting affordable accommodation sometimes to be near their workplace or their children's school.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A new way to envision crisis shelter service delivery, perhaps.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I recall, many years ago, when volunteering at Casa Raudha Crisis Shelter, I brought my daughter along.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There, she saw many girls her age playing with their mothers.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is gated and, some may say, isolated.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When I explained to my daughter why the other girls were there, her reply stumped me.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why can't the bad people move out instead?" Our approach towards family violence has always been to tread carefully with relationships and balance that with the safety of survivors in a confidential setting, mostly away from the public glare.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their interventions break with the traditional "behind closed doors" approach.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It means working with all family members, including, if safety allows it, the ex-spouse or perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The focus is on the impact of family violence on children and safe parenting.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It would also be and must be welcoming to men who are perpetrators themselves but want to seek help.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are wounds that do not appear physically, but they hurt more and leave deeper scars.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such is the emotional trauma caused by family violence and online harms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the White Paper and this Motion and the action plans set out by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must target zero violence and online harms against all.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Men are not just allies because we are good men, but because we are all meant for good.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore women's development has come a long way.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Education, coupled with progressive and women-friendly policies and structures put in place over the years, has enabled women in Singapore to enter and excel in the workforce as both employees and business owners, and contribute to our nation’s growth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We stand on the shoulders of Singapore women who were trailblazers of their time and Singapore men who were enlightened and humble to act on the wisdom that women are first among equals alongside themselves.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, as part of Celebrating SG Women, Singapore Business Federation (SBF) did a research study around the issue of "Uplifting women in the workforce; Investing in the success of women in Singapore".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The study concluded that in a resource-scarce country like Singapore, it is a business imperative to mobilise all available talents, male or female, in order to achieve more robust, sustainable and balanced long-term economic growth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SBF is heartened to see that the industry's views have been taken on board in the White Paper. "Women", as a category, is not a monolithic, homogeneous whole and, hence, policies need to address the experiences of multiple sub-groups, for example, single women, single moms, vulnerable groups of women, women as caregivers, senior women in our ageing society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The White Paper, certainly, reflects this reality and that the Government has listened hard and intently to the challenges and aspirations of our women across generations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Kudos and thank you to everyone involved with the SG Women Conversations and this White Paper.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For my speech, I will focus my discussion primarily on "Making the Workplace Work Even Better for Women in Singapore".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I submit to you that if the workplace works for women, it will more than likely work better for men, too.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I remember back in the 1990s when IBM Singapore was designing policies that would attract and retain women in IBM.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One of the policies was to enable women to go on "Leave of Absence" and return to work after the time-out, where they either had to go as trailing spouse to their husbands who went overseas on assignment, or when they had to care for their elderly parents, or when their son or daughter was in PSLE year.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While this policy was designed with the women's needs in mind, the first beneficiary was a male colleague.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, there you have it – if you do it right for women, the men will benefit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One would ask: "Why the focus on attracting and retaining women in the workforce?" There is a strong business imperative underpinning this, as women form a rich talent pool critical to alleviating skill shortages and boosting organisational diversity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As we say in the corporate world, it is a race for talent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These are FWAs; managing workplace bullying and discrimination; addressing the great resignation; advancing women in leadership; and balance between family and career.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Employers need to recognise that female employees are, generally, the primary caregivers and face challenges in managing work and personal responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: FWAs can better support their women employees to manage both aspects.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore National Employers Federation strongly encourages employers to implement FWAs, regardless of gender, to achieve work-life harmony.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Before COVID-19, I think FWAs were a little bit of a difficult thing for employers to hear, but COVID-19 has resulted in work from home (WFH) becoming the norm.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, the "WFH-during-COVID-19" model is not necessarily the best practice.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The design principles of FWAs should address the workplace flexibility that is needed, especially by the women, and, at the same time, ensure that the workplace will facilitate an innovative, productive and inclusive work culture that builds strong teamwork and shared purpose.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MNCs and LLEs, like Shell, DBS and IBM, have best practice policies that support FWAs, companies can learn from one another's experiences and apply them to their own situations.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Petrine Puah shares with me that at Shell, they encourage flexibility in how, where and when employees work.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, employees are also encouraged to step outside of purely work boundaries to participate in other areas of interest, such as social responsibility projects and employee interest groups, for example, time-off for sporting or volunteering.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At Shell, there is also a general perception that a career in the energy sector is not suited for women, or shall we say Shell recognises that there is such a perception.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, at Shell, they provide their female employees with training to overcome biases that they may face in a largely male-dominated industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Today, they have many stories of how women colleagues at Shell break the biases.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: DBS Bank believes that FWAs are a key element to attract the best people to the bank.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Yan Hong of DBS shares with me that they provide a range of FWAs which include "flexi hours", "flexi place" and 100% "work-from-home" for six months for new parents with young children or those with caregiving responsibilities at home.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: DBS also launched a job-sharing programme where one role can be shared by two employees, giving their employees time to manage family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The bank recognises that FWAs require change management for managers and has launched a new manager learning module to support managers to more effectively manage and lead teams in remote or hybrid work settings.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: FWAs are not just for the large companies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: AKC also allows its staff to leave work a few hours earlier once a month to spend time with loved ones.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: AKC conducts cross-training for staff from different departments, so that they can cover one another, and this also builds stronger teamwork and fraternity amongst the employees.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs may be concerned with their limited capacity to implement good policies and processes for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs can tap on Government funding, and Singapore Human Resource Institute, or SHRI, SBF and TACs can all support the SMEs in their journey.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The largest employer, I think one of the largest, is the public sector.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It can play a key role in setting best practices for FWAs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: KK Women’s and Children’s Hospital (KKH) provides an on-site childcare centre with special rates for employees.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They have policies for FWAs which include compressed work week, flexi-time and part-time work to suit their staff’s needs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, KKH will have lactation rooms for nursing moms but they also organise family events, such as "Eat With Your Family Day".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: IBM implemented many of these policies as far back as the 1990s.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I treasure the fact that I did not have to miss most of my children's significant moments.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I was empowered to be fully mom and fully IBMer, knowing that appraisal and promotion are based on personal commitment to results and outcomes, and not on time clocked in the office.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Because the company was supportive of my personal goals of being a working mom, I probably worked triply hard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I am quite sure all my fellow female IBMers at all levels can say the same.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Fair practice in the workplace and zero tolerance of workplace discrimination are an imperative for a productive and trusting workplace culture.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The issues of unconscious bias and unintentional discrimination are often more acute for women.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have heard some of them in this Chamber today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Managers being unconsciously biased against their pregnant women employees for particular assignments or jobs, or – I am sure you have heard of this one – managers expressing distress that their female staff is going to be away for four months of maternity leave and so on and so forth.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Line managers need to be trained to raise awareness of inclusive behaviours, set expectations on consequences and create a culture that enables staff to feel safe to speak up.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should have a whistle-blowing process, so that victims can safely speak up and have their grievances heard.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Human Resource Institute (SHRI) shares with me that they have a one-stop HR shared services centre that provides HR solutioning for grievance handling, employee engagement, background screening services and compliance audits.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Earlier on, we heard hon Member Seah Kian Peng shared with us that NTUC has the same.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, SMEs can turn to SHRI or NTUC for support.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, addressing the Great Resignation – making the workplace work for our next generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most managers and leaders who are now in decision-making positions grew up in a different era than our millennials and Gen Z women and men who have joined the workforce in recent years.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To address the Great Resignation, leaders need to understand what is important to the next generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: WhatsApp and email without limits and consideration are a big no-no.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, for them, their desire is for work to be purposeful, that is, there is meaning to the work and they can see the impact on clients, the community and society, country, environment, humanity; and they can see how their work aligns with the company’s vision, mission and purpose.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The next generation is prepared to work hard but just not all of the time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They want to live their lives to the fullest.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our next generation can teach us many things, just as our senior workers can offer their wisdom and experience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Employers need to design their workplace and workplace culture to work better for the next generation workforce if they want to succeed in the race for talent.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The next generation is more prepared than us to vote with their feet.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: My fourth topic: advancing women in senior leadership and board representation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Top 100 Institutions of Public Character (IPCs) have close to 30% of their board members represented by women.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Internationally, however, Singapore's 20% lags the average Women on Boards (WOB) percentage of developed markets at 25.8%.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Board diversity is a business imperative for organisations' sustainability and resilience.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: WOB is but one aspect of diversity but a very visible one.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Investors and employees are increasingly looking to putting their money with companies that show up on the radar of diversity, inclusion and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The ecosystem is asking for change and accountability.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Take, for example, Blackrock and State Street Global Advisors expect their portfolio companies in Singapore to have at least one woman director and may vote against the re-election of directors deemed responsible for the lack of female participation on boards, starting from the 2022 proxy season.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While there are some people questioning whether there is an adequate pool of board-ready female candidates in Singapore, Mr Simon Israel, the Board Chair of Sing Post and previously Singtel, once said, and I quote, "If you are prepared to have a much wider profile of what could bring diversity to the board, the gene pool is much bigger than boards probably think it is." Council for Board Diversity, Singapore Institute of Directors and executive search firms are all ready to support Board Chairs to fill credible and talented women on their nomination slates for serious consideration and selection.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I should declare I am a member of the Council for Board Diversity.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is encouraging to see progressive companies make concerted efforts to harness the benefits of having more women on their boards.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Take Venture Corporation Limited, SATS Ltd, Singapore Post Limited, Far East Hospitality Trust and, most recently, Thomson Medical, for example.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These boards had zero women in 2013 on their boards but each has at least 30% women on their boards today.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: They are blazing the trail for others to follow.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's President, Mdm Halimah Yacob, recently said and I quote, "The pandemic has highlighted the importance of diversity in leadership.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Organisations with few or no women directors should cast the net wide for the best talents and experience to contribute to their boards … (and) position their organisations well for long-term success." And on to my final point, balance between family and career.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Long ago, I once thought that I had to choose between family or career and even told my boss, who was a man back then, "You do not have to promote me.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am getting married." Thankfully, I had an enlightened boss who ignored my declaration and went on to give me my first management role while I was on honeymoon.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And they tell me, the joke is, each time I have a daughter, each time I have a child, I got promoted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, they asked me if the factory will keep going.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And thankfully, my workplace was a workplace that works for women like me and my colleagues at all levels to have pretty fulfilling careers while bringing up our families, too.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I must say at this point I am grateful that I have a supportive husband who definitely broke all norms at that time, decided to quit his job and be the trailing spouse when I was offered international assignments overseas and has since been the Mr Mom for our family.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: He broke the record because, when we were in Japan, the Parents' Association was called Mothers' Association.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Janet Ang, you may have four children, but you have 30 seconds left.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: All through my journey, there are many moments when I had to stop, in partnership with my spouse, to discern, decide the choices and the steps to take to move forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: I understand that many young women today are troubled by whether they should focus on their career or plan to start a family.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: And non-therapeutic preservation of human eggs appears to be the solution to their troubles, offering women the freedom to opt for work and delay settling down and defer starting a family.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Will the workplace consider women who choose not to postpone childbearing with the freezing of their eggs, as not being sufficiently committed to their career, thus harming their progress?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang
text: Will this lead to inevitable widening of the inequality?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The proposal to legalise elective egg freezing for women aged 21 to 35, regardless of marital status, is an incredibly important development.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For us women, the passage of time affects our bodies significantly and our health and fertility may not hold up until situations finally allow us to have babies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For couples who have difficulties conceiving, the road to parenthood can be so very tedious, frustrating, demoralising and expensive.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a topic close to my heart and I have been raising Parliamentary Questions on this since 2016.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Last year, I devoted my entire Budget speech on egg freezing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In 2015, I started the Baby Joy Programme in Tampines East, where I would visit families with newborns.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I brought diaper cakes to congratulate them on the arrival of their new bundle of joy.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was at all these house visits that I heard the stories of their journey to parenthood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For many couples, the process was not easy at all.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was clear to me that, with today's improvement in medical technology, we can definitely do more at so many levels to help women make informed and individual choices to preserve their right to motherhood.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Take, for example, Janet, 38 years old, who is struggling with IVF as there seemed to be issues with the quality of her eggs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She wanted to freeze them at 33 but did not because she could not fly out due to work commitments.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said she always dated with marriage as an end goal, but the dating scene was limited for her as a 30-something woman.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Now that she is ready, her eggs are no longer quite as ready.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another, 33 years old, said she is a PHD holder of a Government scholarship and is single not by choice.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She tried online dating, asking friends for help but things just did not work out.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She said "educated women are not overly picky" but she feels she has not been lucky.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She added that she just came out of an abusive relationship.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is it better for her to settle and have a child grow up in a potentially abusive environment, or end it, recover and start her search again for Mr Right?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: She wants to try again and she looks forward to being a mother one day.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The reality is that, for various reasons, marrying and starting families early are not always possible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Even if it is the ideal scenario, sometimes, things just do not work out.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: While I understand scientific evidence shows that the quality of a woman's eggs depreciates significantly after the age of 35, we all know that it has now become relatively common for women to conceive between the ages of 35 and 40 and, some, even in their early 40s.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have spoken to so many women and this seems rather clear.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When I did the Journey to Parenthood survey in 2019, those in the 25 to 29 age range took a neutral stand to egg freezing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is just not something they are thinking of at that age.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They are focused on better jobs and pay, dating, clubbing, travel.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My sense is, even with the new policy, it will be women in their 30s who will form the majority who choose to undergo this procedure.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Another reason why women in their early 20s are not likely to undergo elective egg freezing is the issue of cost.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many understand that egg freezing is an elective procedure and if they want it, they know they have to save for it.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The cost of $10,000 to $12,000, while not cheap, is saveable for many.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, this tends to happen when there is a certain level of financial stability and that only happens when one enters one's 30s.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: A fortnight ago, before the White Paper was out, I did a live Instagram session with Dr Janice Tung, a gynaecologist, and Nicole, a moderator invited by Love Bonito, a local fashion apparel company.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: About 9,000 followers tuned in that night and we had a very lively discussion on egg freezing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many commented that egg freezing is the right of the individual woman, a personal choice – a women's right to preserve her chances of motherhood if she so chooses to do.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: From the Instagram live session, I learnt that people are curious.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We discussed cost, the process, success rate of live birth, how many eggs were needed, what is the annual maintenance cost and, of course, other questions.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But before the session started, I asked the team if they had considered egg freezing and if they had also seen a gynaecologist before.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Most would tell me they have spoken to friends or are researching on it but, so far, I have not had anyone who said they had been to a gynaecologist.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Women need to be better informed and understand their bodies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They need to consult their gynaecologist earlier in order to understand their fertility health.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I have met many couples in their late 20s and early 30s who struggle with fertility issues.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many young couples who struggle with fertility issues were surprised to be in that situation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many assumed that the problem is only after 35 years old.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Ladies do not screen early enough to detect the possible issues.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The role of the media in educating the public was crucial in this.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When I asked a Parliamentary Question (PQ) in 2017, Zaobao had a half page article to educate their readers on egg freezing.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Over the years, there have been many articles to spread awareness – CNA, TODAY, Mothership, Her World and many more.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Celebrities, like Ase Wang, also shared about her egg freezing journey.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We were together on a radio show last year and she shared her views quite candidly with the audience as well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Dr Ann Tan, Dr Loh Seong Feei and many more were taking interviews and advocating for the cause.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will probably be the largest group to be cared for, given our rapidly ageing population.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Caregivers are emotionally connected to their charges, such that even if respite care of two to three hours is offered, they may not take it up because they do not have ease of mind when another person helps to take over.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This situation is most common when the elderly has complex medical conditions or is attached to familiar faces.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I welcome the proposals to enhance respite care options for caregivers of seniors and to offer them more help.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What I would like to see is how we can further tighten the assistance framework so as to help lessen the stress on caregivers and on social workers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, for many caregivers, the issues never really go away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their need for help arises at the most unexpected of times when emergencies arise.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, it is very important that caregivers have a constant, familiar contact to call, so that suitable and expedient help can be offered.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, this may mean just listening and giving some advice on how to handle difficult situations and does not necessarily mean that it always needs to be a physical meeting.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Knowing that there is someone who will be there for them in times of need will take a huge stress off their minds.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The reason for a team is to minimise disruptions in case the case manager has to go on leave, be changed to a different department and so on and so forth.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a team befriend them and be a point of contact (POC) for them so that they know they can turn to that POC for help rather than different persons talking to them will be extremely useful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could AIC consider looking into this, or even to empower partner social service agencies to build up such capabilities as well?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While there is consideration of a community peer support network, the key to making this model work is to recruit volunteers who have the bandwidth to undertake such tasks, as well as to provide training to equip them with the expertise to take care of seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have also received feedback from caregivers about stand-in caregivers to stay temporarily at the seniors' homes who might help relieve some stress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, very often, this arrangement is not suitable because the size and condition of some flats may just not allow it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What may help would be having an institutional set-up with care centres, where seniors can check in for a few days and the caregivers will be able to take a break from caregiving duties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, there are limited provisions for such arrangements and advanced reservations need to be made.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The costs vary but some households may have problems affording them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Presently, the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) refers caregivers to suitable help resources but most assistance is temporary.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, for most caregivers, the problems do not really disappear.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, what is important is that they must have a suitable and familiar contact, in order to get access to suitable and convenient help, especially in emergencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a team, compared to a single case manager, as the point of contact is more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will AIC consider this suggestion, even empower partner social services organisations to arrange likewise?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Setting up institutional care centres may be helpful, where seniors can check in for a few days while the caregivers take a short break.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Presently, provisions for such arrangements are limited and need advance reservations.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The fees vary but some households may find them hard to afford.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If the Ministry can provide subsidies and increase the number of places, these will be helpful.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Indeed, the whole of society can do our part to better support our caregivers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am especially heartened by its support for key issues like equal workplace opportunities, caregiver support and protection against violence, which have been championed by activists and women for many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This White Paper is, indeed, about women's development.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I hope we can all agree that the action plans in the White Paper are good not only for women, but also for men and, indeed, all of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They steer our society towards a healthier, fairer set of norms, cultures and practices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And that is something we should all be able to celebrate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first proposal is that we gradually equalise paternity and maternity leave entitlements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members of this House will be no stranger to my daughters Ella, Katie and Poppy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some Members tell me they feel like they know my daughters quite well now, just from the stories I tell about them through my speeches in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are a huge part of my life and I have learnt a lot from them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Of the memories I have shared, the ones that stick most are from when Ella, Katie and Poppy were born, when they were babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Paternity leave was a special time, and my only regret is that it was not long enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, I will never enjoy paternity leave again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Ms Joan Pereira has said, when you have twins, you will never have more kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But even as paternity leave becomes a thing of the past for me, I want to make sure fathers of our future get to spend more time with their babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I have said many times in this House, "Spend time with those you love.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of these days, you will either say I wish I had or I am glad I did." Study after study show that paternity leave is vital.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Researchers at NUS looked into this and published their findings just a few months ago.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their paper "documents the positive relationship between paternity leave provision and family dynamics and children's well-being in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taking paternity leave not only gives fathers the "immediate benefit" of sharing joy and responsibility of caring for the newborn, but ends up having a "mid-to-long-term impact on children's and family's well-being".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Longer leaves are significantly related to lower family conflict, lower maternal depression, higher marital satisfaction and fewer behavioural problems for the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, paternity leave is good for fathers, mothers and children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some have said that mothers need more leave than fathers because mothers need to physically recover from childbirth.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this is all the more reason why paternity leave needs to be equal with maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fathers need to be there as well, otherwise mothers will spend their 16 weeks of leave single-handedly caring for the newborn; and that is no rest at all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A young father recently reminded me how insufficient two weeks of paternity leave are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My wife was still recovering from labour and was bleeding and had stitches and still needed bed rest, except she could not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Once I resumed work, she had to care for the baby, all while learning the ropes to be a new mom.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It broke my heart to return from work every day to see her collapsed and break.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Two weeks, even if taken flexibly, is not enough.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just about the baby; it is also about the mother.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our wives have gone through enough to bring life into the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Please let us stay home, to take care of the big and little things, so that they can focus on recovery and all the other things we cannot do, like create milk".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It broke my heart to read this and I hope the Government can rethink whether paternity leave should really be less than maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2019 IPS research paper stated that "family policies in Singapore continue to signal that childcare is a woman's responsibility and reinforce gender stereotypes".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We give mothers 16 weeks of maternity leave and fathers two weeks of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mommy stays at home and daddy goes to work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The worst part of the problem is that it is self-reinforcing because we give fathers less leave, they do not get to develop the skills and confidence needed to care for their kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This, the IPS study finds, causes them to leave childcare to mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The IPS study proposes that we increase the amount of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I wholeheartedly support this call and hope that we can set a target year, perhaps 2030, by which time we will have an equal amount of paternity and maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can increase paternity leave in phases, giving our employers time to plan ahead, while also providing a clear signal of our intentions to reduce gendered perceptions of parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Minister will look into this proposal in consultation with the relevant stakeholders, including the tripartite partners and NGOs, such as Families for Life and Centre for Fathering.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having just guidelines does not show that we place a strong importance on this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Survey after survey show that Singaporeans want this and some would rather continue working remotely than receive a bigger bonus.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have also known for a long time that work-from-home narrows the gender pay gap.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The pandemic has also highlighted that work-from-home can reshape gendered stereotypes of "Daddy goes to work, mommy stays at home." An economics research paper titled "The Impact of COVID-19 on Gender Equality" found that the pandemic, by forcing people to stay at home, has likely led to an increase in fathers taking on childcare responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The paper concludes that this increase may sustain only if the fathers continue to have increased flexibility to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The media has also reported stories of how COVID-19 has given fathers a chance to bond with their kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imran, a marketing manager, talked about how his wife and him are so glad that he now has more time to play and eat together with his two toddler children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imran shared that after this increased time together, his kids now miss him even when he steps out of the house briefly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To be clear, fathers taking on more childcare responsibilities is a positive step for women's development.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It spreads out the burden of childcare between the parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It frees women from the stereotype that they will stay home to care for their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Legislating the right to work from home would send a strong signal, like how we are legislating the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices to send a stronger signal that unfair employment practices of all forms, including against women, are not tolerated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can carefully scope this new law together with the tripartite partners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no reason why we cannot design a balanced effective law that is a win-win for everyone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final proposal is that we end the continued discrimination against single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For decades, Members of this House have been speaking up for single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 1997, Minister Shanmugam questioned how it could be "morally justifiable to deny an unwed mother and her child public housing".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2006, Minister Indranee Rajah said that to build an inclusive society, policies affecting certain segments, such as single parents, had to change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2011, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary called for Singaporeans to be compassionate, to treat single parents with dignity and not to punish single parents and their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single unwed mothers now receive the same 16 weeks of maternity leave as married mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their children now benefit from Child Development Accounts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most recently, we have allowed single unwed parents to apply for rental housing and buy subsidised HDB flats from HDB.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As MND has acknowledged, "Single unwed parents are valued citizens and, like all parents, are respected for the love and care they provide for their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are no less a mother or a father, just because their child was born outside of marriage".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the White Paper recognises the need to help single parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It recommends increased support for single parents as one of the six focal areas in the Alliance for Action to strengthen Marriages and Family Relationships.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I am confident the Alliance will help reduce the stigma against single parents, we cannot run away from the elephant in the room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are single unwed parents any less a parent?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are unwed working mothers any less a working mother?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And are babies of single unwed parents any less a baby?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We may answer no, but these policies signal the opposite thing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if it is not the Government's intention, these policies suggest that single unwed parents are a less worthy set of parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This discrimination is a painful one because it is especially hard to be a single unwed parent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister of State Sun Xueling acknowledged during this year's Committee of Supply debates, "It is not easy to bring up children, even more so, single-handedly." The numbers speak for themselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Inflation is hurting everyone but they are the ones who will most have to scrimp and save.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, we deny them the support all other parents get.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We agree that healthy intact families are ideal but staying together is not always possible or even good.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We agree that single unwed parents and their children face stigma and have to overcome exceptional challenges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us felt this stigma first-hand at a recent dialogue session where single unwed parents spoke courageously about the stigma they faced.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As Minister of State Sun Xueling shared after the dialogue, "They shared the pain and hurt felt when faced with the stigma that comes with being a single unwed parent." We can help end this stigma.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What we need to do is end the discrimination in our parenthood support policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, we need to equalise maternity and paternity leave entitlements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, we need to legislate the right to request work from home, which employers can reject only for valid business-related reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am thankful for many of the action plans sketched out in it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, they promise a brighter tomorrow for the women, men and children of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding that women's welfare, rights and development have progressed tremendously over the years, I believe that there is more that we, as a community, can do for the last, the lost and the least.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The working mothers who struggle between providing for their families and in raising their children, the homemakers with dependants with no avenue of financial support, the women trapped in unhappy and abusive marriages as well as those who experience harmful behaviour online – all of them deserve the same opportunities for self-reliance and peace of mind, no matter their situation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As shared earlier by Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, in conjunction with our PAP Women's Wing International Day celebrations this year, we have organised a series of law awareness talks centred on the issue of online harm.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a follow-up, together with Ms Nadia Samdin, we launched an online toolkit to empower all of our PAP branch activists with useful information to assist victims who are facing online harm.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During this period, we realised that many victims have chosen to suffer in silence as they either felt embarrassed and/or thought that there is no recourse available to them even if they were to report to the relevant authorities.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This mentality worries me as it must have been detrimental to their mental well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I share the same sentiment as Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim that more needs to be done to increase awareness and to win the trust of the victims to open up and seek help.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from equipping more community volunteers with what was shared in the toolkit, I also hope that more of such law awareness talks can take place in our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, the Sunlight Alliance for Action can collaborate with the Law Society of Singapore to take the lead, inviting partners such as psychologists, Police and social media companies, to participate and share more on the recourse available to victims.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from discussing topics, such as voyeurism and cyber bullying, we should also venture into tips on combating online scams that many seniors and single women have fallen prey to lately.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the course of my practice as a matrimonial lawyer and in my time volunteering in legal clinics, I have come across many helpless women who have approached me to seek legal advice.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of them would often begin by sharing that they are contemplating a divorce but do not know if they should proceed to do so.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of them had gotten married early, barely worked and accumulated any savings, whether personal or in CPF.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some may have once had a decent career but chose to give it up after giving birth, effectively sacrificed their independence and out of the workforce for years to focus entirely on taking care of their family's well-being.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite being unhappy in the marriage for years, some even suffering from domestic violence in the process, the thought of undergoing a divorce puts them in great fear, the possibility of losing the roof over their head or self-doubt as to whether they would be able to bring up their children single-handedly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some worry that if the divorce proceedings become contentious, it may wear them out both financially and emotionally.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another most practical thing that the Courts can actually do to ease parties' emotional turmoil is to make the Court proceedings in the Family Justice Courts less acrimonious and less strenuous.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Currently, a spouse who has been subjected to domestic violence and deprived of maintenance by her husband will have to file two applications under iFams in order to seek protection and recourse for support for her children respectively.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should she wish to file for divorce thereafter, she or her lawyer will have to apply through another platform, eLitigation, through CrimsonLogic.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unfortunately, she may not be able to afford the fees for her lawyer to represent her in all three applications, as having to appear in different sets of mention dates as well as the need to comply with various sets of Court directions would result in heightened legal costs – keeping in mind the fact that she has yet to be paid support in the first place by her husband.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Furthermore, another enforcement Court application will also have to be made thereafter in the event her husband refuses to adhere to the maintenance order.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some women, despite facing great financial constraints, have become homemakers out of necessity as they have dependants that require constant care.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There is more that we can do as a community to support these women.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Trainees graduating from the programmes are, subsequently, offered opportunities to set up businesses and an online presence for clothes alteration services, along with sewing equipment that allows them to begin operations.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, I wish to take this opportunity to thank our PAP activists, community partners as well as residents who have shared their personal experiences with me and continued to participate in this meaningful journey with me to advance the cause of women's development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many organisations representing both men and women, students' unions and members of the public stepped forward with their feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are extremely grateful to organisations, such as SCWO, NTUC U Women and Family, People's Association-Women's Integration Network (PA-WIN), PAP Women's Wing and Young PAP, Persatuan Pemudi Islam Singapura (PPIS), AWARE and also trade associations and corporates, for putting forward proposals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: My fellow co-chairs, Minister of State Low Yen Ling, Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam, and I are deeply grateful for the inputs from everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the White Paper, we had grouped our 25 Action Plans into five areas not only for clarity but also to allow for thorough and effective implementation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: After all the conversations, it is now the time to take action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are determined to see this through over the decade, just as how the Government has advanced the progress of women over the past decades.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some have shared that the White Paper only seems to focus on Singapore women.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To address their concerns holistically, we have other workstreams, such as a committee which looks at residency and benefits for foreign spouses, which Minister Indranee Rajah chairs, supported by Minister of State Desmond Tan and myself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For today, I will speak about specific groups of women who are vulnerable, their challenges and how, as a society, we can collectively protect, support and empower them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We convened the Taskforce on Family Violence in February 2020 before the full effects of the pandemic on family life became apparent, which signalled our concern and focus on family violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We brought in various partners, including the Family Violence Specialist Centres, such as PAVE, which have spent decades supporting families affected by family violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We firmly believe that, in Singapore, one of the safest cities in the world, no woman, child or vulnerable adult should have to live in fear, jump at the sound of approaching footsteps or be subjected to the abusive words and actions of a perpetrator of violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The home is supposed to be a sanctuary for adult and child alike and we will do our utmost as authorities and as members of the public to protect those whose sanctuary has been violated by physical and sexual violence, psychological and emotional abuse and neglect.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: One example of our firm commitment to tackle family violence is how we have taken steps to expand the National Anti-Violence Helpline (NAVH).

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I had announced the renaming of the NAVH to National Anti-Violence and Sexual Harassment Helpline to better reflect the scope of its services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This one-stop national helpline provides support for all forms of violence, including sexual violence and sexual harassment, in a familial or non-familial setting.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The MSF Adult Protective Service and Child Protective Service will also help to train the new operators to equip them to perform their roles effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: MSF is prepared to set aside more resources if there is a further increase in call volume.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Accessibility is another key area that we are looking at.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will not stand by and watch vulnerable adults, men or women, children be subject to family and domestic violence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Appointed social service professionals will be empowered to go on site and jointly work with the Police to address immediate safety issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is by no means a soft approach, just because social service professionals are involved.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If there is a risk of family violence recurring, the social service professionals will be empowered to decide on the issuance of a time limited protection notice or help victim survivors move out of their home temporarily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Victim-survivors facing immediate risks are not left unprotected and in the vulnerable position of having to take care of himself or herself against a perpetrator.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Court may make an order to authorise Adult Protective Services to remove a vulnerable adult from the place of residence if he or she is experiencing abuse and the removal is required for safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also increase the penalties for the violation of PPOs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Courts will also be able to make other forms of orders, such as non-visitation or non-communication orders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim suggested adopting the Netherlands’ Orange House model of shelter for family violence survivors, for which the shelter is in a visible setting within the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As part of the step-down care to the community, residents of crisis shelters with low risk levels have an option of staying in individual housing units.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Crisis shelters also adopt trauma-informed approaches to supporting family violence survivors and their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, for some aspects of the Orange House model, such as the open location of the shelter where perpetrators know where the survivors live, our assessment is that this may not be suitable at this point in time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Minister Shanmugam had shared about the sentencing framework for sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The relevant Penal Code amendments have since come into force on 1 March 2022.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Victim-survivors can remain traumatised by memories of the episode, have flashbacks that can be triggered by anything remotely related to the incident, develop phobias of interacting and being close to people, and suffer from self-esteem issues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Being sexually violated takes away that feeling of inner sanctity that resides deep in every individual and some survivors may withdraw and develop a sense of detachment to protect themselves from further hurt.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will support victims of sexual violence, not just in the form of Police enforcement and laws and penalties but also in the form of psychosocial support and care.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) have, similarly, further strengthened support for victims of sexual misconduct through various measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They have enhanced training for first responders to equip them with the skills to support victims sensitively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Twenty-four-hour helplines for student care and dedicated victim-survivor care units have been established and counselling services have been enhanced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If the case involves a student or staff from the same institution, No-Contact Orders can be imposed as added protection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we know that the heart of the issue underlying many sexual offences lies in the mindsets that we have in society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We know concrete action needs to be taken to emphasise the value of respect and teach appropriate behaviour and safety, starting from a very young age from our children and our youths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And this is being done through the education journey from preschool, all the way to tertiary education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under the revised Nurturing Early Learners framework, preschool teachers will be encouraged to teach children aged four to six appropriate behaviours around body safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In Primary schools, as part of Character and Citizenship Education (CCE), students learn about personal safety and the protection of oneself from unhealthy relationships, sexual grooming, exploitation and abuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In Secondary schools and at the pre-University level, students learn that respect for boundaries is fundamental for healthy relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The refreshed CCE curriculum brings a greater emphasis on the need to communicate, assert and respect boundaries for self and others, and the socioemotional and legal consequences one faces if they overstep these boundaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These modules aim to promote deeper shifts in culture and mindset that will create a safe and respectful community for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the Autonomous Universities, students discuss and reflect on issues related to consent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Similarly, modules in the Polytechnics and ITEs emphasise the importance of respecting boundaries and the consequences for overstepping these boundaries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But beyond mindset shifts to prevent offensive and inappropriate behaviours between the sexes, it is also important to catalyse mindset shifts so that women and men become equal partners in all areas of life, in both the workplace and at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In school materials, women’s experiences, contributions and achievements are highlighted, alongside those of their male counterparts, as content examples.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The refreshed CCE curriculum has Family Education as a key content area.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Students learn to appreciate that members within families can play different roles regardless of gender, and that shared parental responsibilities should be discussed and mutually agreed upon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Poh Li San and Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin spoke about the need to encourage women and girls to pursue careers in STEM.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The IHLs have ongoing efforts to encourage women to enter STEM fields.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the Secondary level, more than half of our Secondary schools offered the Applied Learning Programme in STEM areas, providing a hands-on approach to enable students to appreciate the relevance of their learning beyond the classroom in community and STEM industry settings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Education and Career Guidance(ECG) curriculum, as part of CCE in schools, also encourages students to explore a variety of education and career pathways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: ECG Counsellors guide students to recognise how gender stereotypes may limit education or career pathways and to instead explore career sectors aligned to their interests and skills, including, but not limited to, STEM.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These efforts in formal education complement the crucial role of parents at home and the efforts of our community partners, such as Family for Life, to change mindsets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is only when respect becomes a fundamental tenet that we can expect that when the children grow up, that men and women see each other as equals and treat each other with dignity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I would now like to touch on our support measures for women with differing needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As part of the work of AFAM, we will work on a new pilot.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is intended to ascertain the demand for such services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Hany Soh and Dr Wan Rizal will be happy to note that the childminding pilot has a built-in flexibility to enable users to specify their requirements, including arrangements for childminders to pick up the child from school and the location of childminding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Based on their needs, DOT will match with suitable childminders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The details of the pilot are being worked out and we will share more details in due course.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: AFAM is also supporting MSF and NCSS’ work with HCSA Community Services to enhance their Single Parent Informed, Involved, Included (SPIN) programme portal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The enhanced portal aims to be a one-stop portal which better consolidates information on support schemes for single parents and other types of useful information, such as the location of nearby child and youth services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many of the initiatives that Minister of State Gan Siow Huang spoke about earlier, including FWAs and support for back-to-work women, will benefit all, including single unwed parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For complex cases that need more time, HDB will provide an interim update that the application is still being assessed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ms Carrie Tan spoke about the housing insecurity that single mothers may face.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have a network of crisis shelters and transitional shelters to help our single mothers who are homeless and require social work intervention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But, at the same time, our Marriage and Parenthood policies seek to support parenthood within marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is because our society continues to strongly value marriage and having children within marriage.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Members spoke about paternity and maternity leave entitlements and shared parental leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I think we can all agree that employees, generally, will welcome more leave – infant care leave, childcare leave, eldercare leave.
